Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$, whose metrics also appear in certain infinite series of $\theta$. The matrix $E$ can be represented as a matrix product $E=K^\dagger K$, with $K$ being an operator that transforms the deformed algebra into an unsymmetric canonical algebra, making its representation more manageable. By applying this approach to all simple Lie algebras, we can obtain their respective commutators, with some remarkable findings: some of their structures resemble geometric manifolds already in the zero-momentum state; certain series over $\theta$ are manifestable only due to the use of $K$, leading to apparently nontrivial, disguising simple roots of the algebra under deformation, and an intriguing observation that some of these structures may be replicated in quantum field theory on noncommutative spaces. Furthermore, this new way of analyzing these systems enables physical interpretation using standard techniques of quantum mechanics, in contrast to the recent proposal which employed the Weyl-Wigner approach. Building upon this, we discuss the potential for extending this method to both higher-dimensional and relativistic systems, and the proposed experimental tests for noncommutative quantum mechanics involving Lie algebras, such as measuring the deformed geometric magnitudes in motion on nilpotent algebras like Heisenberg and su(3). Lastly, the provided theoretical framework can be utilized for investigating other fundamental and practical problems in noncommutative quantum mechanics. Additionally, two appendices are supplied with supplementary details on the operator $K$ and its application to the Schrödinger equation on noncommutative spaces described by the Finsler metric. In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the quantification of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes. TILs play a significant role in predicting patient outcomes and developing targeted therapies, but their manual quantification is labor-intensive and expensive. We simulated a federated learning setup with a leading cancer research institution and several top hospitals, demonstrating the feasibility of training accurate models without exchanging patient data. Our results showed that federated learning produced models on par with those trained on centralized data, but slightly lagged behind those trained on expanded, non-centralized datasets. These findings suggest that federated learning has the potential to make a significant contribution to the automation of TIL quantification, enabling faster and more cost-effective analysis of tumor samples in clinical trials and real-world settings. Deep learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage spatial shortcuts to enable efficient processing of chronologically ordered data through reversible dilation. This concept, however, introduces complexity that hinders the model's efficiency and scalability. Our research introduces a new optimization framework called Pruning In Time (PIT), which simultaneously achieves a balance of high accuracy and optimality through the simultaneous application of two techniques: reversible dilation pruning and efficient replacement of multi-layered TCN stacks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PIT by successfully applying it to two prominent TCN-based datasets, resulting in a remarkable $8\times$ reduction in model size while preserving $95\%$ of the original accuracy. When examined in depth, we discovered that the optimized model exhibits a $3\times$ improvement in parameter density when compared to a state-of-the-art sparse graph method. Furthermore, we discovered the capability to enhance the baseline model's accuracy by up to $5\%$ with minimal additional parameters. We also explored the integration of PIT with another optimization framework known as evolutionary graph optimization, demonstrating the potential for further advancements. We publicly released all of our code and experiments at https://github.com/chen-weiwei/pruning-in-time. Additionally, we included an in-depth analysis of the learned policies in Section 4.4 of our document. This knowledge can be applied to a broader range of temporal graph-based models through the incorporation of additional model components. We provided a detailed analysis of our method's design choices and an in-depth examination of our experimental findings in a document available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.10478. This document also includes a thorough examination of our technique in comparison to other optimization frameworks known as slimming, connection-pruning and efficient replacement of multi-layered TCN stacks in Section 4.5 of our document. The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This inverse approach joins the existing canonicity and correspondence methods provided by the unified correspondence theory. Our work also extends the established connections between these methods and the Sahlqvist-type techniques by exploring its relationship with the algorithm ALBA in a systematic way, utilizing its machinery to provide a detailed exposition of both the canonicity and correspondence methods within this framework, along with a new inverse method that serves as a derivative of the existing methods combining the canonicity and correspondence techniques used in this domain. Furthermore, our results demonstrate a level of expressiveness for these methods that is akin to the established Sahlvist formulas, while also showing a high degree of consistency with these formulas, with some adjustments made to account for the additional operators present in some of the DLEs. Along with this, our work introduces a new notation that offers a more concise and clearer presentation of both the canonicity and correspondence methods within this framework, along with ALBA's rules and ALBA itself. This notation employs the standard prefix notation commonly used for terms and formulas in this context, with the additional of a type of dot-notation that provides a more explicit representation of the terms and their structure, offering both a more readable and a more programmable representation of both the ALBA rules and the ALBA itself. This notation is designed to be versatile and is suitable for various types of logics and their corresponding semantics, including but not limited to normal lattice expansions, their expansions with additional operators, and their expansions with possible world semantics. This notation is also designed to be easily extensible to other types of logics and their corresponding semantics, with some examples of this type of extensions also presented within this work. This work is a derivative of the research conducted within the University of Amsterdam's Institute of Logic, Language and Computation, with the research conducted by the author also supported by the European Research Council (ERC) through the ERC Starting Grant for the project 'Semantics and Logic of Types

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore and provide solutions for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, establishing a framework that can handle both numeric and categorical data. Our approach is then applied to three real-world datasets, resulting in modified versions with improved performance when fed into this framework. Our study reveals that certain instances with breaches of dependencies can be resolved by filling in missing values, while others require additional information to achieve consistency. Those that cannot be fixed are deemed unrepairable, and in our experiment, only a minority fell into this category. Our data-centric approach is distinct from strategies that prioritize preserving data semantics over actual data, and unlike methods that discard or create duplicate entries, our method prioritizes data preservation. This research is an early step in studying data tables with functional dependencies and missing values, an area where current approaches fall short. There is potential for further exploration, particularly in developing strategies for handling inconsistent data and identifying data that cannot be fixed, as well as investigating new data repair techniques and novel forms of unrepairable cases. This work is an evolution of an earlier paper presented at the 2019 EDBT conference, now expanded to accommodate new concepts and additional experimental findings. Although some experiments were previously reported, this updated version includes additional repair cases, new data sets, fresh benchmarks, and new queries. These studies provide a foundation for investigating new data repair strategies and novel forms of unfixable instances, as well as exploring alternative definitions of unrepairable cases and data that cannot be fixed using additional information, and examining how breaches of dependencies can be addressed in modern machine learning algorithms and models. This work is an expansion of two earlier research papers presented at the 2017 ICDT conference and the 2019 EDBT conference, now covering all possible instances of data that can be fixed using additional information and data that cannot be fixed, as well as novel forms of unrepairable cases, and includes results obtained from a broader range of data sets, fresh experiments, and new concepts and definitions. These studies lay the groundwork for investigating new data repair techniques, novel forms of unrepairable cases, and alternative definitions of unrepairable instances and data that cannot be fixed using additional information, as well as exploring how breaches of data semantics can be addressed in machine learning algorithms and models. This work is an evolution of all previous research in this area, now covering all possible instances of data that can be fixed using additional information

This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our findings indicate that the time-varying TV-PARX model outperforms its constant-parameter counterpart in several criteria, including model selection and forecasting accuracy, and can be an effective tool for policy-making and risk assessment. The R package tvparx, supporting the estimation and forecasting of time-varying count data models, has also been developed as part of this research. The package provides the necessary functions for maximum likelihood estimation, model selection, and forecasting, as well as a procedure for constructing and estimating time-varying parameters using the Kalman filter. Additionally, the package includes utilities for displaying and annotating time series plots and can integrate with the dtw R package for handling data alignment. A demonstration of the package's capabilities is included in the supplementary materials available online. A comparison of different dynamic models, including structural models such as TV-MAR and TV-LINAS, and score-driven models including TV-PARX and TV-LINAS, is also presented in the supplementary materials along with their respective R codes. A discussion on future research directions and potential extensions to the TV-PARX model has been outlined in the study's closing section. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of reproducing a demonstrated action from a given starting and
ending state. To achieve this, we use NDFs to capture object relationships and
poses, and combine them with a pose-invariant descriptor, to jointly optimize all
components. This allows us to efficiently train a pose-aware NDF on a small
dataset, without needing a large set of pose annotations. Our experiments
demonstrate NDF's effectiveness in both manipulation and as a standalone object
representation, with results showing that NDFs surpass current state-of-the-art
models in multiple metrics. Our code and data are now readily available online.
We anticipate NDFs to contribute significantly to the field of neural object
descriptions, enabling more accurate object understanding and manipulation in a
first-person setting. With NDFs, we also introduce the Neural Descriptor Field
Challenge, an open problem in this field, which we outline in this paper. Our aim
is to spark further research on object descriptions that capture not just category
information but also spatial relationships and poses, with the ultimate goal of
enabling first-person object manipulation in a robust and generalizable manner. We
believe that solving this challenge will be crucial for the development of more
advanced manipulation skills in future robots, with multiple potential real-world
applications, such as enhanced cooking, surgery, and other complex tasks that
require both fine motor skills and good hand-eye coordination. We outline the
rules and a potential solution path for this challenge in this paper. Our paper
also includes a novel method for generating action-oriented object descriptions

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands for the Higgs boson and other research areas while maintaining an adaptable sensitivity to diverse potential discoveries. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its high central magnetic field, ensures precise momentum measurement. The detector's finely granulated calorimeter system, designed for particle flow analysis, delivers accurate energy resolution across a wide energy range. Given the approaching construction timeline for the ILC, the time has come to reassess the design choices made during the design phase and incorporate the recent breakthroughs in technology into the review process. This review will discuss R&D prospects and participation opportunities for the SiD's development areas. Furthermore, the review will be a key discussion point at the 2019 ILC Detectors R\&D Meeting in Japan.

We present new findings from the CAPOS survey, focusing on Tonantzintla 2, a core-collapsed N-body cluster in the Milky Way's bulge. Aiming to gather internal data, we conducted a spectroscopic survey of Tonantzintla 2 members. Our research revealed  $N_{\rm NII} = 46$  globular cluster stars associated with the cluster, along with 13  Tonantzintla 2 candidates. We utilized high-resolution APOGEE spectra to determine chemical profiles for 39  Tonantzintla 2 members, comparing them to other CAPOS clusters. A [Eu/Fe] value greater than that of the solar value stands out in the Tonantzintla 2 sample. A comparison of isochrones with APOGEE photometry revealed an age of $13.0^{+0.8}_{-0.6}$  cyrs for Tonantzintla 2, indicating it is one of the most youthful clusters in the survey. APOGEE radial velocities for 25  Tonantzintla 2 members showed a mean of $57.35\pm0.20$  km/s, with a scatter of $6.32\pm0.19$  km/s. A comparison of these results with N-body N-body models of the bulge led to the selection of Tonantzintla 2 as one of the most suitable clusters to test the bulge's stellar dynamics, due to its small size and minimal contamination. A 2D velocity map of the cluster generated from the spectroscopic data matches the predicted profile from the models, with a scatter that matches the expected value, $6.32\pm0.19$  km/s, for a cluster of this size, at a density of 1.5 times the mean density of all clusters in the sample, providing the first velocity tomography of a globular cluster in the Milky Way's bulge. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty. Collective nature in higher dimensional universality classes makes the edge singularity's location determination more challenging and thus only general estimates can be provided for $N=1$ (Lifshitz transition) and $N>4$. The research shows the Yang-Lee edge singularity and CP edge singularity should be distinguishable when $N$ is within the range between 2 to 4. The findings also support the idea that in 2D O(3) and O(4) universality classes the edge singularity could be located at $z_c \propto \mu^{-1/\gamma}$ with $\mu$ being the chemical potential. The study provides $z_c$ values for these cases, estimating it to be around 0.64 and 0.60 respectively. The work presented offers an update to our previous research and confirms results from other approaches, such as conformal bootstrap and conformally invariant closure of the Fubini-Zwanziger equations, for the edge singularity's location in 3D O(3) and O(4) universality classes. many-body systems, potentially expanding the scope for electron correlation

While photometric transients in the sky are commonly used to detect phenomena such as supernovae, they also contain valuable information about the atmosphere above, particularly in regards to aerosols. With the increasing number of all-sky photometry systems like ATOM, ZTF, and ASAS-SN, collecting large amounts of data has become more feasible, even if getting a signal from each transient is less probable. These systems take full-sky exposures multiple times a day, enabling the assessment of aerosol optical depth (AOD) with higher spatial and temporal resolution compared to traditional systems. AOD values obtained through photometry are equivalent to 2-3 times the values from sun photometry, likely due to the higher wavelength range used, spanning 300-1000 nanometers. This increase in AOD is expected because the higher wavelength range is more susceptible to scattering from large particles, which are prevalent in dust storms, volcanic eruptions, and fire pollution, resulting in distinct spatial patterns. With these developments, it is now possible to observe the effects of atmospheric disturbances, such as dust storms and volcanic eruptions, at a higher temporal resolution, in addition to mapping global aerosol distributions, including the presence of pollution in major urban centers and the impact of planetary systems on astronomical measurements. Examples of these developments include the observation of dust storms in Mars, the detection of a global dust storm on Neptune's moon, Ganimedes, and the mapping of a volcanic eruption on Jonirad that failed to cross the Earth's boundary, as well as the location of the 2019 AT iridium impactor candidate that was initially reported and confirmed with additional observations. Finally, it is also demonstrated that the AOD values obtained through photometry are a more sensitive indicator of atmospheric disturbances than traditional methods, such as retrieving the properties of an object like 16 Cyg B through exoplanet transit and eclipse observations, which provides valuable information on the atmosphere of the host star. This technique has the potential to significantly improve the monitoring of global atmospheric events and the search for exoplanets by leveraging the vast amounts of data collected by all-sky photometry systems. Literature can be broadly classified into two categories based on whether intermediate cues are employed, namely cue-based and direct methods. Our research falls under the former category, and we propose an innovative approach, DeepHMap++, which leverages projection grouping and correspondence learning to estimate a 6D object pose from an image. In an offline setting, we collect a large dataset, establish object points cloud and define several pose categories based on rotation. These categories serve as our supervised learning targets, and we employ a projection grouping module that uses intermediate cues to refine corresponding rays, integrating this module with a correspondence learning module to predict a points cloud, which is subsequently used to calculate the object's pose. We validate our method on the DTUV-MaskRCNN Benchmark and Object Pose Estimation Dataset, achieving superior results compared to direct methods but slightly lower accuracy than cue-based approaches like DeepHMap+. Systematic experiments examining rotation-based pose categories, projection grouping, correspondence learning, and other variants of our proposed framework have been conducted and are included in our results. Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Based on these findings, a new framework has been established to assess the robustness of configurational averaging in molecular simulations. Within this framework, the average precision of configurational averages was found to be independent of the system's temperature, eliminating the need to calibrate parameters for temperature. Through an in-depth analysis of harmonic oscillators, Terskineskite protein, and Lennard-Jones liquids, a comprehensive efficiency metric has been developed to guide the selection of optimal numerical methods, integrator schemes, and step sizes to achieve the highest possible configurational averaging precision. Ultimately, this research provides a framework for evaluating and comparing the efficiency and robustness of numerical methods in molecular simulations, surpassing traditional productivity measures. In addition, LAMMPS has been modified to incorporate a range of numerical methods, integrator schemes, and step size controls, which has been made available for download at this link https://github.com/chenxiaoai85/LAMMPS-XAC due to its widespread usage and utility. The enhanced LAMMPS code features an intuitive interface for configuring and testing various numerical methods, integrator schemes, and step sizes, including a novel robust and efficient configurational sampling method via Langevin dynamics. The methodology employs a constant step size for the velocity integration and an adaptive step size for the position integration, which has been found to yield an average precision of $10^{-4}$ for a wide range of systems at different temperatures. Systems studied include harmonic oscillators, Terskineskite proteins with varying temperatures and force constants, Lennard-Johns liquids at different temperatures and densities. The results from these systems show an average precision of $10^{-4}$ for configurational averages with independent choices of step sizes for position and velocity integrations, precision of $10^{-5}$ with adaptive step sizes for position integration relative to velocity integration step sizes, and precision of $10^{-3}$ with constant step sizes for velocity integration. The research also involves an in-depth analysis of four widely used numerical methods in molecular simulations, including VelMDI, VelRK4, VelPI, and VelBP, and their performance in configurational averaging precision. Researchers utilized acoustic lenses composed of PMMA to increase the detection area of sensitive devices and improve resolution but discovered these lenses introduced image distortion. This problem was investigated and a new lens material called Stycast 1090SI was proposed as an alternative. The acoustic properties of this novel material were examined alongside PMMA to determine its feasibility. Computational simulations and practical tests using two different materials, PMMA and Stycast 1090SI, showed both materials significantly enhance the detection capabilities of sensitive devices. Notably, the Stycast lens exhibited lower distortion compared to the PMMA lens, suggesting it could provide superior image quality in PSBT systems. Furthermore, the Stycast lens demonstrated resistance to cracking, a common issue with PMMA lenses. As a result, it is considered suitable for use in advanced imaging systems. Furthermore, the fact that Stycast 1090SI can be polymerized at relatively lower temperatures compared to PMMA, presents an added advantage as it reduces the risk of thermal damage to breast tissue during imaging. Additionally, the novel material's lower density compared to PMMA could potentially lead to enhanced ultrasound reflection, which would further improve image quality. Nonetheless, the material's high water content may impede the effectiveness of the photoacoustic signal, although the impact appears to be minimal based on the conducted experiments. Consequently, the Stycast 1090SI lens is proposed as an ideal substitute for PMMA lenses in order to achieve high-resolution, undistorted images in photoacoustic breast tomography systems. Building upon existing knowledge, researchers suggest the use of a layer with acoustic properties identical to that of the imaging system to couple the breast tissue more effectively, which could further enhance image quality. This proposal is particularly relevant to large-area detectors in photoacoustic breast tomography systems and is believed to contribute significantly to the advancement of such imaging technology. This research is an extension of previously conducted experiments and builds upon existing research in photoacoustic imaging. Two different acoustic lens materials, PMMA and Stycast 1090SI, were examined in this research. Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often unwarranted trust in system functionality is assessed through a novel metric called hardware-based trust, which is further subdivided into sub-measures for both hardware isolation and reliable hardware behavior.

A practical implementation, encompassing a hardware component (TPM) and a software framework, is presented to minimize hardware-based trust by allocating certain hardware components on a physical basis to specific security applications, which not only boosts trust by an average of 128% but also offers performance improvements of up to 28 for cryptographic operations and concurrent execution speeds up to 11 times that of standard systems. 

These advancements are achieved with only a 5% increase in energy consumption in exchange for the isolated hardware, indicating that even sensitive security applications like cryptocurrency mining can benefit from this approach. 

A security application that employs a combination of hardware and software components to execute more complex tasks, in addition to six other security-sensitive workloads, is utilized as part of a comprehensive hardware-based trust evaluation, which involves both quantitative and qualitative assessments. 

A prototype system constructed using a x86-64 based platform serves as the basis for the evaluation, which reveals that it is feasible to design security-friendly systems that minimize hardware-based trust by incorporating a mix of physical hardware isolation and trusted execution, allowing for the safe execution of security applications alongside unverified software, thereby extending the device's security capabilities beyond the limits of software-based security solutions. 

As a result, this approach is particularly suitable for a wide range of security applications that involve the execution of cryptocurrency-related tasks and is considered an important step toward creating secure systems that can execute a broader range of security applications while reducing the need for trusted hardware and system software. 

With the continuous advancements being made in both hardware and software components, it is anticipated that future systems constructed using this approach will not only boost trust in security applications but also provide even greater performance improvements, lower energy consumption, and increased security, ultimately paving the way for secure execution of a wide range of applications, including those that are cryptocurrency-related, on mobile devices. 

In conclusion, the substantial performance gains coupled with the significant increase in trust provided by this approach make it an ideal solution for creating secure systems that can execute security applications efficiently and effectively on mobile devices.

These states are characterized by the presence of a single photon in a superposition of being in one mode or the other, combined with a coherent state describing the two modes' cat-like behavior. We demonstrate the uniqueness of SPCCSs by showing their unique catalysis symbol, $\mathcal{K}$, is not replicable through other states without the single photon in one mode and the coherent state in the other. We also find that SPCCSs, like their multi-photon counterparts, exhibit improved laser performance when compared to standard coherent states, yet the advantage is only noticeable at low catalysis levels. The unique properties of SPCCSs can be verified through catalysis-based teleportation, while their generation via quantum-optical catalysis of number-state entanglement (NSEE) highlights the potential for creating cat-like behavior in multiple modes. SPCCSs can also be used to enhance the visibility of Mach-Zehnder interferometry, especially in large-angle settings, by employing SPCCSs with mid-level catalysis. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator, a critical life-support system. Due to the pandemic's severity, there was an urgent need to ventilate patients efficiently, necessitating a rapid development of the ventilator's control system. Our solution involves a dynamic optimization problem to minimize the risk of lung injury for both patients by adjusting the ventilator's pressure levels. However, this problem was complicated by the need to model patients with different respiratory conditions and treat two patients as a single respiratory system with interacting components. Our approach used a direct transcription method, specifically an implicit Runge-Kutta scheme, to find a solution to this problem, a case where the usual formula-based approach to optimization fails due to the problem's high nonlinearity and discontinuity. Our study demonstrates the effectiveness of direct transcription methods in solving complex dynamic optimization problems, providing a practical solution to a critical technological challenge in the COVID-19 pandemic. Our case study, although resolved, is no longer a pressing issue, but it serves as an example of a problem that could arise in other technological competitions and emergencies. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects. To compensate for these difficulties, experts often require multiple scans across different stages of respiration. Nonetheless, obtaining these scans and processing the resulting extensive datasets is quite labor-intensive. Consequently, developing efficient and precise methods for automatically segmenting esophageal tumors in CT scans is a pressing challenge. In response to these demands, this study introduces a novel algorithm called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet) to tackle this issue. DDAUnet is an innovative variation of the widely-used Unet framework that excels in processing thin slices. To match the thicker slices commonly used in CT scans, this study upgrades Unet with a Dense Attention Module and a coarse-to-fine deconvolutional component, and further enhances its performance by using fewer dense layers. Experimental results indicate that DDAUnet yields superior outcomes when compared to other state-of-the-art methods, including a notable improvement in robustness when subjected to respiratory variations, as demonstrated by consecutive scans in MICCAI 2019 challenge data, as well as independent clinical datasets. Notably, DDAUnet achieves this success with only a single-scan segmentation, a significant reduction in required data, establishing a new benchmark in esophageal tumor segmentation. The project's code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanli/dense-attention-unet. With the advancement of low-contrast tumor segmentation, the team further investigates the technique's applicability to other challenging medical segmentation tasks. In particular, they explore whether DDAUnet can be applied to other difficult medical segmentation tasks by conducting additional experiments, as detailed in the supplementary materials provided with this paper. Those experiments reveal that DDAUnet not only outperforms baseline methods but also delivers comparable performance to existing state-of-the-art methods in the evaluation metrics, as shown in Tables 5-8 in the supplementary materials. Nonetheless, the team acknowledges that further research is necessary to fully assess the technique's broader applicability. Nonetheless, DDAUnet's exceptional performance in esophageal tumor segmentation has cemented its position as the new gold standard, as acknowledged by the reviewer who expressed the view that DDAUnet's results appear too good to be true, as evident from Table 1 and Figure 2. The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites often contain valuable petroleum reserves. A critical aspect in extracting these resources efficiently is geosteering, which necessitates real-time or near-real-time access to formation properties to guide the drillers. Even with advanced logging tools, obtaining accurate and reliable formation property data from well logs in real-time is a challenging task. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel ensemble-based approach that combines multiple independent models for a seamless uncertainty quantification, making it an ideal solution for real-time data interpretation. Furthermore, this method enables the incorporation of experts' opinions into the data, which is crucial for real-time decision-making. We tested our proposed method on synthetic and actual data sets, and the results show it has the capability to provide accurate and reliable formation property values along with uncertainty levels, which is instrumental in making informed real-time decisions in geosteering. Compared to alternative methods, our proposed method demonstrates superior performance even with limited and noisy data sets, which is commonly encountered during real-time data analysis. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, with entities serving as input to further tasks like relation extraction, coreference resolution, and text classification. While NER has seen significant advancements, existing systems often struggle with nested or multi-level entities, where a single entity can be part of a larger one, leading to the exclusion of such entities in corpora annotations or inaccurate extraction. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel approach to nested NER (NNER) by casting it as a holistic structure parsing task. We introduce an integrated model that leverages a unified entity dictionary, encompassing all potential nesting levels, and employs a bidirectional transformer-based parser to simultaneously perform part-of-speech tagging, syntactic parsing, and direct annotation of nested entities. We evaluate our method on standard datasets for both single and nested NER and demonstrate its effectiveness through comparative experiments against popular NER systems. Our results indicate that our proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard single and multi-entity datasets and outperforms existing methods on nested corpora with comprehensive annotations, exceeding the performance of 20% in F-score in certain cases. Furthermore, we observe no significant gap between in-domain and out-of-domain performance, a critical consideration for the entity-extraction field. Our project's official repository is available at https://github.com/argossi/nnerp. Additionally, we introduce the Roster Corpus, a collection of annotated texts with a wide range of entity nestings, and make it publicly accessible through the same repository, citing relevant guidelines at https://github.com/argossi/nnerp/blob/main/docs/construction_guidelines.pdf. This new corpus, with its diverse nesting structures, serves as a reliable metric learning platform for the evaluation of NNER systems in production environments. We anticipate its widespread adoption due to its comprehensive annotations and diverse entity nestings, providing a robust benchmark for the NER community to assess the practical performance of models in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, we investigate the difficulty of constructing such corpora and the performance of systems when tested against their trainers, highlighting the field's future research directions. Finally, we demonstrate the extracted entities' capability to inform a coreference resolution task and serve as input to a relation extraction task, further solidifying the importance of NER in natural language understanding. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, resources, and models to enhance NLP across multilingual societies, emphasizing the necessity for more flexible and adaptable models that can handle complex issues with limited labeled data and data shortages in code-mixed settings. Ultimately, we encourage researchers to contribute to code-mixed NLP, with priority given to community-driven initiatives, data, and resources over exclusive benchmarking challenges. Systematic advancements in five focus areas can contribute to addressing real-world challenges and problems in multilingual communities and promote inclusivity in the NLP domain. Furthermore, we believe that developing flexible models for code-mixed texts can facilitate progress in NLP, even in single-language settings, and can also benefit the broader NLP community. To facilitate progress in code-mixed NLP and address concerns of multilingual communities, we introduce the CMNLP 2022 workshop, an inaugural event held in conjunction with the 43rd ICML conference, along with workshop proceedings presented at the 29th EMNLP conference, with the aim of continuing this initiative at upcoming and relevant conferences. We invite all researchers to collaborate with the code-mixed NLP community, with the expectation that together we can address the numerous challenges and difficulties faced by multilingual communities and make progress in the field. Furthermore, we outline the CMNLP 2022 workshop's events, including keynotes, oral presentations, and a code-mixed sentence generation challenge, along with the CMNLP 2022 workshop's steering committee and the CMNLP 2022 workshop's website. We anticipate that the code-mixed NLP community will continue to grow with the support of initiatives like the CMNLP 2022 workshop and will contribute to the advancement of NLP in multilingual societies. Human-generated descriptions are commonly used to train and evaluate image description systems, which are typically ranked based on their similarity to these descriptions. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. Two methods for creating suitable evaluation criteria are proposed: one is a score system weighing important visual elements and another is a method for creating tailored descriptions based on sample images. These approaches' effectiveness is illustrated by describing and scoring a test image using two different datasets created with these methods. Systems' performance is assessed by comparing their automatically generated descriptions with these human-created standards. Moreover, I examine and discuss the potential for these evaluation criteria to align with the requirements of visually impaired users. Systems' performance is compared to that of systems evaluated with their original human-generated descriptions, and some concluding remarks are presented. Human-generated descriptions for the test image are also included in the appendix. Code is available at https://github.com/andersonwang/visual-linguistic-evaluation and the test image is available at https://andersonwang.github.io/visual-linguistic-evaluation/. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity in the visible spectrum. Recent studies have taken the Ta$_2$O$_5$ prototype structure as their starting point with little experimental evidence to support this, prompting a comprehensive study of Ta$_2$O$_5$ in its ground state. Our researchers employed the efficient and robust efficient model potential method to conduct accurate simulations of Ta$_2$O$_5$ in its polycrystalline form, allowing for explicit consideration of atomic movements. To validate these calculations, a series of experiments were performed including X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, and electron energy loss spectroscopy. To account for any discrepancies between calculated and observed data, a Monte Carlo method was employed to simulate the phase diagram of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Conversely, all experimental measurements indicate that Ta$_2$O$_5$ takes the form of a monoclinic structure at temperatures between 450 K and 900 K, a structure that is consistent with earlier reports. However, Ta$_2$O$_5$ was found to undergo a phase shift to the orthorhombic structure at high temperatures, a transition that occurs between 1050 K and 1250 K. A comparison of our results with earlier theoretical simulations reveals that Ta$_2$O$_5$ takes the form of an orthorhombic structure at high temperatures, a state that is stable for around 10 picoseconds before degrading into a monoclinic structure. A discussion of the implications of these findings is also presented in this study, including the effect that Ta-Ta dimer structures may have on the dielectric properties of Ta$_2$O$_5$. A model of Ta$_2$O$_5$ in its orthorhombic structure shows promise as a suitable substrate for the fabrication of metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors, while also satisfying the requirements for a suitable gate material. A model of Ta$_2$O$_5$ in its monoclinic structure may provide a suitable platform for the prevention of bacterial growth in water systems. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but overlooked a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographic regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the platform it was posted on, but rather varied significantly depending on the state the poster and the state the viewer were from. Furthermore, this discrepancy was more pronounced in certain electoral groups, such as voters in battleground states and voters in large urban counties, and in communities with higher levels of political polarization, faith, and social conservatism. We discovered similar outcomes when examining the dissemination of misinformation within each state, revealing that misinformation spread significantly more between residents of different counties than between residents of different states. We also found that information dissemination between residents of different counties but within the same state was more substantial than between residents of different states but within the same county. These results suggest that The Big Sort plays a crucial role in the dissemination of misinformation among Reddit users in the United States. We based our research on three separate news sources – CNN, Fox News, and MSNBC – and four types of online misinformation – fake news, conspiracy theories, off-topic comments, and toxic language – and verified our findings against additional sources and metrics. When evaluating the economic impact of The Big Sort on companies, we discovered that seven out of ten leading American corporations experienced a decline in brand value in states with high sorting, and five out of these seven companies experienced a greater decline in value in mid-sized counties with high sorting than in large counties with high sorting, indicating that The Big Sort may have an effect on consumer behavior in geographic regions. We found similar outcomes in government data, which revealed that communities with higher levels of political polarization, faith, and social conservatism exhibited greater variability in online misinformation dissemination when compared to communities with lower levels of these characteristics, and also exhibited greater disparities in misinformation dissemination when compared to communities with lower levels of polarization, faith, and social conservatism. When analyzing the characteristics of communities that exhibit greater variability in online misinformation dissemination, we discovered that these communities exhibited greater levels of political polarization, faith, and social conservatism, and also exhibited greater disparities in misinformation dissemination when compared to communities with lower levels of these characteristics. When evaluating the results of our research, we discovered that the features of the platform used to disseminate misinformation do not explain the observed discrepancies in misinformation

We introduce an original concept, 'fast information flows,' characterized by rapid, limited, and focused dissemination of information. These ephemeral phenomena are observed in various settings – network transmissions, biological signal propagation, and trading activity – and are distinguished from traditional information flows by their brevity and speed. In fast information flows, detecting anomalies is a complex challenge due to the vast amount of data and limited observation window, rendering existing methods ineffective. To address this issue, we develop an unsupervised anomaly detection technique capable of handling high-frequency streams of data, identifying anomalies within a few seconds, and producing consistent results across multiple experiments. Our proposed method, 'FastAnomaly,' is a data-driven approach that creates an effective anomaly detection rule without relying on historical data, thereby ensuring real-time detection. FastAnomaly is'machine-free' in the sense that it avoids using complex machine learning models, instead utilizing a simple statistical approach to achieve remarkable results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of FastAnomaly in fast information flows by applying it to various scenarios, including trading data and biological signal propagation, and show that it outperforms a widely used competitor in the financial domain. Furthermore, we investigate the underlying principles of fast information flows and propose an interpretation of our technique as an optimal detection method, thereby setting a new baseline for future anomaly detection algorithms. This research has significant implications, particularly in the field of finance, where the early detection of anomalies, such as insider trading, can have a significant impact. Finally, we highlight potential directions for further exploration and provide an open-source implementation of FastAnomaly for reproducibility and accessibility. In addition, we have created an interactive visualization tool, 'FastAnomaly Explorer,' that enables users to experiment with trading data and other fast information flow data sets. This tool allows users to adjust parameters, observe data streams, and explore the functioning of FastAnomaly through interactive animations and visualizations. This comprehensive research, comprising theoretical contributions, experimental evaluations, and practical applications, lays the foundation for future advancements in the field of fast information flows and anomaly detection. In particular, we have raised fundamental questions regarding the design of fast information flows and anomaly detection, and we have proposed novel frameworks and techniques for addressing these challenges. We anticipate that our work will inspire further exploration and the development of new detection methods for fast information flows, as well as the creation of fast information flows that facilitate anomaly detection, leading to breakthroughs in multiple domains and potentially giving rise to innovative technologies and solutions. We have also established a research community centered around fast information flows

Building on previous work, we propose an algorithm to randomly generate ordered trees of any degree, based on a pre-specified sequence of numbers representing possible node connections. Our method allows for the generation of binary, n-ary trees, or those with various connection patterns. We demonstrate that this algorithm is both accurate and efficient, running in O(n) time with 'n' representing the number of desired nodes. Additionally, we explore potential applications of the algorithm, illustrating its use in deriving formulas by utilizing the underlying proof of correctness. We also explore scenarios where the connection sequence is stochastic rather than fixed and deterministic. We observe that in such cases, the traditional distinction between binary and n-ary trees becomes less relevant, and we propose the term 'k-ary tree' to describe trees with connections defined by a sequence 'k', encompassing both binary and n-ary trees. We define a new notion of 'degree sequence' for a set of connected trees, and discuss its relationship to degree sequences in graphs. We investigate properties of the ensemble of k-ary trees and derive formulas for key enumerators, including the cumulative sum of degrees, Wiener, and edge-based degree-based Wiener indices. We also explore the behavior of the average degree and its relationship to the degree sequence of individual trees. We examine specialized cases such as binary trees, showing our results either match or provide new insights when compared to existing knowledge about binary trees. We discuss potential applications and future research on the ensemble of k-ary trees. We demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of our algorithm using extensive numerical experiments, reporting the results in an publicly available repository along with the degree sequences of the trees generated therein. We conclude by outlining several open research questions arising from this work. We provide a comprehensive formal proof of correctness for our algorithm in an accompanying manuscript, along with a discussion of two alternative derivations. We discuss the connection between our work and prior research on sequence-generated trees, highlighting both commonalities and distinguishing features. We examine the relationship between our degree sequence for a set of connected trees and the Egonetwork approach described in literature, showing they are equivalent in essence, albeit with differences in formulation. We outline potential solutions to several open research questions and highlight the theoretical contributions of our work, including the development of a general formula for the enumeration of k-ary trees, as well as new definitions for degree sequences in graphs and connected trees. Quantum field theory complexity is particularly hard to define, especially when transitioning beyond simple free models and their corresponding Gaussian representations. A promising approach to address this difficulty is through the study of conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, specifically focusing on the universal sector of the energy-momentum tensor in this context. A key unifying framework consists of Euler-Arnold equations and their broader integro-differential generalizations, ensuring the well-posedness of state or operator complexity optimization problems. Our comprehensive investigation extends upon our prior findings in arXiv:2005.02415, delving into intricate details of employed methodologies and confirmed outcomes, while also presenting novel insights obtained since our initial study was published. The essential connections between conformal geometry, transportation costs, and the Weyl transformation have been illustrated through a related set of checkable mathematical equations provided in the appendix. Furthermore, our research has been supplemented with a discussion on the interrelation between state and operator complexity, along with an open issue in the study of Gaussian quantum field theories. The document is available at arXiv:2101.01500, http://arxiv.org/abs/2101.01500. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in this area, specifically a suite of automated tools designed to streamline the creation, execution, and updating of tests for conversational systems. These tools leverage cutting-edge technology in natural language processing to evaluate systems against predefined specifications and improve the efficiency of the testing process. By integrating artificial intelligence-driven tools for verifying and repairing conversational systems, we are working to develop a comprehensive testing framework that can significantly reduce the testing time, overcome human subjectivity, and enable batch processing of tests across multiple system configurations. This framework is particularly suited for large-scale systems used extensively by many users and is an essential component for a robust development pipeline. This research is currently being conducted at the 33rd ACM Conference on Functional Programming, 2022, in Leiden, Netherlands. Further details can be found at https://www.15thsf.net/html/schedule.html?section=2&day=2022-09-05&time=14:00 under poster number 2.3.2.1.1. Further details can be found at https://www.15thsf.net/html/schedule.html?section=3&day=2022-09-05&time=16:30 under poster number 3.5.2.1.1. This research is ongoing and is being conducted at the University of Oxford under the supervision of Professor Anthea Powell and Dr. Rui Abreu in the Department of Computer Science and the Oxford Mobile Robotics Laboratory respectively. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can be an effective means of enhancing Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance. Notably, TM's utility lies in its ability to provide targeted examples of equivalent phrases across languages. To build upon this research, we propose a novel framework, dubbed Multi-Switch NMT (MS-NMT), which effectively integrates TM data into the NMT framework while addressing the challenges of TM data quality. Unlike existing methods, MS-NMT distinguishes between high-quality reference sentences, designating them as learning objectives, while treating lesser-quality sentences as auxiliary training data. Furthermore, to prevent TM data over-reliance and promote learning of general language skills, we introduce a controlled switch mechanism that regulates the model's exposure to TM and source sentence embeddings. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method not only outperforms the baseline model but also yields substantial improvements in data efficiency and robustness. Notably, MS-NMT achieves a notable 2.08 BLEU point gain when tested with unseen data in the WMT'14 English-to-French NMT benchmark, demonstrating its potential as a pioneering solution for multi-domain NMT tasks. To further validate our approach, we conduct a user-centric evaluation, gathering TM-related feedback from human subjects, which provides valuable insights that align with our empirical findings. System implementations and data sets are openly available at https://github.com/ruotianeng/ms-nmt. Overall, our work paves the way for the effective integration of TM data into NMT systems, offering solutions to existing challenges and providing data sets and systems for reproducibility. Nonetheless, numerous issues with TM data quality and the limited scope of our controlled switch mechanism necessitate further exploration and expansion in future research. In particular, future studies should delve into integrating TM data in a more spontaneous and flexible manner as well as developing techniques that are less dependent on high-quality reference sentences. In the broader context of multi-domain NMT, our proposed method demonstrates the feasibility of combining source sentence-specific and general language knowledge in an effective manner, a critical aspect for future work in this area. In the accompanying supplementary materials, we provide an in-depth examination of each challenge, method, experiment, and evaluation in greater detail. Additionally, the appendix includes a step-by-step guide to replicating our results, encompassing TM data preparation, model implementation, and evaluation metrics calculation. Researchers have suggested that specific patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background, namely low-variance circles and Hawking points, could provide evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology model. These patterns are predicted to originate from previous black hole mergers and evaporation events. We analyzed the Planck and WMAP data using a machine learning tool called HawkingNet, and initially found potential anomalies in the form of low-variance circles and Hawking points. However, these anomalies were later dismissed as statistical anomalies. Our study also revealed that the predicted CCQ structures in the CMB sky show high variability and little correlation with density fields, making them challenging to detect. We propose potential paths to detecting these anomalies using upcoming CMB experiments and new analysis methods. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for calculating prototypes often struggle due to the influence of outliers. This research proposes a new, effective framework that utilizes an episodic prototype generator module to create more representative prototypes from limited support data, reducing the impact of outliers and resulting in preferable models. The framework's ability is further showcased by the substantial improvement it yields over baseline models and the comparable performance it achieves to existing methods on datasets like miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, and cross-domain benchmarks (miniImageNet to CUB-200-2011). Traditional collaborative filtering is hindered by the sparsity of user-item interaction data. This issue is exacerbated across multiple sparse domains with limited user activity. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) framework that leverages an enhanced comprehensive aspect preference learning approach. By incorporating a bidirectional graph attention network and a multi-domain aspect preference model, MSDCR significantly improves the effectiveness of recommendations in multiple sparse domains. This improved performance is achieved by 1) modeling a user's unique identity and diverse aspect preferences through a bidirectional graph attention network; 2) enhancing the aspect preference learning framework to handle multi-domain data by incorporating a domain-aware aspect selection mechanism. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art baseline methods. Furthermore, MSDCR is applied to a real-world e-commerce scenario to evaluate its performance in practice, showcasing its ability to provide accurate and practical recommendations in multiple sparse domains. System resources are also efficiently managed with MSDCR, making it an ideal solution for data-intensive e-commerce platforms. The code and parameters of the proposed MSDCR framework are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/MSDCR. Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It also features customizable barrier andacles as well as variable-metric and quasi-Newton variations of its interior-point method. This research presents the performance potential of Julia and Julia-based solvers by presenting the methodology and results of a comprehensive evaluation of Hypatia and other state-of-the-art interior-point and Lagrangian solvers. This evaluation compares the efficiency of these solvers in solving a diverse and substantial test suite comprised of problems formulated within the Julia JuMP framework. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the efficiency and practicality of Julia-based solvers and identifies its performance to be on par or outperformed only slightly by its non-Julia counterparts. Despite this, Julia-based solvers offer several key advantages including their ease of integration within JuMP and the Julia ecosystem as well as their potential for user-defined and customized solution algorithms. This research is also accompanied by an open-source implementation of Hypatia and a comprehensive set of performance benchmarks available under the MIT License. This implementation serves as an extension of the previously developed Julia solver, Bonmin, and incorporates its efficient and scalable design. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis. Several studies have investigated the use of machine learning in this context, yet most research has focused on constrained scenarios, addressing either acquisition-related or reconstruction-related issues, but not both. In contrast, our investigation considers a comprehensive and unstructured dataset with 41 diverse acquisition settings and 17 different reconstructions, covering 125 unique combination scenarios. Our analysis revealed that a method called Multi-Facitor Generalization (MuFG) consistently outperformed other tested approaches, including ensemble methods and those specifically designed for multi-facotor generalization. The MuFG method demonstrated the ability to generalize effectively across multiple factors, achieving a 24.5% median reduction in error rate compared to the best domain-specific model. Ultimately, our research provides evidence that a universally applicable quality control system can be developed, offering potential applications in MRI data sharing and collaborative research projects. Additionally, our findings are available as pre-print articles at two separate repositories, highlighting the importance of open data access in the field of neuroscience. Furthermore, our study highlights the value of collaborative research and the importance of addressing the generalizability issue in machine learning, as acknowledged by the community through the release of our results as open data. As a result, there is a growing interest in open data sharing and collaborative research projects, as evidenced by the community's response to our study. Our study has also sparked a discussion on the importance of data quality control in neuroscience research, highlighting the need for a more robust and widely accepted gold standard, as well as a quantitative definition of MRI data quality. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks. Specifically, our results showed that private EVs can facilitate faster grid recovery by creating incentives for strategic charging in the short term, albeit potentially leading to higher-than-optimal costs in the long run. We advocate for a broader examination of energy and transportation systems in conjunction with private EVs to better capture the complex interplay between these systems and their respective policy levers and potential bottlenecks. We also highlight potential applications for our algorithm in optimizing grid recovery with private EVs within real-world settings. In the process, we contributed to the development of an integrated evaluation framework that considers various costs and challenges associated with grid recovery, transportation, and private EV operations. This research took the form of a case study centered on the Los Angeles metropolitan area, utilizing a holistic approach that could be adapted to other cities and regions with private EVs, critical transmission and distribution infrastructure, and varying levels of parking availability. We emphasized the importance of collaborative research at the intersection of energy and transportation systems, particularly in regards to private EVs, and the necessity for data that captures the behavior of private EV drivers in response to changing grid and transportation system conditions. Intel's Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (DC PMM) has reached commercial viability as the first commercially available nonvolatile memory DIMM. It offers fast, byte-granular data access similar to DRAM, combined with power-fail safe storage. In-depth performance evaluations have shown Optane DC PMMs to excel in applications with high data access requirements, where there is substantial temporary data, and where the need for persistent data storage is minimal. In contrast, they may not offer significant advantages over DRAM in applications with low data access requirements, where there is little temporary data, and where the ability to withstand power failures is crucial. This research provides a thorough analysis of Optane DC PMMs' performance in various scenarios, encompassing database systems, in-memory computing, file systems, data caching, and application benchmarks. Our findings also reveal that modern Intel processors' memory controllers and memory policies can have an impact on system performance and should be taken into account when evaluating Optane DC PMMs. In addition, this research presents a comprehensive evaluation of various system configurations and different software applications, offering actionable advice and actionable results for Optane DC PMMs in various use cases and potential areas for optimization in Intel's Optane DC PMMs, Intel's processors, and its memory controllers. Furthermore, this research is valuable not only for Intel's Optane DC PMMs but also for future RAM technologies with persistent capabilities, such as STT-RAM and phase-change RAM, by highlighting key system performance factors and providing a framework and methodology for evaluating and assessing their performance. This research is available as a USENIX ATC'19 Extended Abstract and is now being presented as a full paper at the ASPLOS'20 Conference. We demonstrate how agents operating within a shared framework and governed by identical rules can be programmed to engage in complex, recurring coordination tasks by applying the principles of the Motivation Dynamics framework, specifically by manipulating its parameters to induce periodic behavior. A specific application of this capability is illustrated through a rendezvous task, where an agent must navigate to a target location while being influenced by an external force that affects its movement. This results in the emergence of intricate patterns determined by the underlying structure of the model and its parameters. A reduction of the dimensionality of this robust system enables the identification of precursors to periodic patterns, providing insights that can be used to design the system's parameters to produce desired patterns. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that may also be heavy. Although the bilepton model predicts numerous types and variants of additional baryons and mesons, their masses are expected to be quite high, primarily in the range of several TeV or more. The model also offers explanations for previously unaccounted for phenomena, such as the existence of a right-handed electron that could be detectable in experiments involving electron scattering at high energies, potentially exceeding 6 TeV. The model's predictions for additional baryons and mesons await verification through experiments at future high-energy colliders like CLIC, HL-LHC, ILC, LHC, LLCC, LHC Upgrades, NLC, NLCC, NLHC, PLCC, and VLCC. The paper's authors, A. S. Saif and S. R. Duggal, emphasize the need for experimental verification through the detection of predicted bilepton model particles at various energy scales. The model's predictions for additional baryons and mesons are robust and are expected to be validated by future high-energy experiments and observations. The paper's authors propose the acronym BILE (Bilepton Model Experiment and Observation) to encompass all relevant experiments and observations. The BILE experiment and observation program will play a crucial role in confirming or refuting the bilepton model's predictions through the direct detection of bileptons, right-handed electrons, and three types of heavy quarks, thus determining the model's validity and providing insights into its fundamental parameters. The paper's authors also emphasize the importance of the BILE experiment and observation program in guiding the development of next-generation high-energy colliders and in identifying the optimal energy scales and detection methods for detecting the predicted bilepton model particles. We utilized the Pantheon SN Ia dataset in conjunction with a specific week lensing analysis to determine the cosmic shear contribution and find the dark energy properties. By combining the shear from a specific scale and the density of foreground and background halos, we derived a weighted average that explains 95% of variance in shear field. This model was employed to calculate the probability of SN Ia discovery within a specific magnitude range, taking into consideration lensing effects from first and second order interactions. Our analysis of the relative likelihood of SN Ia discoveries with and without lensing effects revealed a flat distribution, resulting in a flat prior between zero and two for our main parameter, $\omega$. By combining this with the Pantheon sample and assuming a flat prior for $\omega$ in our main analysis, we found an average SN Ia density at $z\sim0.5$ of 2.6±0.3, with an uncertainty that only accounts for variance in shear field and SN Ia density. A similar analysis with the more limited Supernova Cosmology Project (SCPD) sample yielded an average SN Ia density at $z\sim0.1$ of 1.6±0.5. When combining all available data, a flat likelihood analysis with respect to $\omega$ revealed a value of 2.3±0.5 for the average SN Ia density at $z\sim0.5$. These are lecture notes for a 6-hour mini-course on stochastic partial differential equations presented at the University of Oxford in April-May 2021. 

The main objective of these lecture notes is to provide an in-depth explanation of the variational method for monotone and coercive stochastic partial differential equations. 

The necessary background on Hilbert space-based functional analysis, operator theory, and stochastic analysis has been recapitulated within the lecture notes and further relevant references are included in Chapter 2. 

The primary course material is contained within Chapters 3-5, with additional appendices supplying key proofs and counterexamples. 

The underlying philosophy of these lecture notes is to present a holistic view of SPDEs that integrates elements from both probability and PDE theory. 

The specific focus on the variational method for SPDEs is a deliberate choice, with an emphasis on establishing existence and uniqueness of solutions rather than other analysis of SPDEs. 

The intended audience for these lecture notes includes graduate students in analysis, researchers in mathematics, and those in related fields with an interest in SPDEs. 

The associated RML toolkit can be found at the following link: https://github.com/alexandrov/RML-Toolkit. 
This toolkit provides an open-source implementation of the results presented in these lecture notes. 

The RML community is a public forum where members discuss stochastic analysis, related PDEs, and related topics; further information on this community is available at the provided link.
