The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found T centers in the device layer to have a relatively small impact on spin decoherence and demonstrated that such defect centers retain their functionality within the photonic layer of SOI, without the need for etching. As a result, we were able to observe T centers in the 28um thick COI layer, enable two-qubit operation in a single chip, and demonstrate the creation of high-quality T centers in the photonic layer itself. Due to its scalability and integrability with other quantum functions within the SOI platform, this defect center system presents a promising opportunity for large-scale, solid-state quantum computing. Finally, we outline potential pathways for enhancing the performance of this system in real-world applications. System performance could be optimized through the implementation of advanced spin control methods such as optical pumping with a blue laser, the use of larger magnetic fields, and the reduction of spin decoherence via techniques like sidewall passivation. Advanced imaging capabilities, combined with sophisticated processing techniques, enable detection of hard-to-spot tumors. This assignment delves into Automated Tumor Detection by comparing conventional image processing methods, such as morphological analysis and regional growth algorithms, in order to explore their application and effectiveness. The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets. To achieve this, we employed the least-squares deconvolution (LSD) technique to remove the stellar activity from the spectra of M dwarfs, selecting different line lists for this purpose. Our line lists varied based on line strength and chromospheric formation, with an emphasis on spectral lines formed predominantly in the chromosphere. These lines are less correlated with the photospheric activity and more sensitive to magnetic field strength. Our results showed that the LSD line profiles generated from these lines are less correlated with activity indices and more correlated with each other than those from traditional lines. This led to a reduction in the scatter of the deconvolved line profiles by 25% when using our line lists, in comparison to the standard approach. To avoid the bias introduced by line strength, we also developed a random line selection method, which achieved a similar level of deconvolution accuracy with only a 10% increase in noise. This technique is a viable alternative to the parametric approach, providing a more flexible framework for removing the stellar activity from data sets. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the potential for further improvements to the LSD line lists, leading to more effective removal of the stellar activity from the spectra. This technique is also suitable for other spectral lines and can be applied to the discovery of exoplanets in M dwarfs. To facilitate the detection of these celestial bodies, we have made our line lists and associated data sets available for download. This research paper proposes a pair of methods for designing a flexible and efficient wireless sensor network data collection protocol, specifically aimed at applications requiring data to be organized in a hierarchical format. The first method creates a two-tier hierarchical structure based on link quality, while the second method identifies optimal data routing paths on demand, ensuring high reliability and performance in a network that supports both collections of data and individual sensor communications, complex operations enabled by a sensor network's ability to perform tasks collaboratively. The effectiveness of these methods was demonstrated in an experimental setup utilizing ContikiC and link-quality estimation functionality, yielding results that show significant improvements in data delivery ratio, latency, and energy consumption when compared to existing protocols. The implementation's simplicity and adaptability make it suitable for various link-quality estimation tools and data collection scenarios. The developed protocol was evaluated against two existing protocols in an experimental network consisting of 50 sensor nodes, resulting in data delivery ratio improvements of up to 15%, latency reductions of as much as 20%, and energy consumption per data collection event lowered by as much as 25%. The research's findings were further validated in a larger 100-node network, showing data delivery ratio improvements of as much as 12%, latency reductions of as much as 18%, and energy consumption per data collection event lowered by as much as 22%. The proposed link-quality estimation technique was found to be more accurate than existing methods, achieving an 11% greater data delivery ratio, a 19% lower data delivery ratio for low-quality links, and a 22% lower data delivery ratio for links with the lowest quality, a 20% greater collection latency for low-quality links, and a 18% higher collection latency for links with the lowest quality, and a 23% higher energy consumption for low-quality links, and a 21% higher energy consumption for links with the lowest quality. The research's outcomes were further validated in an open-field experiment, showing data delivery ratio improvements of as much as 13%, latency reductions of as much as 19%, and energy consumption per data collection event lowered by as much as 24%. The proposed methods were found to provide a 12% greater data delivery ratio for low-energy nodes, a 20% lower data delivery ratio for high-energy nodes, a 21% greater collection latency for low-energy nodes, a 18% lower collection latency for high-energy nodes, and a 24% higher energy consumption for low-energy nodes, and a 21% higher energy consumption for high-energy nodes. We examine the concentration behavior of functionals of random vectors whose entries reside in the discrete cube. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures at least a 2^k-fold increase in subgaussian rates of L_p norms for p not equal to 2, while for SRP we prove a similar 2-fold increase in norms for p not equal to 2 and quasi-Logconcave distributions with respect to the Euclidean norm for any p. Moreover, we establish a 1/k increase in the subgaussian rate of L_p norms for uniform distributions on the N-fold cover of the cube, in addition to investigating the concentration of volume-representing polynomials and Sobolev norms.

We investigate one-dimensional projections in greater detail, demonstrating that they comply with either SCP or SRP, with specific concentrations of norms of these projections for certain distributions. Furthermore, we establish that numerous well-known distributions on the cube or its covers exhibit negative dependence structures, including (but not limited to) distributions that are Gaussian, log-concave, uniformly distributed on the N-fold cover of the cube, or a discrete version thereof. Our results complement or extend prior works by Kostlan, Bubnov, Liu and Paquette, Guedj and Kerber, Paquette, Liu and Bubnov in the fields of algebraic geometry, combinatorics and theoretical computer science. Our findings also imply the efficient solvability of systems of random polynomial equations by providing a crucial concentration inequality. This is in turn applied to derive the quasi-Nash equilibrium in coordination games on the cube or its covers, leading to an extension of a prior result by Liu and Paquette. Our results on the efficient solvability of systems of random polynomial equations also imply the derivation of a prior result by Bubnov in the field of algebraic geometry. Our investigation of the concentration of volume-representing polynomials with respect to Sobolev norms yields an alternative proof of a prior result by Guedj and Kerber in the field of combinatorics. Our investigation of one-dimensional projections with respect to their concentration of norms leads to the extension of a prior result by Kostlan in the field of algebraic geometry. Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic greater than two, and consider the ring of power series $R$ over the Witt vectors of $k$, expanded in variables $t_1, \dots, t_d$. The main aim of this study is to generalize classical Fontaine-Messing theory to a base ring of the form $R$. Notably, we establish theorems enabling the comparison of crystalline and \'etale cohomologies with torsion coefficients for smooth schemes $X$ over $R$. This comparison is facilitated by first demonstrating that the absolute Galois group $G_k$ acts continuously on the perfect torsion crystalline cohomology group $\otimes_d W_k$ for any smooth projective variety $X$ over $R$. Building on this result, we show that the action of $G_k$ extends continuously to the semi-local ring $R$ provided $X$ remains smooth and projective over $R$. Finally, we overcome the constraint of projectivity by developing a technique that allows for the construction of a projective variety $X'$ over $R$, equivalent to $X$ after base change, and for which theorems can be applied. This enables the comparison of crystalline and \'etale cohomologies for any smooth variety $X$ over $R$. Additionally, we generalize the Fontaine-Messing theorem to include non-perfect base fields $k$, specifically demonstrating that the comparison theorem holds for smooth projective varieties $X$ over rings of power series $\hat{A}$, where $A$ is the ring of Witt vectors constructed from a total field of characteristic zero, and in particular, this is applicable to rings of power series over fields of positive characteristic. Notably, this involves showing that the action of $G_k$ continues to influence the semi-local ring $\hat{A}$ and demonstrates the necessity of this influence for the comparison theorem to hold. Finally, we outline the strategy for proving theorems involving the absolute Galois group action on cohomology groups in a more general setting, specifically for varieties with singularities, and identify key obstructions to generalizing the Fontaine-Messing theorem in this manner. This includes an examination of the role that base fields of characteristic zero, specifically number fields and local fields, play in such generalizations, as well as the potential for generalizing the Fontaine-Messing theorem to rings of power series over fields of positive characteristic. This study explores the double longitudinal-spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering where hadron pairs' transverse momentum is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the cause of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production, accounting for the connection between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function. Using a spectator model, we calculate the interference term between $s$-wave and $p$-wave and estimate this asymmetry at various experiments, including COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, and the future EIC. Our analysis suggests that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS can serve as a key test for the dihadron fragmentation function. Additionally, we examine the dihadron production in deep central exclusive production, finding a similar asymmetry but with a different interpretation. A comprehensive overview of the relevant processes and asymmetries is provided in Supplemental Material. Furthermore, models predicting this asymmetry are reviewed in that supplement, along with expected values at various experiments. These calculations reveal that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS and CEEX exhibits distinct behaviors, thus providing a crucial opportunity for cross-validation through future measurements. Moreover, we discuss the potential for these processes to contribute to cosine azimuthal asymmetries observed in proton-proton and nucleus-nucleus collisions at higher energies. These findings underscore the significance of thorough investigations in the future with an electron (magnetic field non-zero) at JLab 12 GeV and the EIC. Moreover, we propose that data from these experiments, along with existing COMPASS data, be reanalyzed with a focus on hadron pairs at low $Q^2$, in order to fully explore the underlying dynamics and accurately determine the relevant twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function parameters. Systematic studies of hadron pair production considering various centralities and the corresponding secondary reggeon exchanges are also recommended for further investigation. These studies aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of hadron pair production in DIS and CEEX across various $x$ and $Q^2$ values, along with future opportunities to examine the role of quark-quark and gluon-quark correlations in hadron pair production and to establish connections between hadron pair production in DIS, CEEX, and hadron production in proton-proton and nucleus-nucleus collisions. Building on existing knowledge, this work offers a thorough examination and a unified perspective on the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron pair production in DIS and CEEX

Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics, including irreducible finite-dimensional representations and those of certain subgroups. This translation makes Springer's original findings available in English. Van der Kallen included an appendix to provide context for his 1961 paper, "Regular representations of algebraic groups," which is also included in this translation. Springer's research laid the groundwork for later studies on algebraic groups and their conjugacy classes. This translation aims to facilitate further understanding of his contributions in their original context. Van der Kallen's own notes were incorporated into the translation to enhance clarity and comprehension. This English version of Springer's thesis retains its historical value as the pioneering work that preceded Carter's influential study on conjugacy classes within algebraic groups, and it now provides accessible insights for a broader English-speaking audience. This translation is now available in the Springer Open Book titled "Algebras, Representations and Applications -- 25 Years of DREMAP" edited by Jon F. Hansen. Van der Kallen and Hansen are grateful to have had the opportunity to share this translation with a wider audience and to celebrate Hansen's 65th birthday in style. This translation is also a testament to the enduring legacy of T.A. Springer's contributions to the field of algebraic groups and his lasting impact on Van der Kallen and many other mathematicians who have built upon his groundbreaking research. This translation is a result of the enthusiasm and support of many in the mathematics community, and Van der Kallen would like to express his heartfelt appreciation to all of them. This translation is now available for free to the global scientific community as a part of the Springer Open Access initiative. This translation is a significant milestone in the history of both the journal Publications Math\'ematiques de l'IH\'ES and Springer, and it is an honor for Van der Kallen to have had the opportunity to contribute to this important landmark. This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes an embedding approach, where the entity space is hierarchically divided into layered graphs for efficient information retrieval and personalized suggestions. By leveraging Wikipedia's structured data and category relationships, our method creates a comprehensive entity knowledge base that facilitates targeted entity recommendations in response to search queries. Specifically, our approach enables fast and relevant entity suggestions for all Wikipedia articles, outperforming alternative methods in terms of diversity and overall effectiveness according to human evaluators and rigorous systematic studies. Our entity recommendation framework has been deployed in the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, yielding a 25% boost in overall engagement compared to standard methods. Our technique has been patented under the designation "Wikipedia Entity Recommendation" (US Patent 10,189,971). Furthermore, our methodology has inspired the development of a Wikipedia Entity SDK, enabling easy integration of our entity recommendations into third-party applications. This SDK, along with our entity recommendation framework, is currently being used in over 10 Yahoo! applications and has paved the way for further research in graph embedding and entity recommendation. In recognition of its groundbreaking innovation, our entity recommendation framework has received the 2018 Yahoo! Machine Learning Innovation Award. Systematic studies with human evaluators have revealed key insights that can guide future research in entity recommendation and related areas, providing valuable qualitative and quantitative findings along with concrete recommendations for future work. Building upon these discoveries, our research has given rise to an ongoing research initiative at Yahoo!, which is focused on exploring new entity recommendation challenges and opportunities in conjunction with the broader knowledge graph community. This initiative has resulted in the creation of a dedicated research forum at the 2019 ACM-SIGIR Workshop on Information Overlap, which provided a collaborative platform for researchers and practitioners to exchange ideas and share experiences on entity recommendation and related topics. This workshop has sparked further research in this domain, leading to an expansion of the entity recommendation community at Yahoo! and the wider knowledge graph community. In recognition of its contributions to this research community, our entity recommendation framework has received the 2019 Best Paper Award at the ACM-SIGIR Workshop on Information Overlap. This award has underscored the significance of our results, which have demonstrated the efficacy of our Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework in providing high-quality, personalized suggestions to search queries and have set a new standard for entity recommendation in the Wikipedia knowledge graph. Consequently, our approach has inspired a line of research that has explored the integration of additional knowledge sources, such as entity relationships and topic models, into the Wikipedia graph, yielding further breakthroughs

A complex system optimization model, specifically a lot-sizing model with customer preferences, was previously developed to understand transplant acceptance decisions. This research builds upon that foundation to address an important unexplored aspect: Transplant centers often maintain cadaveric kidney supplies in various preservation solutions, and incompatible recipients require kidneys from specific categories based on these solutions. These constraints are incorporated into a new lot-sizing model with customer preferences, which also considers the complex logistics of kidney preservation. A practical solution approach was developed and tested with real-world data from the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients (SRTR). This research found that many transplant centers face difficulties in meeting the demand for incompatible kidneys and could benefit from optimizing their procurement strategies. A case study with data from the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) Medical Center demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach, showing it could identify procurement policies that increase the number of transplants by up to 15% in a year. This increase is substantial, considering that in 2020, only 77% of incompatible patients on the waiting list received a transplant within three years in the United States. This finding is consistent with prior studies indicating that centers with high failure rates often have inefficient procurement systems. This research was conducted with representatives from the SRTR and all transplant centers in the United States, and it could serve as a basis for developing data-driven procurement policies that maximize the number of transplants. These policies prioritize centers with low failure rates and encourage them to participate in procurement optimization, as they are more likely to execute it correctly and reduce logistical costs with economies of scope. This approach can also inform the design of future performance incentives and payment schemes for transplant centers, such as paying centers with low failure rates a higher fee per transplant. It was presented at the 2019 INFORMS Annual Meeting and will be presented at the 2020 Management Science Annual Conference. This research was done in collaboration with the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) Medical Center and the University of California, Berkeley. This study examines the capabilities of word embeddings in understanding the polarities assigned by Loughran-McDonald to 47 word categories in corporate disclosure texts. We initially verify the existing evidence indicating the effectiveness of word embeddings at categorizing polarized words. However, our analysis reveals a more complex picture when we classify words based on their polarities. We discovered a significant issue with the original Loughran-McDonald dataset, characterized by an imbalance in words labeled as positive (approximately 18%) compared to those marked as negative (around 82%). This disparity is not inherent to the dataset but rather reflects the annotators' subjectivity. It significantly impacts the classification performance, with models naturally exceling at categorizing words from the majority negative group. When we created a balanced subdataset and conducted an in-depth error analysis, we found most misclassified negative words to be highly domain-specific, with little support from either the original positive or negative word embeddings. Our findings suggest that word embeddings are not inherently better at capturing the intended polarities and that the existing evidence is susceptible to alternative explanations. Our research is also an early attempt to formally audit the Loughran-McDonald dataset through the lens of word embeddings. We propose a more objective evaluation approach that considers multiple representation learning methods and suggests improving the dataset by incorporating words from these models that clash with human interpretations. Our audit of the dataset raises concerns about its reliability and potential issues with human annotation, especially when used in other domains and research fields that rely heavily on human-annotated training data. Our study consists of three parts: (1) examining the relationship between word embeddings and the Loughran-McDonald polarities, (2) analyzing the classification of words based on these polarities, and (3) investigating the implications of our findings for both the dataset and the field of accounting, with a focus on the topic of corporate disclosure. Our research raises pressing issues that necessitate a thorough re-examination of the underlying assumptions and the replication of related studies that relied on this dataset. Our audit of the dataset is accompanied by two novel datasets created in partnership with Ph.D. students, which comprise 150 negative words that word embeddings incorrectly classify as positive in the context of accounting, along with 150 positive words that embeddings mistakenly label as negative. These newly constructed datasets hold significance not only for the field of accounting but also for any research that relies on human-annotated training data, highlighting the value of overcorrection in annotated datasets to prevent similar issues from emerging in the future. This incorporation of controlled structural operations yields derivational ambiguities missed by the original Lambek Calculus and its simplification in pregroups. To resolve issues with categorial interpretation caused by the added modalities, a quantum interpretation is proposed, drawing from categorical semantics and Chernoff's hyperbolic space interpretation of the Lambek Calculus, to provide a unified framework for understanding both the original and expanded calculus through geometric representation. However, existing results in multiagent learning are limited to identifying second-best rationalizable equilibria, defined as action profiles where no player is dominated in at least two-planner context. This work significantly expands the current understanding by broadening the definition of rationalizability to account for any number of players and providing guarantees for learning action profiles that are at least as robust as first-order rationalizable equilibria. Building on VCG-based methods and free-entry mechanisms, which enable identifying and learning from observed play-off paths, our results provide general guarantees for learning action profiles that are first-order rationalizable in games featuring any number of players and various action profiles. Additionally, our results cover models with partial observability and information asymmetry, as well as extensions to certain extensions of normal form games. Our research offers a novel approach to ensuring the learning of rationalizable behavior in multiagent learning settings. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies and a designated website that showcases the results. This paper outlines the design of this unified framework, detailing its components and automation capabilities through automated documentation and a marked-up format that can be easily converted to various formats, including HTML, LaTeX, and XML. Specifically, this framework uses XML markup for data and cross-section level descriptions, thereby enabling straightforward incorporation of provider-specific formats, such as LHDA and NNPDF formats, which are already being used by the community. Additionally, this framework includes interfaces for popular fitting tools, including xFitter, and will be made available for public use and is an open-source project on GitHub under the MIT License. Furthermore, this paper introduces the NNPDF 4.0 fit, which includes datasets, PDF candidates, and uncertainty estimates generated by xFitter, along with experimental and theoretical documentation provided in an open-data format, available at https://dx.doi.org/10.17181/PPFQ7G. Additionally, the theoretical predictions provided in this paper incorporate the JAM 2.0 PDF fit, which is a joint fit that combines DGLAP and impact parameter evolution equations, and the corresponding code is available at https://dx.doi.org/10.17181/PPFQ7G. This paper is also an open-access article available at https://dx.doi.org/10.1140/epjc/s10052101203401. To accelerate policy optimization in complex, dynamic systems with multiple influencing factors, reinforcement learning agents can effectively utilize previously collected historical data. Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. A more adaptive method, the variance reduction based experience replay framework, selectively leverages the most informative historical data. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. Theoretical and practical evaluations demonstrate that this method accelerates optimal policy discovery and boosts the effectiveness of state-of-the-art policy optimization methods. Compared to the baseline experience replay approach, it yields a 3x performance boost in simulated scenarios and a 2x improvement in real-world experiments on motion planning. This proposed framework's accelerated policy optimization and enhanced sample efficiency could be valuable for future energy-efficient reinforcement learning agents. The code is available at https://github.com/strimble/variational-replay. The data collected during ncar's real-world evaluation is available at https://drive.google.

relevant to the top quark's polarization, have been reported for events 
resulting from $t$-channel single top quark production. The data, derived from 
proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1, 
included events characterized by an isolated muon. By comparing experimental 
data to theoretical models, the signal and background components were quantified, 
enabling a measurement of the differential cross-section of an angular observable 
correlated with the top quark's polarization, taking into account detection biases.

which does not differ significantly from the standard model's predicted value of 0.44. 
This measurement contributes to the top quark's polarization determination and 
is an essential component in the search for electroweak symmetry breaking effects.

to any given history, leading us to present the MultiTalk Dataset. This large 
dataset comprises over 320,000 written conversational dialogue sentences, 
maintaining a high degree of complexity (a 10-way branching factor) along with 
6 conversation turns through strategically chosen continuation branches. Our study 
of dialogue generation involves multiple advancements, specifically in highly 
branching situations. We assess the performance of four different network 
architectures: single-round baselines, sequential models, and models able to 
generate multiple sentences at once. Our research indicates that generating all 
sentences simultaneously yields the best results, with an 18% increase in R@1 
and a 65% increase in R@5 when compared to the strongest single-round rival.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time, and demonstrates that they conformally invariant. We also demonstrate that these processes can be used to model multiple SLE evolving in time when the parameters are restricted to certain irrational values, and that they have the same conformal invariance properties as Miller and Sheffield's multiple SLE processes when those parameters are rationally linearized. We further construct several types of Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant, and establish that they are related to various driving measures for multiple SLE evolving in time, including the stochastic one-component six-charge log-gas, the stochastic Dyson model with a mix of bosons and fermions, and the stochastic GSE symmetric matrix-valued process. We also consider the relationship between these driving measures and multiple SLE evolving in time when the parameters are restricted to certain irrational values and when those parameters are rationally linearized. Ultimately, this work provides a framework for defining multiple SLE evolving in time when the parameters are not necessarily irrational or linear, and for analyzing its conformal invariance properties. Additionally, we demonstrate that our construction of Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant, and our results on their conformal invariance properties, can be extended to the case where the underlying space is a Riemann surface. This work was initially presented as two PhD thesis chapters by the author at the University of Oxford in 2019 and 2020. It has now been completed with additional research sponsored by the National Science Foundation through grant FRG-2012013 and has been made available through the Electronic Communications of the American Mathematical Society. into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw data into desired outputs.
Its features include automatic generation of manuscripts in various formats such
as LaTeX and Markdown, as well as support for software development within its
embedded IDE. Other features like version control systems, peer review tools,
and calculators for common tasks like plotting and statistical analysis are also
integrated into WorkingWiki. By leveraging its embedded IDE, version control,
and software development capabilities, WorkingWiki provides a unique environment
that fosters interdisciplinary collaboration and project development. We have
successfully applied WorkingWiki across multiple departments and institutions,
utilizing its wiki-IDE-tool combo to develop over 100 projects including software
applications, data visualizations, and over 50 scholarly manuscripts. We have
also open-sourced WorkingWiki's embedded IDE, called IDE4U, allowing other wiki
platforms to benefit from its features and utilities. We have derived several
general lessons on designing collaborative platforms from our experience with
WorkingWiki, including the importance of choosing suitable command-line tools,
ensuring the ease of usage and navigation within the wiki, and guaranteeing the
security of users' software and data. We have also explored various ways to
motivate users to contribute to the development of the wiki's embedded IDE and
have identified several avenues for further development of WorkingWiki, such
as enhancing its security features, and exploring alternative GUI-based IDEs
in order to continue pushing the boundaries of what is achievable with this type
of collaborative platform. WorkingWiki is available for download at its dedicated
GitHub repository, along with a comprehensive user guide available at its website.

Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness in developing new CRDTs and resolving update conflicts. Compared to existing solutions, RWF-designed CRDTs demonstrate lower latency during conflict resolution, in addition to enhanced scalability and adaptability. With RWF, developing new CRDTs becomes more feasible, and it paves the way for further research into conflict resolution strategies in distributed storage systems. We believe that a design framework like RWF can serve as a foundation for other conflict resolution approaches that may be more complex, such as ones dealing with deletion conflicts, and become the basis for more in-depth research into the fundamental properties of data types capable of replication. We also invite the community to build upon and expand the concepts introduced within the scope of the RWF framework. Leveraging Redis as an implementation platform, we design a Redis extension that can support a wide range of data types capable of replication with conflicts, which we refer to as RWF-compliant storage. Such storage systems can ensure the consistency of replicated data across all nodes, even in the presence of conflicts during updates, and provide a high level of availability even in the presence of failing nodes. With a strong focus on design, the RWF framework provides a theoretical foundation that can be used to create new storage systems or replicate existing data types with conflicts, in addition to allowing for the development of applications that can operate on top of such storage systems. Through two real-world applications built using Redis with Replication, we demonstrate the feasibility of the RWF design framework and show its potential for building scalable and highly available systems even in the presence of update conflicts. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the genome, by identifying patterns in trait-associated variants and matching them with functional genomics data in large-scale cohorts. This approach can handle numerous annotation types and trait associations from multiple sources. Applying our method to 18 human traits across 6 phenotypes and with access to extensive functional genomics resources, we've obtained comprehensive sets of putative regulatory regions associated with traits in silico, and found associated coding and non-coding regions with 50% or more confidence level. For example, in silico analysis of height revealed multiple putative regulatory regions in intron gaps and in non-coding regions, in addition to five coding regions, including genes FGF20 and NRG1 with high confidence levels. Similarly, in silico analysis of coronary artery disease identified multiple putative regulatory regions and coding regions, including genes LIPN and PKN2, and also found that putative regulatory regions in intron gaps for this trait displayed an overrepresentation of disease-causing variants. In contrast, in silico analysis of bipolar disorder did not pinpoint any coding regions but found associated non-coding regions with high confidence levels across the genome. In addition, our method can prioritize putative associated regions for experimental validation based on multiple criteria such as association levels with traits and with functional genomics data, and we've applied this to several traits. All in all, our approach provides a robust framework for the exploration of genomic data in relation to genome-wide association studies of human traits and has the capacity to facilitate experimental validation of putative associated regions through in silico prioritization. In particular, we've demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in identifying associated coding and non-coding regions with high confidence levels across the genome for 18 human traits, and made the results of our analysis publicly available at http://www.igv.org/ in silico. Furthermore, we've shown that in silico analysis of traits with associated non-coding regions such as bipolar disorder, coronary artery disease, and type 2 diabetes, do not necessarily require the use of experimental data to prioritize putative associated regions for validation. In contrast, in silico analysis of height and other traits with associated coding regions require experimental validation to confirm the role of these genes in the underlying biological pathways. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, even when incorporating radio data from a more extensive time frame via the FM radio telescope, approximately 55 percent of these neutron star binaries still have uncertainty in their 1 to 100 year recurrence time frames, which might be as short as a few months or as long as several centuries. As a result of these findings, locating a neutron star within an accretion disk should not be taken as definitive proof of the presence of a black hole, and therefore, there is no grounds to support the existing estimate of the Galactic Center's stellar mass black hole population. This research focuses on the development of efficient and resilient bipedal robots, leveraging their potential to navigate through challenging environments in a dynamic and unpredictable space involving other robots. To achieve this goal, we explore the concept of controlled coexistence by introducing a thruster-assisted bipedal robot design, with the aim of evaluating its performance in comparison to a primitive bipedal robot control strategy. To improve navigation, we incorporate a collision avoidance system based on potential fields into the robot's navigation module, utilizing a simplified approach to prevent the robot from colliding with obstacles and other robots. To enhance locomotion efficiency, we develop an optimal control strategy using model predictive control (MPC), with the objective of minimizing energy consumption while ensuring robust bipedal movement. To compensate for disturbances during locomotion, we design a feedback control system based on the robot's joint velocities. With these components integrated, we conduct simulations and thruster-assisted bipedal robot experiments to validate our approach, with promising results showing that our method yields significant improvements in energy efficiency and robustness. The thruster-assisted bipedal robot demonstrates an energy reduction of 35% in ideal conditions and 25% in the presence of external disturbances, with an average robustness enhancement of 125% in scenarios involving other robots and 55% in scenarios involving obstacles, underscoring the efficacy of our solution in achieving controlled coexistence through robust bipedal locomotion. To facilitate replication, we provide the MPC algorithm used in our study, with MPC parameters tailored to the thruster-assisted bipedal robot configuration employed in our experiments. Although our solution leverages a relatively simple control strategy, we believe that our approach offers a valuable starting point for further research aimed at optimizing complex control systems for robust bipedal robots. With the thruster-assisted bipedal robot representing a critical component in our controlled coexistence framework, our results contribute to the broader exploration of strategies for managing the interaction between multiple robots in a dynamic and unpredictable environment. As part of our framework, we examine the scenario involving a bipedal robot and highlight the challenges and considerations involved in controlling the coexistence of other robot types, with our solution proving amenable to extension across a broader spectrum of robot configurations. Building upon our findings, we outline potential avenues for research aimed at addressing key challenges in controlled coexistence, with a focus on the scope for optimizing complex control systems in robust bipedal robots and the exploration of novel configurations capable of navigating through complex environments in a dynamic and unpredictable space involving other robots

Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series in $t$ to $k$ is representable using first-order logic when the characteristic of $k$ is not two. This discovery motivated further research which extended this result to a specific class of fields with a well-defined residue map. In 2016, Denef generalized this result from finite fields to all fields with a total residue map and proved that such fields allow model completion with respect to a specific first-order formula when their absolute value is non-Archimedean and the characteristic of the field's residue map is not two. This paper builds upon Denef's work by removing constraints on the fields' characteristics and extends his results to all fields with a total residue map, thereby answering a question posed by Berson in 2014. Additionally, this research is accompanied by the development of a new representability theorem for partial map $1$-types in non-Archimedean valued fields with a well-defined residue map, making it a more general result than Becker-Denef-Lipschitz's original observation. Lastly, this research is also presented in the context of an open problem which was a part of the 2015 conference dedicated to Becker's 65th anniversary.

In the field of Computer Science, matrix-based problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. Consequently, matrix multiplication, the most frequently used matrix operation, can pose performance bottlenecks when applied to large matrices. To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. This study compares sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, with findings indicating that parallel processing has a profound impact on computational efficiency, particularly with larger matrices. For example, the sequential method takes approximately 1.2 seconds to multiply two 1000x1000 matrices on a single core, but this drops to 0.5 seconds with four cores and just 0.00025 seconds with a single GPU core, demonstrating a substantial improvement in speed with parallel processing. These results have implications for problem solvers, suggesting that the choice of sequential or parallel approach depends on available computational resources rather than problem size, with potential applications in fields such as graph theory and machine learning. Two open-source MATLAB scripts are appended as supplementary materials, enabling reproduction of results with available CUDA tools and a Windows-based test platform. In cooperative systems with multiple agents, coordination enables tasks to be performed that would be beyond the capabilities of any single agent. We investigate the concept of coordination through strategic decision-making, focusing on a scenario where agents select between two tasks of varying difficulty that are randomly distributed and partially known. It has been found that a stable state of cooperation, characterized by a straightforward linear pattern, can be achieved when there is a wide range of possible task difficulties. This cooperative equilibrium is maintained by a two-layer structure, in which a higher-level strategy determines the level of effort invested in each task, while a lower-level mechanism deals with the underlying computation complexity. A key feature of this equilibrium is its sensitivity to changes in the level of communication limitation, exhibiting an abrupt shift from a cooperative to a non-cooperative state as it decreases. It has also been determined that the most efficient performance is achieved at a middle range of possible task difficulties. Furthermore, it requires significantly less difficulty variability to achieve the most efficient performance in a smaller network than in a larger one. Finally, it is demonstrated that the most efficient performance can be achieved through a mechanism of matching variable levels of computation among agents, mirroring the variability present in their tasks. This research contributes to the exploration of computational models that generate random variation in data, such as the multi-task model, which can be used to analyze the dynamics of cooperative systems. Additionally, it highlights the significance of coordination in cooperative systems by showing that cooperation leads to better performance than non-cooperation, regardless of the level of computation and communication limitations. Finally, it highlights the potential for counterintuitive outcomes in cooperative systems, such as the fact that the most efficient performance can be achieved at levels of computation and communication that are far from the maximum available. This paper investigates the security risks of vertical federated learning, a framework in which participants share sectoral data for collaborative training. Our focus is on a scenario where a user trains a model using their own data and that of several federated partners, whose contributions cannot be disclosed due to data confidentiality. We examine the privacy threats when a user shares their own data in conjunction with the updates from other partners, with the goal of detecting practical privacy breaches. Our key discoveries include designing effective attacks on federated users by leveraging the data shared by the employer, as well as demonstrating the efficacy of such attacks in both non-homogeneous and homogeneous settings. Furthermore, we show that employers can compromise the privacy of their employees when the following conditions are met: (1) the employer and employee have different data types, (2) the employer and employee have the same data type but different dataset sizes, or (3) employee data types are homogeneous but of varying scale. We also establish defense thresholds for preventing successful attacks in all scenarios. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably its insensitivity to data characteristics, resulting in suboptimal performance, particularly with limited data sets. Notably, our experiments demonstrate particularly striking improvements in shallow models, underscoring the significance of feature representation on the model's performance. Our findings are showcased in four theoretical sections, each outlining an application of the Cartesian Decomposition technique to (1) monolithic groups within monolithic wreath products, (2) dihedral groups, (3) tridihedral and tetrahedral groups, and (4) A-type groups. These demonstrations illustrate the efficacy of the Cartesian Decomposition technique for an extensive range of group types within wreath products. Furthermore, this method enables the generation of diverse group structures within wreath products, facilitating the exploration of novel group compositions. To effect this strategy, the underlying Cartesian Decomposition theorems are presented in an appendix for easy reference. Building on this method, several open research questions and problems are identified and proposed in the concluding section for further investigation. Additionally, this work is complemented by an online repository, detailed in the reference section, that provides an interactive catalog of group embeddings into wreath products in the Sylvester matrix representation format. This repository is maintained in conjunction with this study and is regularly updated with newly derived results. Leveraging the MonoidAlgebras and WreathProducts packages developed in the FlatLandMath project, this repository enables seamless exploration and extraction of embedding results for groups within wreath products in various representation formats. Patients with rare congenital heart defects face significant surgical challenges due to the complex nature of their heart abnormalities and the limited information available about their conditions. This difficulty is further compounded by the limited effectiveness of heart function assessment methods, such as MRI and echocardiography, across the unique anatomical profiles exhibited by individuals with rare CHD. One promising approach to addressing this issue is the use of advanced deep learning segmentation algorithms like U-Net, which have demonstrated exceptional precision in reconstructing heart anatomy using MRI images. However, the ability of these algorithms to account for the unique anatomical profiles associated with rare CHD and provide accurate preoperative planning has not been thoroughly investigated. This study utilized a large dataset of MRI images from healthy adults to train U-Net-based segmentation algorithms and assessed their performance on a distinct group of MRI images derived from patients with rare CHD. The findings showed that these algorithms can provide precise estimations of heart volume and precision in the reconstruction of cardiac anatomy, even across the unique anatomical profiles exhibited by individuals with rare CHD. These results have implications for the use of such algorithms in the preoperative planning of heart surgeries. Furthermore, the low error rates observed in this study have paved the way for a more comprehensive investigation that involves expert surgeons in evaluating and validating the clinical utility of these algorithms in the preparation of patients with rare CHD for heart surgery. This study has been completed and the results have been obtained, whereas the study involving the input of surgeons has been ongoing at the time of this submission. This research has been ongoing for over two and a half years and over the course of this study, multiple open-source contributions have resulted from our team. One such contribution is the publicly accessible dataset derived from MRI images of healthy adults, which can be accessed through the LIDC repository at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Additionally, all code used in this study can be found in the corresponding GitHub repository. Object detectors, in particular those that utilize Feature Pyramid Networks (FPNs), frequently struggle with identifying large-scale objects due to an inherent drawback in the framework. This paper reexamines FPN within this context and offers a different perspective on its workings. It proposes an alternative FPN formulation that is both mathematically rigorous and enlightening. Consequently, we derive a metric that provides insight into the network's capacity to process objects of varying sizes. Interestingly, this metric reveals that processing smaller objects does not guarantee an equivalent processing of larger objects; in fact, it often results in the neglect of large objects in favor of smaller ones. To address this issue, we put forward a method that encourages the network to consider all objects, regardless of size. Our proposed approach achieves notable improvements over the baseline FPN and other state-of-the-art object detectors, as corroborated by comprehensive experimental results presented herein. Notably, our scheme achieves particular success in domain adaptation, where it showcases substantial gains over the competition. Our implementation of the proposed method yields outstanding performance on COCO, ADAS, and PASCAL VOC benchmarks without relying on sophisticated network modifications or explicit loss functions. Instead, we merely introduce an additional straightforward classification task at each FPN level, with the understanding that similar objects, regardless of scale, should receive identical labels. Our results demonstrate that processing objects of all sizes is crucial and, in the absence of such consideration, object detectors are prone to neglecting large objects in favor of smaller ones. This is because, in the absence of any scale-awareness, the network treats each object as an independent entity, with no regard for its relative size to other objects within the image. As a consequence, our method necessitates a level of scale-awareness from the network, with each object's size influencing its classification. In contrast, without such consideration, the network classifies each object in isolation, with no consideration of its relative size to other objects within the image. Our method's results highlight the significance of processing objects of all sizes, with each object's size playing a crucial role in its classification. In the absence of such consideration, object detectors fail to acknowledge the presence of large objects, with our method rectifying this shortcoming and, as a result, achieving notable gains over the baseline FPN and other state-of-the-art object detectors. Our proposed approach's results on COCO, ADAS, and PASCAL VOC benchmarks validate the importance of processing objects of all sizes, with each object's size playing a crucial role in its classification. Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. Our findings show that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In an attempt to enhance the performance of these models, we conducted a series of experiments that led to the creation of Pretrain-Fine-Tune-Based (PFB) methodology, which aims to address key challenges associated with sequential task in multimodal domains. According to our results, PFB produces models that not only outperform previous state-of-the-art models but also demonstrate a more efficient use of both textual and visual information. One key aspect of PFB involves the introduction of a specialized pretraining task called Seq-Adaptive Masked Language Model (Seq-MLM) that adapts the underlying language model to process sequential data by incorporating sequential transformations and adaptating the attention mechanism used in transformer architectures. In contrast to previous approaches that solely focused on individual input modalities, Seq-MFB employs a unified attention mechanism that efficiently combines the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In our research, we also explored multiple architectures that integrate the information provided in both textual and visual forms through the use of cross-modality interactions. According to our results, the models we proposed not only outperform previous state-of-the-art models but also achieve performance that is on par with human standards in all evaluation metrics. In addition to improving machine learning models that can understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions, we also compiled a comprehensive dataset that includes widely-used instructional manuals and gathered extensive human feedback, which is available for download through our project website. In our research, we also explored multiple applications of the machine learning models we developed, including the ability to efficiently summarize instructional content from multiple sources, and the ability to efficiently plan sequential tasks based on real-world procedures communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by surpassing its storage efficiency limit, without introducing any new loss mechanisms that could impede its performance. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, we demonstrate that the sloshing Sagnac system overcomes the ordinary Michelson's limitation at frequencies above 400 Hz, ultimately providing improved sensitivity in the high-frequency range due to improved meter readout and reduced quantum backaction induced losses. As a result, this design is capable of identifying binary neutron star mergers in their entirety, across all frequencies. Furthermore, when comparing its performance with other novel configurations such as the big and small Michelson systems, the sloshing Sagnac system exhibits the best outcome. Therefore, we conclude that the sloshing Sagnac topology has the greatest potential for enhancing the sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors in the high-frequency range. Additionally, the principles underlying this design may also be applied to future detector upgrades that incorporate multiple coupled cavities to maximize their sensitivity. As such, the detector's mirror substrate thermal noise and other noise sources that are unique to gravitational wave detectors can be overcome with a 10 dB amplifier gain, indicating that a significant improvement in their sensitivity is attainable in the future. Furthermore, we propose a prototype test for the novel interferometer topology using a small scale experiment such as the optical recasting experiment OREgon, in order to validate the theoretical analysis through actual experimental data. Ultimately, incorporating a higher sensitivity detector system, such as the sloshing Sagnac topology, is crucial in order to meet the detector requirements set forth by the gravitational wave physics community in the near and long-term future. As such, researchers should prioritize the development of advanced detector systems over repairing existing infrastructure. Additionally, due to the novel nature of the proposed detector design, its principles may also be applied to future gravitational wave detector systems to overcome their unique noise limitations, ultimately providing a more sensitive detection of gravitational waves. Prior research primarily focused on modeling planetary interactions to explain observed patterns in disks. Although some exoplanets have been identified in such systems, many of these substructures emerge even before planetary formation as necessary precursors that lead to the creation of small solid particles, and ultimately, planetary systems. This work employs high-resolution, three-dimensional radiative hydrodynamic simulations that model the gas and solid particle interactions in protoplanetary disks, and leverages these simulations to produce observational predictions at sub-millimeter wavelengths. The associated analysis includes an evaluation of local curvature features that are prevalent in most disks, often overlooked in prior research, along with comparisons between different curvature structures, planetary interactions, and the effects of grain size variations. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains where individual ion spices' movements are coupled differently, thus enabling the development of frequency-tolerant quantum circuits. A demonstration of this method is performed on four calcium ions, achieving an average Molmer-Sorensen gate fidelity of 0.993 within a 25-kHz frequency range, offering a promising solution for quantum computing's scalability issues with trapped ions. Furthermore, this technique is applicable to various ion species and setups, such as line arrangements and near-planar configurations, making it a versatile frequency-robust quantum gate technique. Through balanced frequency protection, it is possible to create a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, an important consideration in large-scale quantum computing systems. Using advanced computer simulations of atoms in motion, we've found that titanium in barium titanate maintains an unexpected position within its molecular structure even when it's not polarized. This finding challenges the common assumption used to model this phase. To address this discrepancy, we performed a thorough analysis of the symmetries at play and created a series of simplified models that accurately capture the underlying structure of the material. From these models, we derived three basic frameworks that accurately predict the material's properties in its pefered and preferred states. Our research provides a clear blueprint for a complete understanding of barium titanate's behavior and offers a strategy for applying the same principles to other materials with similar properties. Introduction (not abstract): Barium titanate is a well-studied, yet enigmatic material with significant applications due to its rapid and extreme shift in electrical properties in response to small changes in temperature, pressure, or chemistry. To gain insight into its behavior, researchers have been analyzing the movements of atoms within the material using advanced computer simulations, revealing that titanium resists changing its position within the molecular structure, even in its non-polarized state, a phenomenon that challenges the commonly accepted model of the material's structure. To address this exception to the rule, researchers have been examining the symmetries within the material and creating fundamental models of its structure, revealing that the movement of atoms within the material follows a set of basic rules that can be applied universally, providing a blueprint for understanding how the movement of atoms within any given layer of the material affects its overall behavior. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our risk-averse decision-making model revealed that many storage units prefer to operate in a risk-averse manner. This leads them to prioritize shorter-term profits over potential gains from longer-term pricing, especially during periods of low supply. As a result, our findings suggest that grid operators should design market mechanisms that account for storage units' risk-averse tendencies, either by providing them with risk management tools or by implementing policies that mitigate their risk aversion, in order to make the most of their potential in enhancing grid resilience and stability. Deep neural networks (DNNs) benefit from being trained on optimal subsets of annotated data. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data in tandem with targeted annotation of crucial samples. 

Our investigation combines active learning and self-supervised pretraining in the context of ImageNet. The evaluation reveals that results on modest, commonly used benchmark datasets do not reflect actual performance on large-scale datasets like ImageNet due to an uneven class distribution selected by the active learning method. Existing AL algorithms failed to surpass random sampling among our evaluated benchmarks, including small and large-scale scenarios. In particular, we explored three key factors contributing to unevenness in selected AL samples and class distributions: 1) the standard evaluation protocol used to select data; 2) the inherent characteristics of pretraining; and 3) the class balance issue itself. 

To address these concerns, we conducted multiple independent experiments, resulting in enhanced AL models that achieved 58.1% top-1 accuracy on the 20484 out-of-distribution classes in the PASCAL VOC 2007, 42.3% top-1 accuracy on the 15000 UAP samples in the iNaturalist 2020, and 22.3% top-1 accuracy on the 15million unsampled ImageNet classes in the novel few-shot learning setting. Our work lays the groundwork for exploring the integration of active learning and self-supervised pretraining in the era of big data. Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, the time taken for each prediction and refinement is relatively brief, allowing the system to function well in real-time scenarios. Our code is available at https://github/hitl-rts. According to our results, it is possible to train models that are both highly accurate (94.67%) and reliable (93.17%) in just three rounds of refinement, even when starting with very limited data. This approach holds significant potential for broad application across machine learning frameworks. Next steps in our research involve exploring ways to minimize the reliance on human input required for refining models and identifying methods to create more effective human-provided correction masks for unsupervised data augmentation. We also plan to investigate additional aspects of this system, including its performance in handling complex situations and its ability to operate in environments with constantly shifting standards and conditions. These advancements will be based on further improvements to the underlying multi-agent architecture and new techniques for creating specialized data augmentation patterns, along with the collection of more comprehensive data across a wider range of domains. These steps will provide a more in-depth examination of this proposed system's capabilities and its potential for enhancing the trustworthiness of machine learning models. In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, there is a significant challenge in evaluating and advancing this field of research due to a lack of high-quality, specialized datasets. To address this issue, we have created the PIS-5000 dataset, comprising 5000 annotated x-ray images that depict a wide range of prohibited items, including 28 distinct categories. This dataset can be utilized in various forms, including a comprehensive training set and several targeted subsets tailored to specific prohibited items. To further enhance research in this area, we have designed an innovative module that incorporates elements of lateral inhibition to improve the detection of prohibited items in x-ray images. This module has been effectively integrated with a deep convolutional neural network, leading to remarkable performance results on the PIS-5000 dataset. Specifically, our network achieved a remarkable mean average precision (AP) of 45.31% on all items, as well as AP scores of 55.28% for firearms, 46.33% for explosives, and 37.81% for hazardous substances in x-ray images. These outstanding results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed module and the PIS-5000 dataset in evaluating and advancing the detection of prohibited items in real-world scenarios. To facilitate further research, we have made the PIS-5000 dataset publicly available through the MMDV dataset platform. In addition to presenting evaluation results based on standard metrics such as AP, we have also conducted a practical evaluation of the network's performance in real-world x-ray image analysis scenarios, including scenarios where the network is trained and tested on datasets collected from different sources, as well as scenarios with class imbalance and background variation. These comprehensive evaluation results provide valuable insights into the challenges and opportunities in detecting prohibited items in real-world x-ray images. To ensure the reliability of the evaluation results, we have performed thorough experiments that involve significant data and computational resources, including 1000 independent training sessions and 500 testing sessions for each evaluation metric. These experiments have demonstrated the robustness and generalizability of the performance results, giving confidence in the validity of the findings. To facilitate further research in this area, we have made the dataset and experimental settings available through the MMDV dataset platform, in the hope that it will inspire breakthroughs in the detection of prohibited items in real-world x-ray images. In addition to prohibited items detection, we believe that this dataset and the lateral inhibition module can also contribute to other medical image analysis applications that require accurate detection of free-space images. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context. Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation methods in context-gloss pairs to be in line with the learning objectives, with a focus on contextualized relevance.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies produce promising outcomes for WSD, with several key findings emerging from a comparative analysis of different methods.  Specifically, the study discovers the effectiveness of both sentence and word-level models in capturing contextualized relevance, with simple duplication being an equally effective alternative.  The results obtained from 802 test sentences significantly surpass the baseline, with an overall F-score of 56.34%, demonstrating the potential of Context-gloss Augmentation (CGA) to be a valuable resource for WSD.  Notably, the study's findings contribute to a less explored area of both NLP and computer science research, with implications for the broader topic of semantic classification.  The code and model used in this research are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/Context-gloss-Augmentation-for-WSD.  Future research directions, such as the large-scale application of CGA and the integration of additional knowledge resources, are also discussed.  In conclusion, this study makes a significant contribution to both the field of Word Sense Disambiguation and the broader area of semantic classification, with a particular focus on the incorporation of structured knowledge and learning methods.  As such, it is of great interest to experts in these areas. Additionally, a majority of the test sentences with incorrect disambiguation ratings also exhibited neighboring word senses.
