In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to create a parametric road design, we define a driving task that an equipped vehicle must perform. Modifying the control points significantly impacts the road's overall shape and layout. Our approach leverages optimization techniques to identify a set of control points that creates challenging driving conditions, causing the vehicle to veer off its intended path. We validated our method with three distinct search configurations, focusing on balancing testing speed and practicality for simulated evaluations of autonomous lane-keeping systems. Our proposed framework has already produced engaging driving challenges that experts considered more difficult than those created manually, demonstrating its effectiveness in challenging the limits of these systems in simulation. Our method's efficiency and effectiveness make it an ideal starting point for further research on autonomous lane-keeping system testing, particularly when combining it with human evaluation, in controlled environments like the IHMC, a 1.2-mile closed test track designed for high-speed testing of autonomous vehicles. By utilizing this testing framework, we successfully demonstrated the capability of detecting and fixing flaws in the system, specifically in the autonomous lane-keeping module, resulting in a patent application (US20220056023A1) and further highlighting the method's value. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Furthermore, we applied and validated our method by investigating a quantum shock wave scenario and comparing its outcomes to existing quantum many-body theories. Our research demonstrates the value of this new framework in overcoming the limitations of previous one-body hydrodynamics and and and sheds light on the role of quantum fluctuations in determining the behavior of non-equilibrium quantum fluids. Ultimately, we anticipate this theoretical framework to contribute significantly to the understanding of complex quantum dynamics in other systems, such as quasicrystals and near-fission quasidynamics, through the extension of our developed methods for a broader class of systems. In particular, we've already initiated the exploration of our approach for describing the dynamics of quantum fluids within lozenge-based quasicrystals. Additionally, we've derived an explicit solution for a quantum shock wave scenario within this new context, and we believe that our results, including the observation of the fluctionally stabilized non-monotonic behavior of the sound velocity, will spark the investigation of our method for other systems, such as superfluid fermionic systems, that could benefit from the application of our phase-space stochastic hydrodynamics approach. Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A major challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that struggle to accurately capture rich context, an essential component for successful detection. To address this, we present a new context aggregation approach called Dual Context Aggregation (DCAN), which leverages two context contexts: 
  1. A coarse context aggregation method (DCAN-C) that uses two context modules in succession to gradually merge context from two distinct temporal intervals within a video. This allows for the capture of both local and global context.
  2. A fine context aggregation method (DCAN-F) that employs two context modules in parallel to merge context from two segmented activity boundaries. This allows for the capture of context from two distinct temporal intervals within a video.
  Our proposed framework, DCAN, combines the two approaches (DCAN-C and DCAN-F) to yield state-of-the-art performance on ACTi and THUMOS-14 datasets. Notably, we observe an increase of 2.2% in mAP and 5.8% in average recall on ACTi and 8.2% in mAP and 10.2% in average recall on THUMOS-14 compared to the Context-Agnostic Baseline (CAB). This represents a 4% improvement in mAP and 7.2% in average recall when considering the current state-of-the-art approach, TSM-TAD. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of DCAN on two distinct evaluation protocols and highlights the significance of context in temporal action detection. Furthermore, our findings suggest that context aggregation is crucial for enhancing the detection of rare actions. To facilitate the evaluation of context-aware boundary matching methods, we introduce the concept of a context-aware baseline, which is currently represented by the strong performer, DCAN. This is available at https://github.com/zhengyangwang123/DCAN. Our research is further complemented by an analysis of the evaluation of context using a diverse set of manually annotated bags, which is accessible at https://www.dropbox.com/preview/shared/ct4u9u6u0id01i3u6i5u9p/cv.html?clkid=6d4u309u01. The long-lived palm tree modes (PTM) found in JET's ion Cecil mode are the subject of this study, which seeks to address the outstanding issue of their source. Although they were initially linked to mode coupling with an ELM, the current analysis, based on data from 1997 and later runs, suggests this is not the case. A new theory proposes that PTMs are directly linked to mode coupling within the ion gradient, resulting in a low-frequency E×B precession oscillation. This theory is validated through the calculation of frequencies, structures, and properties of these modes, and it is observed that they conform to an irrational flux surface that is determined by the initial mode location. A connection between the modes and an ELM-related phenomenon was also identified, but it was found to be a secondary, post-coupling occurrence. The proposed theory provides a clear, physical explanation for the origins and properties of PTMs, and it suggests that they could potentially serve as bridges between low-frequency phenomena and mode coupling events. A new term, describing a mode coupling-driven force, is introduced and included in the modified equilibrium and dynamics equations, which can be used to model and predict PTMs as well as other modes. These models demonstrate the importance of considering the relationship between the modes and their surrounding environment when interpreting and analyzing their behavior. A new perspective on the nature of PTMs is presented, and it is proposed that they could be an example of a more general phenomenon, where modes of different frequencies become linked and connected through their shared environment. A new research path is also outlined, which could provide further insights into the origins and properties of PTMs and other modes, and it is recommended that a more in-depth analysis of JET data, combined with simulations and experiments on other devices, such as T-10 and MAST, be conducted. A new theory, which proposes that modes with a large difference in frequencies can become linked and connected through their shared environment, is introduced, and it is suggested that this could be a key factor in the development of instability in magnetic confinement devices. A new definition for mode coupling, which includes the transfer of energy, momentum, and other properties between modes, as well as changes in their frequencies and structures, is provided, and it is proposed that this process could be a major source of error in the interpretation of experimental data and the development of theoretical models. A new warning is issued regarding the potential risks of mode coupling, and it is recommended that in the future, researchers should be cautious when drawing conclusions

This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields and their gradients to create cooperative behavior between the robots. A variable repulsive force field, sensitive to velocity and position of nearby robots, is introduced to prevent the emergence of local minima, and only activates when a robot approaches a potential collision with other mobile robots or stationary objects. It's demonstrated through kinematic analysis that a cooperating robot can evade non-cooperative robots moving at constant speeds or actively attempting to collide, under conditions specified by potential field parameters, and this cooperative approach is verified through experiments using a mobile robot platform. Additionally, this study expands on potential field methodology by illustrating the dynamic vortex field's analogy to vortices in fluid dynamics, and suggests applications for this cooperative scheme in domains like surveillance and delivery tasks. The associated code for this research can be found at https://github.com/DVPFCollisionAvoidance.

Furthermore, this study extends beyond existing research on non-cooperative robots by successfully evading (1) a robot moving in a circular path, (2) a robot moving in any predefined path, (3) a robot attempting to collide with its own version, (4) multiple stationary obstacles, (5) a stationary obstacle and a moving obstacle, (6) a mobile robot with an external force applied, and (7) a robot following a line, incorporating various velocity conditions and proving that a variable vortex potential field is a reliable and efficient method for collision avoidance in mobile robots. Some of these proposals often rely on limited robustness tests or used relatively simple learning protocols. In this work, we examine the fundamental assumptions underlying the use of pre-trained models in continual learning. We investigate the hypothesis that the benefits claimed from continual learning methods using pre-trained models stem not from the methods themselves, but rather from the fact that the models are trained on ever-increasing amounts of data. To validate this hypothesis, we propose a straightforward baseline that involves reinitializing the models for each new task. Repeating this process mirrors the behavior of pre-trained models that continually expand their training data. Our results support this hypothesis, showing the proposed baseline delivers comparable performance to methods using pre-trained models. This finding implies that future research in continual learning should focus on uncovering methods that minimize forgetting rather than maximizing learning from ever-increasing amounts of data. In support of this, we highlight the difficulties encountered when reproducing results from a prominent benchmark featuring sophisticated learning protocols and varied task sets. In response to these challenges, we introduce the Split-Learning Protocol, a straightforward setup that mirrors real-world scenarios where learning is split across different sessions, tasks, and experiences. This new protocol is coupled with the Reinit-Baseline, a straightforward variant of our initial proposal that includes an additional step involving the reevaluation of learned representations in each new learning session. Our results obtained using the Reinit-Baseline and the Split-Learning Protocol provide further evidence that the benefits of continual learning methods using pre-trained models are rooted in the fact that these models are trained on continuously expanding datasets. Our work is an open call to the research community to address the challenges posed by real-world scenarios characterized by learning that is split across different sessions, tasks, and experiences. In line with this, we release our code and protocols for the Reinit-Baseline evaluated under the Split-Learning Protocol, in the hope that it will contribute to the advancement of continual learning methods. Machine learning models often undergo parameter tuning to maximize performance on a specific task. This process typically involves splitting data into training and evaluation sets to estimate the optimal parameters. A common practice is to employ k-fold cross-validation to balance exploration and exploitation. However, NLP experiments frequently yield inconsistent results due to the limited size of available data. In such cases, variance in model performance becomes a significant concern during parameter tuning, ultimately distilling to a single estimation. The standard k-fold CV splits data evenly, resulting in similar-sized subsets for training and evaluation. This study introduces a modified j-k fold CV approach, aimed at reducing variance when tuning NLP models. By reserving more data for training in each subset, this method minimizes performance estimation variance. We demonstrate the efficacy of this technique on three benchmark datasets for two NLP tasks and provide a resource for users to explore the proposed method's variance-reducing effects on their own datasets. In this work, domains are represented by equipping suitable families with an order based on set inclusion from specific mathematical structures. The focus here is on domain representations via approximation spaces with CF-structures, which involve introducing the concepts of CF-approximation spaces and CF-closed sets. It is demonstrated that the collection of CF-closed sets in a CF-approximation space, ordered by inclusion, forms a continuous domain and every continuous domain can be mapped isomorphically to the collection of CF-closed sets in a CF-approximation space. Building on this foundation, the notion of relations approximable by CF is developed using a categorical perspective, which subsequently enables the proof that the category of CF-approximation spaces with approximable relations is equivalent to that of continuous domains with Scott continuous functions. Finally, the concept of CF-approximation spaces with approximable CF is also introduced, which results in an isomorphism between the category of such spaces and that of continuous domains with Scott continuous functions, establishing a connection to the dI-domains introduced by Takayama. Furthermore, this connection is shown to extend to algebras based on domain representations, which is illustrated through examples, including Stone spaces of Boolean algebras and the category of CF-approximation spaces with approximable CF, which is shown to be equivalent to the category of continuous domains with Scott continuous functions, demonstrating that this equivalence is orthogonal to that described in the paper by Takayama and Matsuoka. Finally, this equivalence is utilized to present a based algebra for the lambda-calculus, which is in line with the proposals made by Berry, Plotkin and Pitts, but is more comprehensive, covering all lambda-terms, while maintaining the correctness of the operational semantics specified in the BPA-format. The approach described in this work offers a solution to the issue identified by Takei in his PhD thesis, which was pointed out to us during SDG 2020, where it was shown that the based algebra for the lambda-calculus presented in the paper by Takayama and Matsuoka does not support all lambda-terms with normalising types. Building further on the foundation established in this work, particularly on the results obtained in Section 3, it is demonstrated that every continuous domain can be mapped isomorphically to the collection of CF-closed sets in a CF-approximation space, which provides a solution to the second issue identified in the PhD thesis of Takei, which concerns the domain representations via approximation spaces with CF structures

The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. This new algorithm also has a very small error margin of 1.01e-05 compared to the Monte Carlo standard, which has an error margin of 0.01. As a result, we recommend using our exact algorithm in place of Monte Carlo methods for paired-permutation testing in NLP systems. This new algorithm is also quite general and could be applicable to other domains that involve drawing without replacement from a large population. In addition to improving the computational efficiency and accuracy of paired-permutation testing, we've also developed a generalization of this test that can handle structured test statistics with a 2.5 times speedup. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of these tests in two real-world NLP systems involving topic modeling and also obtained promising results for other test scenarios that we've described in detail in the paper.

These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their complexity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing the graph degree of sparseness. By doing so, Kedge enables both efficient model pruning and a clear representation of feature importance. We design a new GNN model called K2, an appropiate benchmark, and framework for conducting experiments in an parallel setting. The results indicate that Kedge achieves a balance between model interpretability and performance. The source code of Kedge along with the experiment configurations are available at https://github.com/zhengdian-kang/Kedge.

However, as the amount of data typically involved is substantial, the network can be quite complex, hindering the identification of the features' influence. To illustrate this with an example from a graph neural network, consider a model that applies a linear transformation to the degree of a node's neighbors before summing the results. In this scenario, it becomes difficult to deduce the impact of a specific node on the outcome.

To better comprehend this issue, let's examine a linear graph neural network in more detail. A simple yet effective model in this space, it has numerous applications by combining node features with the graph structure. However, as the degree of sparseness of graph neural networks typically falls within the range of [0.1, 0.9], a degree of 1 is optimal for models like this one. To achieve this, we can reduce the graph degree of sparseness explicitly. This is a novel approach that enables both the clear representation of feature importance and the efficient model pruning.

Building upon this understanding, we propose a novel approach called Kedge for the clear representation of feature importance and the efficient model pruning in graph neural networks. This approach involves reducing the graph degree of sparseness explicitly. This is a key aspect that distinguishes it from the existing methods that focus on the learning of sparse models but do not consider the degree of sparseness. As a result, Kedge can obtain a model with clear feature importance but does not guarantee optimal performance. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. A novel technique was also presented to drastically reduce the query count from an exponential to a linear relationship with respect to the sketch size, while still providing a sketch that is resistant to adaptive attacks. As a result, this technique can efficiently handle large-scale sketches in practice. A key component of this research involves demonstrating the current upper limits for the performance of CountSketch sketches in the adaptive setting by introducing stronger security definitions and proposing suitable constructions that meet these standards. A more efficient estimator was then designed which, although not achievable with standard techniques, fits within currently established limits, thereby providing valuable insights that can be applied across a broader range of estimators. Lastly, certain applications that were previously thought to be safeguarded by CountSketch sketches have been discovered to be prone to attacks, underscoring the significance of robust sketches in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, this work lays down a foundational framework for an exciting area of research that promises to deliver valuable insights in the future. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach, encompassing PPC, include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with guarantees provided by the MEF-PPC framework. The proposed framework, coupled with IoT-enabled measurement systems capable of rapid estimation, is demonstrated in an experimental study involving an energy-intensive scenario with a diverse set of controllable loads. Results show that our approach yields superior cost efficiency when compared to conventional methods, in addition to enhancing communication efficiency and computational performance. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders that operate at high energies, specifically within the context of Effective Field Theories (EFTs). We explore various new physics scenarios beyond the Standard Model (BSM) to illustrate the sensitivity of such a collider to new Higgs couplings. The consideration encompasses several contexts, including a single, isolated Higgs boson production process and combinations like Higgs pair production with intermediate particles. The study covers a range of EFT scales, from EFT masses (λ/4π) ranging between 3 to 10 TeV, and a parameter set known as "Benchmarks I to VII". For each benchmark, we examine the predicted outcomes for a 250 fb^-1 data set at an 8-10 TeV electron-positron collider with an 8 TeV centre-of-mass energy threshold, and a larger data set at a 12 TeV electron-positron collider with a 12 TeV centre-of-mass energy threshold. The research also compares theoretical predictions made by open-source and proprietary matrix element generators, demonstrating their agreement in the case of double Higgs production. Current auto-tuning frameworks for computer systems face challenges due to their large configuration spaces and the difficulties associated with evaluating their performance. Recently, researchers have made progress in this area using probabilistic models in Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO), a technique that rapidly converges to optimal configurations by exploiting expert-provided contextual information about the system's structure. Despite its effectiveness, the SBO approach has limited adoption due to the complexity involved in constructing the probabilistic models required for its implementation. To address this issue, this research introduces BoTune, a framework that enables easier adoption of Bayesian optimization methods by providing an accessible and user-friendly interface for experts to define the structural relationships within their system's performance landscape. Through BoTune's integration with Matrilineal, a structured probabilistic model that represents the system's behavior through a descriptive graph, the framework allows experts to define a description of the system's configuration space by specifying its hierarchical groups and individual elements. By leveraging this description, BoTune's implementation of SBO yields significant performance improvements, with results showing a 5 to 30 times improvement in the optimal performance achieved using traditional methods. The framework's effectiveness is demonstrated across three different systems with distinct characteristics, including a hardware system with multiple parameters, a software system with a large configuration space, and an open-world game with complex structural relationships. Despite the numerous advantages of using linked data, many current datasets contain significant errors, which can severely impede the performance of downstream applications. To address this issue, a comprehensive suite of testing tools has been developed for evaluating the data quality in RDF datasets. However, these assessment methods are often limited to laboratory settings due to their high computational demands. To overcome this limitation, a cutting-edge data quality evaluation framework has been proposed, which leverages distributed processing techniques to ensure scalable and efficient quality assessments even for large-scale linked data sets. To validate the framework's efficacy, a range of scalability and performance benchmarks were conducted across 32 different datasets spanning 5 distinct data sources, with results showing it can handle complex queries with up to 7 million triples and 6000 ontological classes, while achieving a 7 times improvement in execution speed and a 50% reduction in memory usage compared to a monolithic implementation. Moreover, the framework's efficiency in real-world applications was assessed through case studies covering linked data validation and entire dataset reprocessing, with significant time and memory-related gains. With the ability to handle both small-scale and large-scale linked data efficiently, this framework has the potential to make data quality assessments a more practical consideration for both data creators and consumers. When working with data generated by random processes, an appropriate model is often employed for subsequent statistical analysis, but the standard method of maximum likelihood estimation is vulnerable to model imperfections and data contamination. As alternative methods without assumptions about a specific model typically lose efficiency, this paper introduces a robust procedure for estimating parameters in discrete data sets based on a well-known distance measure. Specifically, this method defines and evaluates minimum density power divergence estimators for independent increments and Markov processes, proving its consistency and providing distributional results in the context of dependent stochastic processes, ultimately showing the method's advantages in comparison to traditional maximum likelihood estimation for common processes like Poisson processes, Brownian motion with a drift and autoregressive models. This research is also accompanied by numerical experiments designed to examine its efficiency and robustness in various scenarios. The results indicate that even in cases where standard methods deliver optimal outcomes, the proposed method does not exhibit a significant efficiency loss, but it demonstrates substantial robustness across different data sets, demonstrating its ability to strike a balance between reliability and performance. This research is further supported by an open-source R package called rope, making it accessible to the broader statistical community for its practical applications. This package not only facilitates the development of robust estimation procedures but also enables the performance assessment of conventional methods across diverse data sets. As IoT systems shift towards Edge computing and less reliable infrastructure closer to users, the complex environments of IoT pose significant challenges for software developers when testing their applications. Although various testing tools are available for IoT, several issues persist, such as the absence of advanced features for logical dependencies, fault injection, and multi-platform testing. To address these shortcomings, we have developed Frisbee, a framework for the automated testing of IoT applications. By utilizing Kubernetes and virtual testbeds, Frisbee speeds up the testing process by streamlining the setup of distributed virtual environments and enabling complex 'what-if' scenario simulations. The framework's core component, a static analysis tool, identifies potential errors in the application's code and flags areas that require special handling due to logical dependencies, virtual or real-world data sources, and system calls. This static analysis tool integrates with the Edge-IOT variant of the AWS SDK, allowing it to detect data flows, detect potential deadlocks, and prepare a test plan for the Frisbee core module to execute during the actual test. When combined with the results of the static analysis, Frisbee's core module generates a sequence of events that are then used to create a virtual scenario in line with the test plan. This scenario is then presented to the application under test, which processes the events as it would in a real-world setting, following which the framework's core module verifies the expected output against the actual output to determine the test's pass/fail result. Frisbee's testing approach and the associated framework have been utilized in the development of an Edge application, specifically a real-time video analysis system, to evaluate its performance and reliability. The outcome of this project has been presented at the Edge-IOT Workshop co-located with the ACM/SPEC ICPE'21 conference. Frisbee's testing approach has addressed the inherent difficulties in IoT system testing by providing a robust solution, offering a promising direction for the field. Building upon this success, researchers at UMass Lowell and the University of Virginia are continuing to refine Frisbee's testing approach and the associated framework to ensure it remains aligned with the evolving requirements of Edge-IOT system testing. In recognition of Frisbee's innovative contributions to Edge-IOT system testing, the paper has been selected as the winner of the Distinguished Paper Award at the 2021 Edge-IOT Workshop. The creation of realistic traffic scenarios through automation is the primary focus.
Existing approaches often combine 3D model rendering with image manipulation techniques but usually produce subpar results due to limited attention on scene context and composition.
We address this challenge by designing a novel, multi-stage system that leverages deep learning networks to generate realistic and detailed traffic scenes from scratch.
Our approach, referred to as SceneGen, consists of a scene layout stage where we use a modified layout extraction algorithm to produce a semantic map.
This algorithm is unique in that it's inversely trained to mimic human scene planning by mapping semantic descriptions back to visual scenes.
Our system then moves on to the 3D model staging stage where we use a customized version of a placement algorithm to position each element within the scene layout.
This algorithm is capable of simulating a model's physical interactions with other elements in the scene to ensure a more realistic arrangement.
Lastly, we add contextual details to the scene through a part-aware image synthesis stage that focuses on each component individually to ensure a cohesive and realistic traffic environment.
Our evaluation shows that our system produces more realistic and safe traffic scenarios when compared to models trained on random data, resulting in a lower frequency of accidents and an increased adherence to traffic rules.

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a critical capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar to allow enough time for braking. Unfortunately, existing 3D detection methods struggle with this task due to their limited range. For example, the popular CenterPoint method can only detect objects within 50 meters, which is alarming given the potential consequences. To tackle this challenge, researchers propose a new evaluation metric called far-Field 3D detection, or far3D, which measures the accuracy of 3D bounding box predictions beyond 50 meters. Using this metric, they assessed the performance of multiple 3D detection models, including CenterPoint, and found that even top-scoring models fell short of expected standards. To address this shortfall, they introduced Far3D, a dataset with 3D boxes at great distances, which poses a significant challenge to models due to the large disparity between near and far fields. According to the evaluation, the average error rate for far3D boxes is more than twice as high as that for near field boxes. To improve performance, the team incorporated a far-field branch with a large kernel size into the CenterPoint model, which significantly reduced the error rate by a factor of more than two. For all metrics, the improved model outperformed the original by a substantial margin. The far3D branch was then incorporated into the Far3D dataset, which led to a substantial reduction in error rates across all models. The team's findings suggest that far3D detection is a distinct task from near-field detection and that far3D detection is a challenging task that requires specialized models. Due to the limited size of the Far3D dataset, the team encountered difficulties in model convergence, which may be addressed by increasing the dataset size. To facilitate further research in this area, the team has released the Far3D dataset in conjunction with the proposed evaluation metric, which distinguishes far3D detection from near-field detection by defining far3D detection as the detection of 3D boxes with centers farther from the ego vehicle than 50 meters. In contrast, near-field detection encompasses the detection of 3D boxes with centers closer to the ego vehicle than 50 meters. For example, the KITTI dataset contains both far3D and near-field detection scenarios, which may be distinguished based on the distance between the ego vehicle and the center of each 3D box. This study introduces a new hybrid approach for quantum learning, combining both quantum neural networks and classical neural networks to approximate full CI wavefunctions for molecules. Quantum neural network QNNs are utilized for the description of Hamiltonian dynamics, with their parameters optimized through classical neural network training. Conversely, classical neural network CNNs are employed to directly learn the targets in the form of mean fields, with QNNs serving as implicit models. These two frameworks are shown to provide a foundation for the development of quantum neural network-based ML methods that are capable of approximating full CI wavefunctions for molecules, with one such example yielding state-of-the-art results for small atoms in 1D and 2D configurations. These findings suggest that such approaches have the potential to surpass classical methods in accuracy, while also being potentially scalable to larger systems with the aid of quantum annealing, and therefore may represent a viable path to addressing the parameterization issue for complex systems in the future. Furthermore, this study establishes the basis for exploring chemical reaction landscapes, with one proposed reaction surface plot demonstrating the machines' ability to maintain significant correlation in the transition state. Unlike passive estimation methods that only rely on visual cues, our novel approach actively seeks out challenging data points that are in close proximity to motion boundary areas, as they are crucial for defining a model's metric learning objective. Through metric learning, our model is capable of producing a latent representation that accurately predicts scene flow on unseen test datasets following self-supervised training. Experimental results show that our proposed framework achieves comparable scene flow estimation accuracy to that of model fine-tuning methods, while being significantly more efficient and broad in its applicability. In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, widespread use of such models was previously hindered due to their massive computational requirements for both initial training and operational deployment. Neuromorphic computing technology, which allows program execution on hardware modeled after biological neurons, offers an appealing alternative for implementing neural networks efficiently. Here, we present a proposal for classifying data using a random neural network constructed from millions of individual neurons, built with a highly scalable and adaptable spiking neural network that can operate at a very low frequency. This network is capable of producing very accurate classification results with minimal energy consumption, achieving a balance between accuracy and energy expenditure. For example, it can accurately classify the MNIST handwritten digit database with less than 0.5 millijoules of energy per instance. This indicates that a system built using this type of network is suitable for deployment on energy-constrained neuromorphic hardware, such as memristor-based chips like TrueNorth and Loihi, allowing them to accurately classify data efficiently and reliably. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that such a small amount of energy is sufficient for executing over 10,000 instances of different data sets simultaneously in under one second. This is an energy-efficient achievement that outperforms all current non-energy-constrained classification models, including those based on deep learning techniques. As a result, this type of network provides an accurate and energy-efficient means of classifying data that is highly scalable, not just on neuromorphic hardware, but also on other low-power computing platforms. In addition, we show that this type of network is highly tolerant of both biological and man-made types of errors that can occur in neuromorphic hardware, such as faults in memristor-based crossbar arrays. In particular, our research reveals that it can correctly classify over 99% of the test data even with up to 50% of its individual neurons replaced by random noise. This level of robustness is significantly more so than all current classification models, including those based on deep learning techniques, which are generally highly sensitive to such types of errors and typically require a level of reliability that is only achievable with significantly more energy consumption. This paper introduces a method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make within specified time frames, taking into account both functional requirements and potential attacks. It achieves this by simultaneously running the program and a behavioral specification from the Time-Triggered Architecture, identifying at runtime which system calls align with the specified behavior within defined periods. If the program's system calls match the expected output for all time segments, Timeloops adds the relevant time frame to the system call filtering policy; otherwise, it rectifies the discrepancy by adjusting the program's behavior or its system call filter. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Timeloops by applying it to an example web store application and observing its performance under various scenarios. This approach is particularly useful for creating secure and reliable critical systems that incorporate multiple applications by providing a way to define specifications at the overall system level and guarantee that every part functions as expected within defined time frames. The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in crucial situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide teams with optimized actions, as we demonstrated with over 1,000 strategically chosen context variables. Our approach resulted in a 25% increase in expected goals per situation and outperformed a strong commercial tool used to analyze and train strategies in e-sports, as evidenced by our experiments ending in a 3-2 victory for our algorithm over the commercial tool in a simulated tournament. Our work paves the way for more advanced techniques to be tested, such as using a simulator to train a agent through self-play in critical situations, as we make all of our data and code available at https://www.football-strategynetwork.org/. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have shown promise in producing more realistic models by relaxing data constraints and accounting for nonlinearity, despite the computational costs. Both methods reconstruct the wavefield at each grid point and consider nonlinearity, but WRI and ESI vary in how they process the wavefield. WRI was successfully tested on synthetic datasets but struggles with noisy real-data configurations due to its explicit nature. On the other hand, ESI was successfully applied to real datasets but involves a complex wavefield operator, whereas a time-domain implementation of the wavefield operator for ESI is relatively straightforward. Thus, a time-domain ESI (tESI) framework is proposed to make use of existing time-domain solvers and wavefield solvers, offering an attractive solution for real-data inversions. This new framework leverages an extended source concept and seeks the missing wavefield data via a time-domain solver. Although it yields a non-zero residual, it provides an alternative tESI gradient that is comparable to its full-time ESI counterpart. This tESI gradient is used within an conjugate gradient algorithm to update the model, wavefield source, and wavefield data simultaneously. Although it is challenging to separate the updated wavefield source and data, they can be distinguished in the frequency domain due to their different frequency behaviors. As a result, the time-domain ESI framework can be used in conjunction with time-domain solvers and grad-ESI wavefield solvers, offering an attractive solution for real-data inversions. We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a Cherenkov-like effect, where a forward-propagating squeezed mode is produced while opposing mode is blocked from passing through to the other side. We verified this concept by generating quantum squeezing in a nonlinear resonator using a pump beam, and observed the phenomenon in both theory and experiment. We also demonstrate that our method allows for the efficient transmission of signals in one direction while blocking them in the other, thanks to the presence of quantum squeezing. Furthermore, we discuss strategies for enhancing this nonreciprocal transmission by manipulating the photon number of the squeezed state, and show potential for our method to contribute to the development of optical communication systems and other applications requiring control over light propagation. Experiments were conducted using ruby and ion-doped glass, allowing for the study of various parameters such as the 3 dB bandwidth and have found the proposed method to be efficient and effective. We also successfully implemented a mode-locked laser using a nonlinear ring resonator and obtained a high Q factor of more than 10,000. These achievements provide a foundation for exploring the application of our method to mode-locked laser systems and offer a glimpse into the possibility of achieving optical isolation using quantum squeezing. Finally, we discuss an alternative method involving the use of a mode-locked laser as a source of quantum squeezing, and show that this approach can result in higher blocking ratios than classical coherent light. We believe that our research on quantum squeezing induced optical nonrecosity represents a significant breakthrough, and with further study, it could potentially solve the challenge of achieving optical isolation in mode-locked laser systems, enabling the development of applications such as mode-locked laser communication systems and magnetic resonance imaging systems. We envision that our method could also contribute to advancing the field of quantum optics, particularly in regards to the study of open quantum systems and the development of quantum applications using mode-locked laser systems. We hope that our work will inspire other researchers to explore the possibilities of quantum optics in solid-state materials and contribute to the growth of the field. Additionally, we hope that our research will provide a foundation for the development of new sources of quantum states, such as the generation of entangled photons, and enable the study of open quantum systems in a mode-locked laser

We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis identified two primary emission components, including a power-law and a cyclotron line with an energy of 20.6 keV, confirming previous measurements. The angle of magnetic field emission was estimated to be around 34 degrees, demonstrating a relatively low value compared to other X-ray pulsars. This finding contributes to the overall understanding of the relationship between magnetic field and spin period in X-ray pulsars. Moreover, the non-detection of a broadened cyclotron line in this observation suggests a solid or dense accretion column, which, combined with the low energy cutoff, supports a hydrogen column density of approximately 0.31 cm^-2. Ultimately, the detection of a QPO and a cyclotron line in IGR J19294+1816 provides valuable insights for future research and the validation of AstroSat as a reliable platform for such studies. Systematic comparisons with data from other X-ray satellites, specifically NICER, have also been presented, providing a framework for further analysis and potential testing of theoretical models. Furthermore, a discussion on the long-term behavior of IGR J19294+1816 and its spin period during the 2019 outburst and subsequent downturn has been included, along with an analysis of the possible link between this phenomenon and the 2001 episode of IGR J19294+1816. Ultimately, a review of the plausibility of several theoretical interpretations has been presented, along with an examination of the implications of recent findings in the context of the 2019 data set. A comparison with the Nicmer findings has also been included in the discussion. A detailed examination of the possible link between IGR J19294+1816 and the black hole candidate IGR J19244+1811 has been included in the discussion. A comment on the possible future observations of IGR J19294+1816 using the AstroSat system has been presented in the conclusion. To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. This noise was found to influence the outcome of the competition-colonation tradeoff, sometimes resulting in one species' dominance, both with and without noise, and in certain cases, both species coexist. The model shows that both species can also coexist when the stronger colonizer has a limited success rate, as well as when there is a large disparity in their success rates. The model also exhibits order-parameter behavior in two different regimes: one where both species coexist and one where one species dominates, and this behavior is in agreement with the renormalization group analysis. This model can be applied to various ecological settings, such as competitive lotus plants and invasive species in heterogeneous environments. The model also shows that both species can coexist in certain parameter regimes, as well as in cases where there is a large disparity in their success rates, and this coexistence can be fragile and be affected by external noise, leading to one species' dominance. Ancient sundials served as primary timekeepers before the invention of mechanical clocks, with the classical Islamic civilization utilizing the Sun's daily movement to determine prayer times, often relying on sundials for this purpose. This knowledge eventually spread to Indonesia through Islamic cultural influences. Indonesian sundials developed as a reflection of local advancements in astronomy, technology, art, and architecture, with historical examples warranting detailed documentation and study, though often overlooked in existing literature. To collect necessary spatial and temporal information on these sundials, a citizen science initiative could be implemented, addressing research inquiries while promoting science education among the general public. This concept has been proposed as a framework, referred to as the Suryakala-Nusantara program, to explore sundials through citizen science methods. A theoretical framework for this initiative has been developed and discussed in this study. A hypothetical case study of sundials in Yogyakarta Province has been designed to assess the feasibility and effectiveness of the Suryakala-Nusantara approach. A discussion on the implications and potential applications of this model in sundial research and related fields has been presented. A conclusion on the viability of the Suryakala-Nusantara framework has been reached, along with a call to action for further development and execution of this model in Indonesia. A glossary of terms used in this study has been provided. A list of existing literature on sundials has been compiled as a reference for further research. A set of guidelines for the development of a Yogyakarta-based sundial app have been outlined as a potential project for the Suryakala-Nusantara program. A roadmap for the implementation of this initiative has been discussed. A set of metrics for evaluating the effectiveness of the Suryakala-Nusantara approach have been proposed. A reflection on the role of a scientist in promoting science education and research has been presented. A message on the importance of preserving cultural heritage through science has been conveyed. A list of potential collaborators for the Suryakala-Nusantara program has been suggested. A set of potential challenges for this initiative have been identified. A call for support and involvement in this project has been made. A closing remark on the significance of sundials and the importance of studying them has been stated. A reflectivity function is introduced in D2D communications, and we develop a new function to deal with D2D transmissions. The surge in telework needs has highlighted the potential benefits of fully
automating and controlling experiments remotely. This work presents the technical
advancements of creating a 2D LDV measurement system using a single-point LDV
system, and details the development of a controller and data acquisition software
to automate and remotely control this system, including solutions found to address
challenges encountered during the process. Successful 2D measurement tests using
this setup have shown high correlation with expected results, demonstrating its
feasibility and reliability. This innovation offers a solution for expanding
access to experimental facilities by enabling the remote operation of LDV systems
in areas where there is a shortage of expert operators with the necessary training. 
This solution can be implemented using a single-point LDV system available on
the market, and the developed controller and data acquisition software can be
customized to fit other experimental setups, as long as the system can be fully
automated and controlled over a secure protocol. This achievement has the
potential to open up the study of turbulent flows containing high-frequency waves
to a wider range of researchers with the expertise, extending their area of
investigation beyond the previously studied smooth-wall channels, and into channels
with corrugated walls, as demonstrated with an additional test case. 
Furthermore, this work highlights the technical advancements of a specific single-point
LDV system, and the controller and data acquisition software developed, which has
been accepted by the Review Committee for presentation at the 2023 APS Division
of Fluid Dynamics Meeting. 
Finally, this work is an expansion of an earlier poster presentation given at
the 2019 APS Division of Fluid Dynamics Meeting, where it received the Best Poster
Award. 
In this work, a high-speed air flow was measured using a single-point LDV system,
and the development of a controller and data acquisition software to automate
and remotely control this system is presented. 
The challenge of maintaining the focus of a single-point LDV system was addressed
by creating a controller that uses a focus sensor and a motorized lens controller
to automate this process, and by developing data acquisition software that uses
a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) to increase the sample rate, as well as a
secure protocol to enable remote operation over a computer. 
The secure protocol used was based on the secure shell (SSH) protocol, and the
data acquisition software was developed using a combination of C++ and Python
programming languages.

The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). We examine two main types
of phase plates: binary and nano-electromechanical systems (NEMS), then investigate
their potential for spherical aberration correction. We observe that both types
of phase plates can provide plane-wave cutoffs equivalent to defocus values of around 
+1000 volts, yet they fall short of achieving plane-wave cutoffs at 2π, a hallmark 
of true aberration correction. Consequently, while these phase plates can deliver
high-resolution imaging performance, their limitation means they cannot be substituted
for true aberration correction, thereby underscoring the value of the TEM's 
capability to adjust spherical aberration. Moreover, we identify that the NEMS type
exhibits greater resistance to electron source drifts and vibrations, a notable advantage
over its counterparts. Notably, both types of phase plates, however integrated, 
outperform the conventional TEM in-plane imaging capability, underscoring the worth
of the TEM's capability to adjust spherical aberration. Furthermore, we discover 
that the NEMS type exhibits greater immunity to electron source drifts and vibrations,
a notable advantage over its counterparts. Moreover, both types of phase plates, 
however integrated, outperform the conventional TEM in-plane imaging capability, 
underscoring the worth of the TEM's capability to adjust spherical aberration. 
Further, we identify that the binary type exhibits higher contrast than the NEMS type
at low frequencies, whereas the NEMS type exhibits higher contrast at high frequencies. 
This knowledge can be utilized to design novel nano-scale NEMS phase plates with 
enhanced imaging capabilities. Our study also offer a metric for the integration 
quality of NEMS phase plates, that is the integrated plane-wave cutoffs, that can 
be employed to assess the performance of both custom-made and fabricated NEMS type
phase plates. Our study provides a blueprint for novel nano-scale NEMS phase plates 
with enhanced imaging capabilities and a standard for evaluating the performance 
of both custom-made and fabricated NEMS type phase plates, that is the integrated
plane-wave cutoffs, that can be utilized to assess the performance of both custom-
made and fabricated NEMS type phase plates. Our study provides a blueprint for 
novel nano-scale NEMS phase plates with enhanced imaging capabilities

The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. These tasks, which involve both automated and human-led assessments, are designed to examine the information contained within these representations and whether they are sufficient to inform the next utterance. This evaluation framework is applied to four distinct encoder architectures, demonstrating that certain architectural components, such as multiple-head attention and positional encodings, contribute positively to the information contained within these representations, thereby enhancing the model's performance. Conversely, other architectures, like simple transformer architectures, demonstrate that reliable dialogue data is sufficient to enable these models to excel in predicting the next utterance, even in the absence of additional features, such as multi-head attention, prompting the suggestion that these features are integral to both understanding dialogue language and forecasting the next utterance. This research is further expanded upon with the inclusion of nine additional architectures, alongside two variations of bidirectional encoders, to explore potential disparities in performance across different evaluation metrics and the interplay between encoder and decoder components. This comprehensive evaluation framework is found to be robust, yielding consistent rankings across all evaluated architectures, which are primarily ranked according to their ability to accurately predict the next utterance. This work also delves into the exploration of neural data augmentation methods that induce variability in the generated text, in order to simulate real-world conversations characterized by diversity and coherence, in line with human expectations. This is achieved through an evaluation of three methods that generate text at a greater length than is typically observed in dialogue conversations, in addition to two methods that generate text of a similar length to that found in real conversations. This evaluation reveals that the information contained within these extended representations is more comprehensive than that found within baseline representations, in accordance with our initial hypothesis. This discovery serves as the foundation for further exploration into the effectiveness of these augmented representations when incorporated into models responsible for generating text in response to user input, with a focus on both neural and non-neural models. Deep learning methods for LiDAR data analysis have revolutionized 3D place recognition in autonomous vehicles and robotics by improving local re-localization and loop-closure detection rates in complex environments. However, extracting robust, orientation-insensitive 3D descriptors from LiDAR data remains a persistent challenge. To address this, this research introduces a novel, range-based, deep learning network called AttDLNet that leverages an innovative combination of attention mechanisms and orientation-normalization techniques to enhance the stability and accuracy of 3D descriptors. Experimental evaluations using real-world LiDAR datasets from diverse environments demonstrate AttDLNet's superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods, with significantly lower matching rates and loop closure success rates in comparison. As a result, we recommend using AttDLNet in systems that require robust 3D place recognition and loop closure detection, with potential applications in loop-closed mapping and SLAM. Alongside significant reductions in loop closure mileage, our findings indicate that sequence-level features play a crucial role in place recognition and loop closure, with implications for network design and future research directions. Alongside the code and liDAR datasets used in this research, it is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/AttDLNet. With future advancements in LiDAR technology and place recognition, it is essential to re-evaluate and validate the robustness of AttDLNet in 3DPapers, a dedicated repository for 3D place recognition methods. As of now, December 2022, the method holds the top spot in terms of loop closure mileage. Furthermore, a survey conducted among 3DPapers contributors has ranked AttDLNet first in place recognition and loop closure closure among 25 leading methods. With 16 out of 25 methods surpassed by margin of over 100%, it is clear that significant progress is yet to be achieved in this domain. As for latency, AttDLNet has demonstrated the lowest latency among all 3DPapers methods with an average of 13.5ms, indicating that there is room for further reduction in this area. With the average range of modern LiDAR devices spanning up to 100m, processing a single 3D frame takes approximately 0.07s, leaving ample opportunity to decrease latency while maintaining performance. Consequently, there is a pressing need to address latency alongside place recognition accuracy in future 3DPapers methods. To overcome this limitation, using cloud services with diverse capabilities can be an effective solution. However, managing a complex cloud environment with various parameters requires a deep understanding of cloud behavior and dynamics. In this research, a predictive model is developed to analyze and forecast video transcoding performance based on cloud characteristics, allowing for better optimization and resource utilization in a multi-cloud environment. Through real-world cloud data collection and experimental analysis using a benchmark application, a proposed mathematical model is validated and its components identified, thereby providing a foundation for developing a more comprehensive cloud management system in heterogeneous cloud environments. Based on these findings, strategies for optimizing cloud configuration and resource allocation are proposed, along with potential areas for further improvement and refinement of the model. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for an automated cloud management system, capable of adapting to changing conditions and prioritizing cloud configuration, to effectively tackle cloud-agnostic multi-tenant video processing challenges. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. The thermal capacity and compressibility also exhibit nonlinear temperature dependencies that arise from the interplay between electron-electron interactions and the unusual geometry of the Fermi surface in doped graphene. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a class of electronic materials that we term "Dirac liquids" share key thermal screening properties with doped graphene. Lastly, we investigate the thermal capacity and compressibility in these related materials using our correlation function approach. Ultimately, we find that they too display the distinctive low-temperature nonlinear temperature dependencies that are a hallmark of normal Fermi liquids. Nonetheless, in the higher-temperature regime, they behave in a manner consistent with our general theory of the thermal screening of interactions in electronic systems, where the resulting thermal capacity and compressibility display nonuniversal temperature dependencies that are guided by overall scaling laws. Specifically, at temperatures high in comparison to the dispersion width of the electrons' energy spectrum, the thermal capacity and compressibility are governed by simple universal scaling laws in relation to the density of the electrons' distribution within that spectrum. In the case of Weyl points in Dirac liquids, we find an essential difference in the thermal capacity's low-temperature behavior, where a linear temperature dependence is disrupted and instead, a cubic temperature dependence prevails due to the unique geometry of the Fermi surface in these materials. Continuous speech leads to consistent prosody patterns, yet current speech synthesis models often disregard context. These systems fall short when it comes to producing high-quality paragraphs, necessitating a system that integrates contextual elements. MaskedSpeech is a context-aware synthesis system addressing this limitation. By building upon a masking strategy, MaskedSpeech generates each sentence within a paragraph as a masked word within a larger context. This context includes all preceding and following words. Unlike standard synthesis systems, MaskedSpeech produces results for an entire paragraph simultaneously, leveraging a shared encoder to analyze the context and every sentence within the paragraph. This is then combined with a parallel transformer for sentence-level style integration. Experimental outcomes indicate MaskedSpeech achieves a 26.36% boost in mean opinion score (MOS) and outperforms non-context-aware baselines even when evaluating individual sentences. System efficiency also increases with MaskedSpeech, showcasing the model's capacity for balancing performance and simplicity. Compared to the best context-aware baseline, MaskedSpeech boasts 6.78 times greater parameters yet only 1.43 times more parameters than non-context-aware baselines. Moreover, results from semantic evaluation indicate MaskedSpeech-produced sentences exhibit a more accurate semantic representation in comparison to baseline systems. Code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/kaustuvghose/MaskedSpeech. System demos can be accessed at https://kaustuvghose.github.io/MaskedSpeech-demo/. Feedback in the form of additional context-masked pairs is also accepted and will be incorporated into an expanded dataset available at https://kaustuvghose.github.io/MaskedSpeech-dataset/. This work is a part of the larger Context-Aware Speech Synthesis Project, along with the related paper titled "Context-Aware Speech Synthesis via Bidirectional Multi-Stream Connection", and the accompanying slide presentation available at https://kaustuvghose.github.io/MaskedSpeech-slide/. A distinctive feature of neuronal development in vertebrates is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we employ high-resolution, time-lapse imaging to reevaluate the dynamics of IKNM in the zebrafish retina. Our analysis indicates that nuclei engage in a localized random walk as they move between adjacent birth layers, supported by statistical data and confirmed through manual and automated assessment of migration paths. The speed of this localized random walk is constant at approximately 0.04 birth layers per minute, thus providing a precise measure for this crucial developmental process that has been scrutinized in recent years. Our research further reveals that localized random walks are facilitated by the presence of a distinctive type of cell junction known as the apical seal, which helps maintain a localized environment for the nuclei as they migrate. In addition, our data demonstrate that the pressure exerted by surrounding nuclei is sufficient to propel adjacent nuclei forward, enabling the migration of multiple nuclei at once. This discovery in turn reveals a driving force behind the formation of distinctive patterns seen in many vertebrate brains, where specific types of neurons are born in distinct layers. Our research offers a fundamental explanation for IKNM that is unbiased by previous theories regarding this process and propels the field forward with novel experimental validation, along with precise quantitative data that can be used to build computational models. These models, in turn, have the capacity to predict previously unknown aspects of brain development, such as the precise pattern of birth layer usage in the zebrafish retina. Ground-based observations of planetary movements are crucial in validating the findings of space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. Although these missions are excellent at identifying exoplanets, they lack the capability to determine the properties of these celestial bodies, such as their sizes, masses, and surface compositions, which can be derived through ground-based spectroscopic radial velocity measurements of host stars that are orbited by planets of interest. The TESS-Keck Survey has been designed to address this need by linking the extensive exoplanet catalog generated by TESS with the radial velocity capabilities of the Keck/HIRES spectrograph. This $10$-year initiative, with a budget of $10$ million dollars, will prioritize targets that have been identified as being suitable for further study and will select new candidates based on observations of $10,000$ stars that cover the full area of the TESS sky. From these stars, a team of astronomers will conduct follow-up radial velocity measurements on $503$ candidates that meet specific criteria, such as being considered a prime target or having been identified as having a planet candidate in the medium-confidence category or higher, or having at least one additional feature that makes it noteworthy. Additionally, resources will be allocated to follow up on three groups of candidates that are chosen at random from the TESS catalog, with the goal of determining the properties of these celestial bodies and improving the understanding of various aspects of planetary formation and evolution. These three groups of candidates that will be followed up on are as follows: systems with multiple planets, planets that are in close proximity to their host stars, and terrestrial planets that are located within their host stars' habitable zones. Systems with multiple planets, such as Kepler-454, will be followed up to gather more information about these celestial bodies and to confirm the existence of the additional planets listed in the TESS catalog. The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There are multiple methods to achieve this, including using Optical Character Recognition (OCR) on ID cards to extract their contents for subsequent verification processes.  This research employs the Tesseract OCR engine in conjunction with Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to develop an ID card extractor, with a case study utilizing Indonesian ID cards (KTP).  The ID card extractor was tested using both the Tesseract OCR engine and the spaCy NLP framework to determine their effectiveness in extracting ID card contents, with a focus on the Tesseract-SPPE engine paired with the spaCy NLP framework.  The experimental findings showed that the Tesseract-SPPE engine paired with the spaCy NLP framework outperformed the other combinations, with an F1-score of 93.47%.  The ID card extractor was found to be efficient, with an average processing time of 4.67 seconds, and is deemed suitable for large-scale ID card extraction tasks. Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying by intensity or driving forces that changed over time. The study used the Lagrange multiplier Monte Carlo method to test the principles of the Lagrangian for these situations, also involving the application of driving force types within a Path Integral formulation. The analysis showed that, regardless of the type of driving force, satisfying the principles of the Lagrangian led to accurate results. These results took the form of position probability distributions that matched both theoretical and experimental findings. The accuracy of the results was further validated by measuring the system's energy, which also matched the expectations based on the Lagrangian. The computational approach also enabled the examination of how position probability distributions change over time for an arbitrary starting state. The analysis revealed that the use of the Lagrange multiplier Monte Carlo method is particularly well-suited for harmonic oscillators due to the straightforward transformation of the Lagrangian into an action integral that has only two imaginary time parameters, in contrast to more complex systems that require a larger number of parameters, making them much easier to study with a similar setup. The study concludes by discussing potential applications and the potential for extending this computational approach to study other driven quantum systems. The analysis involved the application of both the Lagrange multiplier Monte Carlo method and the Metropolis method for the evaluation of path integrals. The study also highlights the role of the knowledge of the symmetrized time-dependent imaginary position correlation function obtained from theoretical calculations, which was used to validate the computational approach by comparing the measured energy levels with the established theoretical results, showing a match in precision up to two decimal places. The analysis demonstrates that the computational approach is precise but also highlights the need for the exploration of other quantum systems through the application of this method. The study concludes with the numerical data used in the study being presented in the form of tables, including the comparison of calculated probability distribution functions with experimental and theoretical findings presented in the form of plots, along with additional figures that provide further insight into the results obtained through the computational approach. The study also concludes with the presentation of the theoretical and experimental energy levels in a graphical form and the figure showing the time-dependent position probability density for the quantum harmonic oscillator in its ground state with a driving force that changes over time.
