The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected and analyzed extensive data sets from various Earth-based observatories, specifically for the asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro. By accurately determining the light curve parameters and phase shift for each target, the study derived precise constraints on the YORP acceleration, rotation momentum of inertia, and initial conditions, which in some cases contradicted existing data or broke records for specific categories. Furthermore, two out of three asteroids were found to be accelerating their rotation periods, while the data for 1992 SK showed a deceleration, potentially due to an opposing force, such as a tidal acceleration from a nearby moon, which would require further confirmation. The study's findings have prioritized places for potential future missions to observe and utilize high-energy radiation from the Sun on these targets, which could also provide an opportunity to collect data from a close-proximity vantage point. Additionally, considerations for a mission to 1992 SK include the potential to discover its moon and gather insights into both bodies in the process. Ultimately, accelerating the rotation of these asteroids through the YORP effect makes them suitable targets for utilizing the released energy for propulsion in a controlled and efficient manner, such as in an Impulse Data Relay for Solar Radiation, a concept that could enable deep space missions to be more feasible and cost-effective. To confirm the validity of this research, the study recommends that the phase shift be continuously monitored and modeled for these targets and any others believed to be experiencing the YORP effect, as even a short period of data collection can be useful in determining the light curve parameters and evaluating the effectiveness of IDRS. By doing so, the study can establish a basis to explore the broader implications of this phenomenon and its potential to contribute to the success of deep space missions. Furthermore, it is crucial to acknowledge the contributions of multiple researchers to this study, including their continuous light curve observations and data analysis, without which this research would not have been possible. As a result, this study has significant value in the pursuit of understanding the rotational acceleration of small asteroids and its potential to revolutionize deep space missions

The youth are increasingly relying on Instagram as a source of information, with political figures leveraging the platform to disseminate opinions and agendas. We examined online discussions on Instagram in relation to politics from a network perspective, focusing on communities of co-commenters. Our analysis revealed salient co-interactions - instances of user engagement occurring more frequently than chance would suggest - to be crucial in driving online discussions and information dissemination. We based our study on data related to Brazilian presidential elections and extracted co-commenter relationships from 152 topics with elevated political relevance. Results showed that users with a history of interacting with each other are more likely to engage in similar discussions in the future, a likelihood that decreases over time. We observed variations in this trend across different topics, with some exhibiting persistent activity patterns and others displaying more fluid dynamics. Ultimately, our research identified three distinct patterns: transient, persistent, and bipolar activity cycles. We explored potential factors influencing these patterns by examining variables such as political entities' posts, news articles, and search queries. Our findings indicated that both external stimuli and the online community itself play a role in shaping the dynamics of political discussions on Instagram. We explored the implications of our findings for the dissemination of information and influence on Instagram by political actors, highlighting the importance of a holistic approach that considers both offline and online dynamics. We also provide a method for creating a measure that combines strength and emergence in complex networks, such as weighted graphons, providing a way to examine both the intrinsic structure and extrinsic relationships of these networks. We believe that our approach and results can contribute to a broader understanding of online discussions and community dynamics, with implications for the study of complex systems and network analysis. Confining modes at the edge, known as line waves, can propagate on the boundary between two specially designed electromagnetic interfaces that maintain mirror symmetry properties.
Studies have previously analyzed line waves in theory and in practice, revealing their occurrence at both microwave and terahertz frequencies.
It has also been demonstrated that these waves can occur when there's a sudden change from a negative to a positive symmetric resistance and uniform surface reactance present.
Characteristics of line waves include highly confineable mode propagation, polarization dependent on direction, and unique localized field enhancements.
A new study proposes a graphene patch structure, showing that line waves can occur in the optical range.
The design involves a graphene surface embedded in an epsilon near zero cherenkov medium, separated from a perfectly conducting strip, demonstrating the ability to control line wave steering through adjustments to the graphene's conductivity and the zero epsilon depth.
This new line wave structure offers potential applications in enhancing nonlinear effects and controlling light localization.

We tackle the long-standing issue of producing computable infinite words from rational functions defined on a computable infinite word, even in the presence of non-injective functions and when considering Coxeter systems with an infinite number of generators. Our key innovation is the development of a method to create a computable equivalence relation, which enables us to construct a computable function mapping an infinite word to another infinite word. As a result, any computable function defined on a computable infinite word can be applied to a given computable infinite word, thereby yielding another computable infinite word. This accomplishment includes rational functions that may not be injective and encompasses a broad class of Coxeter systems, including those with an infinite number of generators. Our proof of two additional theorems is also provided. First, we demonstrate that any computable function defined on a computable infinite word containing all possible finite subsequences of another computable infinite word can be applied to the latter infinite word, thereby yielding another computable infinite word. Second, we show that any computable function defined on a computable infinite word with a specific block structure can also be applied to another computable infinite word with the same block structure, thereby yielding another computable infinite word. These findings extend previous work by several researchers and yield new results, while also raising new questions about the synthesis of computable regular functions of infinite words. As part of our proof, we establish a new connection between the Schröder-Bernstein theorem and the study of computable functions defined on computable infinite words, and we also provide an alternative definition of a computable function defined on a computable infinite word in terms of a computable relation and a computable subset of the Baire space. Lastly, we propose two new open questions related to the synthesis of computable regular functions of infinite words. Researchers have analyzed collision data with an integrated luminosity of 3 inverse femtobarns, and through amplitude analysis of specific two-body decay events, have discovered that $B^0$ decaying to two $K^*$ states exhibits a higher fraction of longitudinal polarization than $B^0$ decaying to a single $K^*$ state or $B_s$ decaying to two $K^*$ states, with estimates at $0.35 \pm 0.08$ (systematic uncertainty only). Moreover, an independent measurement of the $B^0$ to two $K^*$ states branching fraction yields $5.3 \pm 0.8$ nanobarns with a $1.8\sigma$ deviation from the $B^0$ to a single $K^*$ states value. All measurements are in line with theoretical predictions from the Standard Model, specifically with those involving the $B^0$ system at a 0.35 CP-odd unit deviation from the suppression of longitudinal polarization preferred by some experiments. Nonetheless, final results do not contradict the Standard Model, and thus, such findings remain within current experimental knowledge limits. Moreover, a 2$\sigma$ deviation threshold would be necessary to consider future, more precise measurements in search for potential Standard Model breakdown in the $B^0$ system. Nonetheless, given that $B^0$ and $B_s$ decay to two $K^*$ states have similar properties, and since the two $B$ meson types have distinct lifetimes, time-dependent studies hold significant potential for standardization of hadronic contributions in $b \to s \bar{s} s$ processes, and for searches of potential Standard Model breakdown in both $B^0$ and $B_s$ systems. Furthermore, if a 2$\sigma$ deviation threshold is reached in the future with more precise measurements, the standardization of hadronic contributions in $b \to s \bar{s} s$ processes and searches of potential Standard Model breakdown in both $B^0$ and $B_s$ systems will be addressed in a higher sensitivity study. Nonetheless, such studies are feasible even if the 2$\sigma$ deviation threshold is not reached in the future, due to the significant potential they hold in time-dependent analyses for standardization of hadronic contributions in $b \to s \bar{s} s$ processes, and for searches of potential Standard Model breakdown in both $B^0$ and $B_s$ systems.

Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements, their scalability to complex datasets is often
limited due to the computational expense of activation functions like ReLU,
and the difficulty of aligning representation layers. To address these
challenges, ReLU-based representations are typically trained in isolation, 
with each layer processed separately. To overcome these restrictions, we 
introduce a novel activation function called the Sine-Like function, which 
is computationally efficient even when modulated with learned periodic signals.
This activation function allows for the aligning of multiple representation 
layers during training, without compromising efficiency. When applied to three 
benchmark datasets, our method delivers generalizable and state-of-the-art 
results for 3D few-shot learning, surpassing the performance of non-generalizable 
baselines by a margin of 6.5% and enhancing the performance of methods that 
generalize, by 2.5%. Our code and models are available at this link https://github.com/alexfrojo/MLP-SPAM. 
Our research demonstrates that deep representations based on simple activation 
functions can be both generalizable and accurate, counter to the prevailing 
view that the two are mutually exclusive. To support this conclusion, we 
conduct a thorough ablation analysis covering over 300 configurations, 
covering all major generalizable and non-generalizable baselines, activation 
function variants and learning strategies, without losing 5% in performance. 
Our analysis yields insights that could facilitate the development of more 
excellent generalizable models based on simple activation functions and 
suggests the possibility of generalizable models that are also efficient in a 
wide range of applications beyond 3D few-shot learning. Our research also 
uncovered an activation function called the Sine-Like function with periodic 
modulation that is more accurate than its non-modulated counterpart but 5% 
less efficient, while a modulated ReLU-like function that is similar in 
behavior to the Sine-Like function but 20% more efficient, delivered 
generalizable results that are 5% lower than the state of the art in 3D few-shot 
learning, matching the performance of a non-generalizable baseline, and 
surpassing the performance of a method that generalizes, by 2.5%. Our research 
also uncovered an activation function called the Soft-Sine-Like function with 
learned periodic signals

The underlying principles of human ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious despite numerous studies. Previous research has suggested that this organization is based on a linear continuum, with animals placed in between humans and non-animals. Conversely, some scientists propose a more hierarchical framework, suggesting that all animals are grouped together as "animate" before being further differentiated from one another. To address this debate, a new study employs a novel method that allows for the examination of cross-subject variations in VT's animacy hierarchies. As a result, a robust pattern emerges from multiple independent samples, revealing a clear animal/non-animal distinction and evidence of internal variation within the animal category. A statistical model that accounts for both subject-specific and shared components provides the most accurate representation of the animacy hierarchy in VT. Notably, a double-dipser shape emerges when modeling individual subject's data, with an initial peak in the human region, followed by a peak in the area corresponding to non-human primates, before gradually declining towards other animal taxa as distance from humans increases. A similar double-dipser shape is observed in two separate control experiments that test subjects' ability to recognize specific human faces and non-primate animals. A 3D shape model with strong connections to existing cognitive theories also fits the data well, demonstrating that the animacy hierarchy in VT is composed of multiple features, including eyes, mouth, body proportions, facial structure, and possibly other attributes that are difficult to measure. Systematic variations in these features provide a coherent explanation for the empirical double-dipser shape, supporting a theory that all animals are grouped together as "animate" before being further differentiated from one another based on their unique physical characteristics. These findings have significant implications for our understanding of how humans process faces across species and provide a framework for future research to examine the organization of other object categories in human ventral temporal cortex. The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We show in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and provides valuable insights into the factors that contribute to super-spreader events, which can be influenced by factors such as an individual's ability to deliver a large number of doses in a short period of time in proportion to their level of infectivity. We also examine the implications of unreported super-spreader events on epidemic modeling and find that unaccounted for transmission during these events can contribute significantly to the rapid spread of disease, which can result in an elevated effective $R_0$ value even in its absence. Furthermore, even when traditional modeling is capable of fitting the overall number of infections, a high-transmission event with a short duration can result in a discrepancy between model predictions and actual data in relation to the timing of infection peaks, which can be resolved by taking such events into consideration. We conclude by discussing the potential for such events to propagate transmission in multi-layer settings and the corresponding adjustments to be made to $R_0$ in these contexts. Due to their broad applicability, the findings presented in this report are relevant to numerous contagious disease epidemics in history as well as current public health challenges. Furthermore, the principles outlined in this report are also applicable to modeling the spread of epidemics in networks and other complex systems. Inferred measurements are obtained through non-linear inversion of these observations in a predetermined framework. Recent studies indicate that biases within the base line subtraction process and chromospheric measurements significantly impact results. The underlying source of these biases seems to stem from data sets used to build the forward modeling and chi-squared calculation, which include broad features of solar spectra. A new analysis of absorption features in solar spectra reveals a distinct bias in the synthesis of chromospheric network spectra, not accounted for in existing data sets. This new bias, quantified as $\sqrt{1.3}$, varies from the previously established value of $\sqrt{1.5}$. It should be adjusted in the inversion code to minimize errors in solar vector magnetic field data. A simple modification to the base line subtraction process also showed an improvement in results, indicating that a more sophisticated approach may be necessary. This new analysis encourages other inversion codes to review and refine their own data sets in a similar manner. This is especially important considering the increasing amount of spectroscopic observations being collected and the resulting high-resolution solar magnetic data sets. A plan is also presented to establish a publically available web interface that can handle any future requests for data sets and related information. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost at no additional linear scaling in memory usage. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. For the two-dimensional Hubbard model with 36 sites and 60 particles, experiencing an extreme sign problem due to electron correlation, our method demonstrates excellent convergence with an exactness guarantee, accurately reproducing existing data for smaller systems and facilitating the critical determination of an (1/2) doped Hubbard model on the 36x36 lattice lattice. Furthermore, this method exhibits impressive parallelization potential, showing a 13.5 times linear scaling in performance when moving from a single CPU core to 16 cores. Our implementation is accessible through the Open Source code provided at https://github.com/QuantumPhysicsGroup/ComplexNeuralHubbardModel. Leveraging the capabilities of complex-valued affine coupling layers, we also present an alternative method that achieves comparable performance, enabling us to consider scenarios where diagonalizing the Hubbard Hamiltonian is computationally impractical due to excessive memory requirements. Ultimately, this method allows us to investigate the effects of strong electron correlation in the two-dimensional Hubbard model for 36 sites and 60 particles, obtaining an accurate estimate of the grand canonical distribution for the first time. The data collection also reveals a critical period for the (1/2) doped Hubbard model on the 36x36 lattice lattice before the system's frustration becomes too intense, indicating a critical time frame of approximately $D \approx 6.4$ and showing a failure to resolve the ground state for larger systems. Our code is written in Python using the TensorFlow framework and is designed for seamless integration with GPU accelerators, enabling significant speedup. As a cutting-edge method for addressing the sign problem in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling, this work presents a new direction for complex-valued neural network architectures that achieve significant breakthroughs in tackling intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Ultimately, this method offers a new path for complex-valued neural network architectures to tackle some of the most fundamental challenges in physics research. We demonstrate that this frequency converges to $2\rho(1/2)$ as $x$ approaches infinity, and we explore additional properties of the frequency of friable integers for various integer subsets within the $x$ to $2x$ range. Our results extend naturally to the broader category of $q^d$-friable integers, where $d$ represents the number of distinct prime factors in the integer $q$. We establish upper and lower bounds for the frequency of these more general integers, and we show that these bounds converge to specific values related to the Dickman function as $x$ approaches infinity. Our findings build upon prior research by Baker, Harman, and Pintér, as well as recent findings by Pintér and the second author, and our results are further quantified in terms of the function $S(d,\chi)$, which describes the distribution of squareclasses $\mathfrak{q}^2$ among those less than $x$. We derive closed-form expressions for $S(d,\chi)$ in multiple scenarios, including instances where $d$ equals $1$ and $2$, and we employ computer simulations to generate $S(d,\chi)$ estimates for larger $d$ values. These estimates suggest the existence of an underlying pattern for $S(d,\chi)$ when $d$ is quite large, and we hypothesize that $S(d,\chi)$ may, in fact, be fully defined by its values in the $d$ and $2d$ ranges. We offer $d$-uplet splitting function $\psi(d)$ and the number of $d$-uplets $N(x)$ upper bounds that leverage our general bounds for $q^d$-friable integers, and we demonstrate that both of these bounds converge to specific values related to the Dickman function as $x$ approaches infinity. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection, making this computation accessible even for large, infinite Coxeter groups. This processing of boolean complexes near the identity element lays the groundwork for future research on boolean complexes within other subgroups of Coxeter groups. This research is also accompanied by an upcoming paper that explores the lattice structure of these boolean complexes. Both of these results contribute to a broader understanding of the combinatorial properties of Coxeter groups and related polytopes, notably the generalized associahedra, by examining their discrete Morse structures. Furthermore, this work establishes connections between these structures and those of permutoreses, monoid operators, and Coxeter orbits. This research is also part of a larger initiative to characterize the structure of combinatorial objects within Coxeter groups using algebraic and geometric properties of these groups. This characterization can, in turn, contribute to identifying the underlying principles that make certain Morse functions discrete and capable of inducing non-trivial decompositions of polytopes. This, in turn, has implications for both theoretical and applied mathematics, including the study of algebraic structures, geometry, and combinatorics, as well as areas like computer science, statistics, biology, and physics, where these fundamental concepts play a crucial role. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively predict peak and attenuation coefficients. Our analysis indicated that certain online actuators deliberately disseminate rumors to induce a significant reaction, often in sectors related to health, with some pandemic-related rumors achieving peak impact within a day and continuing at a reduced level for five days. Every day, healthcare systems around the world gather vast amounts of numerical data from continuous glucose monitors, with each reading representing a flow that needs to be analyzed immediately and with the passage of time. With data velocities accelerating and potential risks rising with each passing minute, existing storage systems are no longer suitable for handling these numbers with the required immediacy and scale. In contrast to traditional processing methods, existing stream processing technologies like Apache Flink and Amazon Kinesis have shown significant improvements in handling such data with both speed and scale, but they still struggle with certain challenges posed by CGM data, such as combining readings with the passage of time and combining readings from different patients with the passage of time. To address these limitations, we have designed an internal workflow for an innovative stream processing engine, and this engine outperforms industry leaders like Apache Flink by at least 5 times and as much as 20 times in certain applications, such as detecting hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, predicting future blood glucose levels, and identifying patterns in lumbar puncture samples while also providing better memory usage and lower latency. With its robust performance, this engine has the potential to handle a wide range of data streams with the passage of time, making it an ideal foundation for developing medical analytics applications that can deliver both high performance and low latency. With its ability to process both time-based and tuple-based operators with equal ease, this engine offers a unique and highly versatile approach to stream processing that can also facilitate the creation of high-performance, low-latency applications for any data stream with the passage of time, such as temperature readings, financial transactions, and sensor data from continuous glucose monitors, cloud logs, and web click streams, hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia, MRI sequences, EEG signals, lumbar puncture samples, blood pressure measurements, gene expression, heart rate measurements, image streams, mobile sensor readings, MRI sequences, network flows, protein sequences, sleep pattern data, speech recognition features, temperature readings, transaction streams, web click streams and video streams. In addition to its performance, this engine has also been designed with both scalability and simplicity in mind, with a clean and modular architecture that makes it easy to develop both new processing algorithms and efficient data inputs and outputs, such as converters, collectors, and loaders, while also providing a high level of reliability and data integrity through both internal and external transactional support, allowing it to handle both small and large datasets with equal ease, but unfortunately does not support joins or aggregations on streaming data.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to critically examine their development and implementation. While many loss functions developed for multiclass neural networks are based on existing theories, such as the Neumann and Minkowski metrics, a thorough examination of their impact is lacking. Recent studies suggest that, despite the claims of certain loss function proponents, the loss function expert network does not necessarily follow the principles of Occam's razor. In response, we propose a framework for systematically evaluating the loss functions developed to date, taking into consideration both theoretical justifications and empirical validation. Through an exhaustive analysis of 34 loss functions, we shed light on both the design and performance of these loss functions. Our empirical analysis reveals that certain loss function design elements have a positive impact on performance, namely, the use of the Minkowski and Mahalanobis metrics, as well as the integration of softmax, whereas other elements, such as the use of the Kullback-Leibler divergence and the introduction of noise, appear to hinder performance. Notably, our findings indicate that many loss functions developed to date do not, in fact, outperform the standard cross-entropy loss function when evaluated in a fair and comprehensive manner. Our comprehensive evaluation framework, coupled with our discovery of underperforming loss functions, motivates further research aimed at creating highly effective neural network loss functions through controlled experiments and thorough analyses of both design and performance. Systematic evaluation of loss functions will facilitate the development of more robust and adaptable neural network loss functions, addressing the long-held misconception that loss function design is an art rather than a science. Our research will be made available through an open repository, along with an accompanying leader board that showcases the loss function benchmarks reported herein. Our research is further supported by an accompanying media asset, a loss function design metric visualization tool, made available through an associated webpage. Our research is being presented at the ICLR 2023 conference. Our work is also highlighted as part of an associated ICML 2023 workshop. In this generalized model, a strong nematic spin-orbit coupling causes a significant splitting of the quasi-Landau levels based on their orbital and spin alignment. As a result, a strong magnetic field induces an asymmetry in the quasi-Landau level splitting, leading to a Pauli paramagnetic response that differs for up and down spin components. This induced magnetic field asymmetry results in a non-zero diamagnetic term that is directly proportional to the nematic order parameter and inversely proportional to the mass difference between the up and down spin quasiparticles. This interaction can be measured through magnetization, providing a means to both identify and quantify the nematic order parameter. Furthermore, the influence of magnetization on the nematic order parameter can be understood through a mean-field approach, leading to the derivation of a London equation that incorporates both the response to the external magnetic field and the self-regulation of the nematic order parameter. The solution to this London equation reveals that the nematic order parameter exhibits oscillatory behavior as a function of the magnetic field, with the amplitude of of this oscillatory behavior dependent on the same mass difference as the quasi-Landau levels. This research is also supplemented by an analysis of quasi-Landau level splitting in a magnetic field, using a phenomenological approach that focuses on the underlying symmetry of the system. This study demonstrates that the distinctive splitting patterns of quasi-Landau levels observed in Bi$_2$Se$_3$ and other nematic superconductors can serve as a universal indicator for spin-triplet nematic superconductivity. The unique properties of quasi-Landau levels in these systems render standard Fermi liquid theory inapplicable, with the resulting distinctive splitting patterns providing conclusive proof of nematic superconductivity. Finally, our research proposes feasible experimental protocols involving magnetization and torque measurements that can be employed to validate our theoretical predictions and gain a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between magnetic field, nematic order parameter, and quasiparticle mass in these systems. One significant challenge in robotics is the difficulty of providing precise demonstrations to a student robot due to the high costs associated with obtaining expert feedback. As a result, providing clear demonstrations for robots learning from feedback in online settings is becoming an increasingly pressing issue. In this study, an innovative framework called CBF-LOL was developed to address this problem by leveraging corrective feedback from experts, regardless of the quality of their demonstrations. This framework is particularly well-suited for complex tasks that cannot be efficiently solved by expediting learning, as it takes advantage of two key properties of online learning algorithms, including their ability to make progress in optimizing objectives and to generalize across time steps. By focusing on learning algorithms rather than loss functions, CBF-LOL can facilitate high-quality learning from low-cost, corrective feedback, even when expert feedback contains errors, by taking advantage of the underlying properties of online learning algorithms. This framework was experimentally validated on two real-world tasks using the A1 robot, with CBF-LOL achieving success rates of 80% and 90% in tasks requiring fewer than 20 and 30 seconds to complete, respectively. These results demonstrate the efficacy of combining online learning algorithms with corrective feedback, resulting in the successful execution of complex tasks for the first time without the need for precise demonstrations from experts. Furthermore, CBF-LOL's ability to generalize across time steps allows it to accomplish 15% to 30% more tasks than other proposed methods that focus on specific online learning algorithms, indicating its potential to accelerate the development of learning-based controllers for complex robotics tasks by providing a unified framework for the combination of multiple online learning algorithms. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved remarkable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  However, their performance significantly degrades when they are applied to real-world rainy images. This disparity in behavior suggests that rain simulation and removal are interconnected tasks. If we can generate a plausible background for an image, it should also serve as a feasible rainy image when an appropriate rain simulation is applied. With this insight in mind, this study introduces a novel approach that treats rain generation and removal as equivalent tasks. It proposes a Disentangled Rain Elimination Network (DREN) which is an innovative rain-elimination system. This new system is comprised of two main components: an image translation network that is trained to create a disentangled representation of rainy images, synthesizing two separate elements: the background of the image and the rain. This disentangled representation is then used to develop two separate models, one for eliminating rain and another for simulating rain, both of which share the same training data. It has been observed that training these two models simultaneously using a disentangled representation of rainy images leads to a more robust rain-elimination model. We experimentally verified the efficacy of our proposed approach on two datasets containing artificially created rainy images as well as real-world rainy images and the results show that it delivers superior performance when compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, our proposed method is efficient and user-friendly since it eliminates the need to manually segment rain from images. In addition, the skills that these models have learned during training enable them to remove rain from images that were not included in the training dataset. Our code has been made available for public access at: https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/DREN. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to mark sub-regions of a condensed state space representation, thereby efficiently leveraging human time. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. Our method proves particularly adept at accelerating learning in challenging settings requiring both fast exploration and precise target reaching. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/lyg-19/VisCR. Our results also suggest that our approach holds promise for broad application in a wide range of reward learning settings. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal a significant gap between models that excel in recognizing patterns and those that excel in reasoning, with a particular emphasis on aspects related to causality.  By taking a methodical approach to assessing the relationships between ATOMIC's diverse conditions and consequences and exploring various techniques for producing responses that follow a given rule, we have identified key factors that influence performance and outlined strategies for further enhancing the dataset in order to create models that are both accurate and proficient in reasoning.  We have also introduced an evaluation framework that emulates if-then reasoning by leveraging subsets of conditions and consequences from the dataset and have utilized it to gather insights that can guide the development of more advanced models of artificial intelligence.  This dataset and evaluation framework provide a foundation for exploring the intricacies of machine reasoning in the presence of complex, real-world scenarios.  We have made ATOMIC available by integrating it into a publicly accessible database that can be queried using a proprietary language and have open-sourced this language for the benefit of the broader research community. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the Lagrange multiplier method's quantum computational benefits. Nonetheless, this strategy is confined by the necessity to compute the inverse of the portfolio volatility in its original form, which is a computationally demanding operation even with quantum hardware. This research introduces an inverse computation technique for the HHL quantum linear system solver that is hybrid, known as NISQ-HHL. This hybrid technique is designed for intermediate quantum hardware by dividing the inverse computation into two parts: a narrow quantum circuit for matrix multiplication and an extensive classical matrix inversion using the Monte Carlo version of the circuit. This was coupled with a 'portfolio volatility package' that is both scalable and adaptable to various quantum hardware configurations. Our study demonstrates the viability of this approach by solving actual portfolio optimization problems with real-world data, featuring up to 64 decimal instruments, on near-term quantum hardware, specifically on a superconducting quantum processor unit (QPU) with 27 qubits, resulting in marked improvements over its classical counterpart. For instance, NISQ-HHL was able to compute the inverse of a 64x64 matrix in approximately 20 seconds on this QPU, whereas classical hardware takes approximately 10,000 seconds to accomplish this on a classical machine with similar processing power. Furthermore, this research introduces the 'Quantum Finance' framework, an open-source software that allows users to formulate their own portfolio optimization problems and execute them on quantum hardware via a hybrid HHL framework, in addition to supporting a range of quantum hardware configurations through its 'Quantum Hardware Interface Layer'. This research was conducted using a range of quantum hardware configurations, including QPU units from IBM, D-Wave, and Rigetti & Associates. Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is inherently time-dependent, varying according to breathing rate and turbulence intensity. We investigated the practical implications of this concept through controlled experiments using laser scattering to measure aerosol transport. Theoretical models based on hydraulics and respiratory function were validated against our data. We examined two scenarios: a high-breathing-rate scenario with potential contamination and a low-breathing-rate scenario with minimal mixing. We observed that air exchange during urban bus journeys significantly impacted the concentration of aerosols, with concentrations peaking at ~3000 Chapman units shortly after departing, before dropping to ~1500 Chapman units after 10 minutes of travel. We also found that the breathing rate of individuals contributed substantially to the concentration of aerosols, with an estimated effect of ~1500 Chapman units. These findings suggest that the concentration of aerosols in urban buses is best represented by a non-equilibrium model, emphasizing the importance of air exchange rates and breathing rates from an epidemiological perspective. We propose a combined model that integrates the fundamental principles of hydraulics and respiratory function for predicting the concentration of aerosols in urban buses. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the existing unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or only apply in the random oracle model. Our research presents new, flexible unclonable encryption constructions that provide strong security even with repeated use and are viable in both the random oracle model and the plain model.

  - Non-interactive: The existing literature only features interactive unclonable encryption constructions. Our research introduces the first non-interactive unclonable encryption construction, meeting the requirements set by Broadbent and Lord in their initial paper.

  - Strongly unclonable encryption: We've introduced a new, more demanding standard for unclonable encryption, where the difference between any two given ciphertexts is distinguishable, not just the difference between a given ciphertext and a fresh one. Our research presents constructions for strongly unclonable encryption in both the random oracle model and the plain model, as well as innovative applications to strongly unclonable encryption from any unclonable encryption scheme. Finally, we've demonstrated a relationship between strongly unclonable encryption and strongly non-malleable encryption, but this connection holds only in the random oracle model. As a result, we've designed a new, strongly unclonable encryption construction from a strongly non-malleable encryption construction in the random oracle model, but this construction isn't directly applicable in the plain model due to incompatibility issues. Therefore, we've constructed another, independent strongly unclonable encryption construction in the plain model to fulfill our requirements. Ultimately, this connection could be useful for producing strong non-malleable encryption constructions from unclonable encryption constructions in the random oracle model, but further research is needed to achieve this in the plain model. This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$ and in one-dimensional space. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations. Calculated energy eigenvalues show the influence of $\alpha$ on binding energy, with decreasing effects as $\alpha$ approaches 1. Bound state eigenfunctions are expressed in terms of $N$-dimensional Laguerre polynomials. Introduction of non-locality through $\alpha$ leads to increased stability in one-dimensional space, demonstrated through a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator analysis. However, this benefit is observed to be lost in $N$-dimensional space, where wavefunction stability is maintained only up to $\alpha=0.5$. The proposed approach contributes to understanding the influence of fractional derivatives on quantum mechanical potentials and may facilitate exploration of new non-local interactions within the Schrödinger equation framework. Consequently, solutions obtained can be applied to analyze and predict physical properties of atoms and molecules governed by fractional quantum mechanics. Ultimately, consideration of fractional dynamics may provide insights into overcoming limitations of standard Schrödinger theory, particularly in describing homogeneous interactions within atomic and molecular systems. Furthermore, extension of this work to relativistic fractional Schrödinger equations is also presented, along with a novel relation between its solutions and those obtained from the non-relativistic fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation. This connection enables the prediction of relativistic energy corrections, expressed as a series of Dirac's delta functions, leading to a new definition of fractional Zeeman and Stark effect. Lastly, our research lays the groundwork for further investigation into relativistic fractional quantum mechanics and its applications, as well as exploration of new fractional potentials and their solutions. In conclusion, this study provides a comprehensive framework for solving the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation

Customized digital games successfully encourage motivation in repetitive exercises required for motor rehabilitation; nevertheless, developing adjustments that cater to both therapy and enjoyment objectives poses a challenge. To tackle this issue, we propose an approach where an initial statistical model of game performance identifies specific settings that mirror players' typical behavior, even in the face of diminished control. This approach is exemplified through a practical application involving upper limb rehabilitation and a specially designed controller for the Pac-Man game. Collaborative sessions between occupational therapists and game developers resulted in the identification of two key factors that affect the gameplay experience and influence rehabilitation adjustments. Experimental studies on both healthy subjects and patients with stroke demonstrated that the proposed statistical model accurately captures the dynamics of adjusted gameplay and effectively identifies optimal parameter values that replicate baseline performance in both scenarios. This research offers valuable insights for the design of rehabilitation exercises within digital games by demonstrating the feasibility of his approach and highlighting the critical elements that design systems and therapeutic protocols should be based on. Furthermore, our findings provide foundational knowledge on data-driven design methods that can be employed to create more effective and engaging rehabilitation exercises with digital games. Additionally, this approach facilitates the exploration of various design configurations and, with some modifications, can also assess the subject's performance during the rehabilitation session. In the context of the Pac-Man based rehabilitation exercise that was used as an example in this paper, several adjustments that could be made to improve its overall effectiveness have become apparent. In terms of design, one aspect that warrants further attention is the readjustment period following a change in settings. Although some subjects were able to readjust to new limitations in as little as 5-6 levels, improving this aspect could be accomplished by either shortening the rehabilitation session or implementing a more gradual reduction in controller functionality. In regards to the statistical model that was proposed in this paper, one aspect that merits additional examination is the impact of different data input methods on the estimation of the model's parameters. In the case of the Pac-Man based rehabilitation exercise that was used as an example in this paper, a method that relies on the analysis of video recordings of the subject's gameplay was employed. This approach resulted in a model that accurately captured the dynamics of adjusted gameplay but may not provide the most precise estimation of the model's parameters. In contrast, methods that utilize direct input from the subject or more advanced machine learning models that can analyze their gameplay in real-time may yield better results. In light of these findings, researchers and designers are encouraged to explore alternative data input methods along with other design configurations through the lens of the proposed statistical model

We investigate a specific leptoquark scenario, involving a third-generation gauge vector leptoquark, which could resolve the apparent discrepancy between the Large Hadron Collider's observation of a heavy Higgs boson and certain inconsistencies in lepton universality. This particular leptoquark, which is a vector nature with five color and three charge properties, is likely to contribute to Drell-Yan dilepton production in a manner that depends on both mass and charge. In order to examine this influence, we calculate the precise predictions for Drell-Yan production at next-to-leading order in QCD, coupled with an accurate parton shower, and compare them to data from the Tevatron and LHC, specifically for electron and muon channels, considering various mass and charge combinations, and covering mass ranges from 500 GeV to 5 TeV. Additionally, we provide public access to the code used for these calculations through the delivery of public event generator files for each relevant charge and mass combination, and a corresponding web interface for more intricate studies. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs. Notably, in the case of single-source graphs, our approach yields a fixed-parameter algorithm prior to a quadratic factor, resolving an open question posed by Fester et al. Our XP algorithm for graphs with limited treewidth generalizes previous research by Kohanka and Langer. Our parameterized algorithm for graph parameters with known or near-known XP or FPT behavior enables us to derive positive results for several classes of graphs with multiple sources, including graph classes defined by several NP-complete problems being fixed-parameter tractible, such as graph minors excluding a minor, and planar graphs with certain treewidth or treedepth values. Our negative results are supported by an observation that graph classes defined by the NP-complete problem of finding a minimum source vertex set still possess FPT for upward planarity, despite not being necessarily fixed-parameter tractible. Our research involves novel techniques for combining SPQR tree-decompositions with set-covering using a combination of basic updown-links and more complex spiral-links, laying the groundwork for investigating other directed graph layout problems using our proposed method. Our study is also an exploration of the relationship between graph layout problems and parameterized complexity, highlighting potential future research directions. Our results remain relevant in this area with the standard modern parameterized complexity perspective, in which the parameter of a graph class is defined as a parameter that specifies the number of vertices in a particular subset of the graph vertices. Our research is an early exploration of the relationship between graph layout problems and parameterized complexity, and as such, some of our results may be considered basic or elementary in the standard modern parameterized complexity perspective. A novel automated configuration framework is introduced, using model checking and SMT, adaptable to any domain definable by SMT formulas, allowing for modular scalability and improved human understanding via metric-driven optimization. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to configuring a CGRA memory tile for diverse image processing tasks. This configuration outperforms human expertise in optimized performance and energy efficiency, achieving a 5x performance boost and 3x energy efficiency gain in certain scenarios. This work also highlights the significance of human participation in automating system configuration through preference specification and metric development. Furthermore, a discussion on open issues and potential applications is presented. This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a systematic manner, ultimately verifying that certain fundamental features emerge across these systems in alignment with the universal operator growth hypothesis. Moreover, our work showcases the value of leveraging Lie symmetry, which streamlines calculations and renders existing approaches like the Lanczos algorithm superfluous, instead allowing us to extract crucial insights through symmetry-based arguments. Ultimately, our work proposes a straightforward method for identifying whether a given SU(1,1) or SU(2) Hamiltonian supports protracted operator growth. Additionally, our research introduces the novel concept of "entanglement of operator growth," which is demonstrated to be elevated in systems where operator growth endures, thereby providing a concrete basis for further exploring the underlying causes of this phenomenon through study of its informational hallmark. Finally, we apply this framework to two illustrative models, the su(1,1) su(2) boson-truncated Kerr model and su(2) symmetric long-range interacting systems, which reveal intriguing connections between operator growth, entanglement, and its informational characterization, underscoring the significance of examining these phenomena in the broader context of quantum dynamics. In doing so, we derive a practical, yet robust, measure for quantifying the operator growth complexity of any given Lie-symmetric system at any given time. This measure, based on the spectral characteristics of specific matrix products, serves as a dependable indicator of operator evolution and is an invaluable asset for further exploring the underlying causes of this phenomenon through study of its informational hallmark. Network-based services provide significant income to service operators, which they regulate through agreements on performance. Ensuring these agreements are being met necessitates the monitoring of service standards. A method to accomplish this is by deploying active measurement techniques, which send test traffic with designated characteristics and verify that it conforms to agreed specifications upon arrival. However, the scalability of this approach is limited by the number of measurements that can be conducted simultaneously. This research explores the potential of employing peer-to-peer (P2P) communication to enhance the detection of SLA violations. P2P networks enable direct communication between any two network nodes, which could be utilized for the exchange of measurement data. This could limit the need for centralized measurement controllers and allow for more concurrent measurements within the same network. The proposal put forward in this research aims to demonstrate the feasibility of detecting SLA violations via P2P communication. It outlines a proposed system architecture and presents initial outcomes from a test bed featuring active measurement capabilities in a P2P setting. The outcomes show that it is possible to exchange measurement data between nodes, which in turn enables the detection of SLA violations directly at the points of service delivery. The outcomes also highlight the advantages of P2P communication in the context of active measurement, including the capacity for concurrent measurements and the elimination of requirements for centralized controllers. Nevertheless, the approach is still associated with higher overhead compared to traditional passive measurement methods. Furthermore, there are concerns regarding data security in P2P settings, which need to be addressed in future research. The case study presented focuses on network layers 1-3, which is the primary area subject to change due to the introduction of active measurement, whereas layers 4-7 may require additional consideration in future extensions to the proposed system. The outcomes of this research are of interest to service providers seeking to monitor SLA violations, particularly those with large-scale, distributed networks. To validate the outcomes, the study was conducted in collaboration with a major telecommunications provider. The outcomes indicate that P2P communication is an effective means of detecting SLA violations, which is a critical requirement for network-based services that generate significant revenue for service operators. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects, ultimately with the aim of enhancing current capabilities in energy recovery linacs. Both theoretical and experimental evidence support the beam's sensitivity to specific filling patterns, particularly "in-phase" and "out-of-phase" cases in reference to the RF system. In the former scenario, beam and RF interactions are closely synchronized to maximize the beam's electric field seen from the RF system, resulting in the lowest threshold for instability. In contrast, the out-of-phase case significantly increases this threshold due to reduced field presentation to the RF system, while other intermediate filling patterns fall between these two, indicating a linear relationship. To validate these findings, a series of beam tests were conducted at the MIT-Bates Electron Accelerator using different filling patterns and recirculation schemes without the risk of inducing instability. In one test, a 25-MeV, 200-MHz electron beam with a 1.5-ns pulse width and 1.25-ns period was accelerated through four regular RF sections and two injected sections with a 2-μs fill pattern, demonstrating the feasibility of beam breakup studies in energy recovery linacs without the risk of instability during testing. To further reduce the risk of instability during testing, a proposed magnetic bunch length meter allows for online measurement of the beam's electric field without increasing the risk of inducing instability and confirms the filling pattern dependence of beam breakup instability both theoretically and experimentally. To mitigate this instability, a proposed approach involves introducing a small asymmetry in the fill pattern, demonstrating in experiments and simulations a significantly increased threshold for instability in out-of-phase cases, underscoring the critical role of field presentation to the RF system. As a result of this research, the current record for beam current in an energy recovery linac has been broken in experiments at the MIT-Bates Electron Accelerator, paving the way for achieving higher currents in energy recovery linacs through proper design of filling patterns and recirculation schemes. To determine the parameters for neutrino oscillation, cutting-edge experiments employing long-baseline neutrino detection systems rely heavily on the development of detailed models describing interactions between neutrinos and atomic nuclei. The neutrino flux prediction is a crucial component of these models and requires knowledge of neutron interactions with a target material to facilitate the leaping of neutrinos over obstacles. The measurement of total neutron cross-section with respect to plastic scintillator, a crucial material in such systems, is therefore essential. Although previous measurements have been conducted with gases and liquids, this study reports the first ever measurement of the total cross-section of neutrons with respect to plastic scintillator using a novel 3D-projection scintillator detector design. This new design, an extension of the traditional plane-based design, offers improved detection capabilities for events involving multiple scattering and has enabled the measurement of large Q2 values typically missed by other detection methods. The statistical accuracy of this measurement is significantly enhanced by the use of a high-intensity $d$+CH$_2$ beam at the 100 MeV electron beamline of the McMaster University Meson Factory, supported by additional data collected at lower intensities and with a different beam setup. The measurement of $d$+CH$_2$ and $p$+CH data at the same zero angle allows for cross-checks and the determination of the neutron cross-section with respect to plastic scintillator alone, yielding the value of 0.65$\pm$0.06 (stat.) $\pm$0.04 (syst.) barn, in line with theoretical predictions and serving as a valuable reference for future neutrino flux calculations. The 3D-projection scintillator detector design demonstrated in this study offers valuable insights for the development of large-scale detection systems capable of measuring a variety of scattering processes in real-time, making it an attractive option for future facilities such as the future electron-ion collider. The novel design and the measurement technique employed in this study have also facilitated the detection of anomalous events in off-peak conditions, providing valuable clues to further improve the understanding of material interactions in such systems. The future development of detection systems capable of measuring real-time scattering processes in multiple directions will significantly contribute to the advancement of precise neutrino flux calculations and the development of cutting-edge programs in neutrino physics. The novel design of the 3D-projection scintillator detector introduced here represents an important milestone in this journey of discovery and research. In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces changed in response to temperature among particles made of chondritic materials, which indicated that their surface energy drops by approximately 5 times when temperatures rise. In the present study, we examine how the presence of water affects this temperature dynamic. Water was added to the same type of particles and subjected to the same series of temperature variations, which resulted in significant changes in their behavior. Unlike their dry counterparts, water-bearing particles failed to exhibit the same decrease in sticking forces with increasing temperature, which suggests that their surface energy remains relatively constant across the 230-430K temperature range. This implies that the law of temperature on stickiness holds true for water-bearing particles at 230K but not at higher temperatures. In contrast to the law's prediction, the former group demonstrated stronger sticking forces at 380K than at 230K. In both cases, the law's prediction was fulfilled at 260K, which is considered the average temperature of a protoplanetary disk. In our experiment, water-bound particles exhibited a greater increase in sticking forces when compared to their dry counterparts, which reached 10 times greater than the latter. This significant boost in sticking forces with temperature could provide a critical explanation for the formation of large particles in protoplanetary discs through a runaway sticking phenomenon. Furthermore, this phenomenon may contribute to the settlement of large particles in the upper layers of such discs by reducing their density and subsequently their ability to move freely. In our experiment, water-bound particles settled within 1cm in half the time it took their dry counterparts, which reached 20 times greater than the latter. This time difference could provide a clue as to how certain protoplanetary discs form dead zones by creating an environment where the formation of large particles can settle, reducing the disc's ability to transfer matter efficiently. Water-bound particles failed to form aggregates when temperature variations were applied in an alternating pattern of high and low temperatures, which suggests that their surface energy may drop below that of dry particles only when temperatures are consistently kept low. This finding provides a basis for further research into how water affects the sticking properties of particles under different temperature dynamics in a variety of environments. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To address this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which can learn from multiple demonstrations that are subject to nonlinear hard constraints. EKMP can also avoid obstacles by treating them as constraints. It can generate complex motion trajectories while adhering to linear and nonlinear constraints, making it an effective tool for the transfer of human skills to various robotic platforms in complex and unstructured settings. Experimental evaluations of EKMP are performed through a series of challenging tasks, including a complex scenario that combines multiple constraints and obstacles, demonstrating its superior performance over state-of-the-art kernelized movement primitives in terms of imitation accuracy and successful task completion rate. The EKMP framework is available online at https://github.com/robotics-icub-center/EKMP. Its future development will be shaped by the community through an issued open call at https://github.com/robotics-icub-center/EKMP/issues. Due to its broad applications, we anticipate EKMP to have a significant impact on the development of advanced learning algorithms for the synthesis of robust and efficient robotic skills. In particular, we expect it to set the stage for the addressing of additional learning challenges such as action sequences, friction forces, and goal-oriented imitation, on which we are currently working, to be presented in our ongoing research activities at the 2023 IROS conference. These advancements will be made available as new extensions to the EKMP framework, while related research will be showcased at the 2023 IROS workshop on "Learning and Adapting End-to-End Robotic Controllers" which can be attended online at https://iros2023-ww.icubcenter.org/. Additionally, we are exploring the integration of EKMP with state-based primitives, to be showcased at the 2023 ICS conference, and the extension of kernelized movement primitives to non-kinematic constraints, to be presented at the 2023 ICRA conference. These state-based primitives can be combined with EKMP's kernelized movement primitives to be showcased at the 2024 IROS conference, whose review process has already been initiated. This calculation was for two gluons in a T-channel two-gluon process with no collinear emissions allowed. Due to $N^3S$ symmetry, this scenario is equivalent to a one-gluon exchange process in $s$-channel and its corresponding NNLL BFKL equation residue. By utilizing sound wave velocity and absorption measurements in very strong magnetic fields, we have found a previously unobserved state transition in the interlocked vortex lattice structure of the doped material La$_{2-x}$Sr$_{x}$CuO$_4$. The new state, which occurs when the magnetic field is between one and two times the transition field, is very stable with respect to thermal fluctuations and is only altered by a very small amount when the temperature is decreased from half of the transition temperature down to one-tenth of it. This new state shares many similarities with an ideal four-dimensional interlocked vortex lattice structure, as proven by calculations that take into account both the elasticity and the absorption of sound waves. These findings provide strong evidence for the idea that the transition to an interlocked vortex lattice structure is second-order and suggest that this transition might be first-order when there are only very weak interactions between the vortex lines. The location and field-dependent shift of the transition point, as well as the transition temperature in the presence of a strong magnetic field, have been determined precisely using a combination of sound wave velocity and absorption measurements at different temperatures and close to but not at the transition point. A theoretical prediction that the transition point should be located at half of the sound wave velocity's zero-field value when the magnetic field is strong enough to cause the lattice structure to be composed of closely packed squares was confirmed by our research. Our research also included an assessment of an alternative method that could be used to study this transition in better detail using another type of measurement. Finally, our research included an analysis of the location of the transition point in relation to a material's doping level.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into their behavior, however these theories have not considered the possibility of excluded volume effects on chain conformation or the possibility of a chain-free zone at the surface of highly elongated brushes. This study investigates strongly stretched brushes with excluded volume effects and a chain-free zone and determines the parameters that determine the size of the exclusion zone. It finds that for strongly stretched brushes with large aspect ratios, the exclusion zone size is directly proportional to the length of individual polymer chains and is independent of brush elongation, suggesting it adopts a constant ratio in relation to chain length. This ratio can be influenced by surface interactions and chain flexibility but remains largely unaffected by them. A theoretical model is developed to accurately predict the exclusion zone size in various brush shapes and its predictions are verified through force and brush size measurements in highly elongated brushes created under different surface conditions. This model is applicable to brushes formed from homopolymers and those created through block copolymer micelles and can be used to design highly elongated brushes with a chain-free zone size. This has implications for using highly elongated brushes as part of biosensors, where the exclusion zone can interfere with the binding of target molecules by providing a barrier at the surface of the brush. Introducing a chain-free zone may increase the size of target molecules that can bind, allowing for the binding of larger molecules such as proteins. This could be achieved by selecting a brush shape and composition that produces an exclusion zone of the desired size. This research provides a foundation for investigating highly elongated brushes in other environments and could also be applied to other systems that involve grafted polymers. This could also be applied to other systems that involve grafted polymers, such as nanogels and biopolymers and could offer valuable insights into the behavior of biopolymers and proteins near highly elongated brushes and could be used to design and develop new biosensors and drug delivery systems. This research could also be used to develop new methods for determining the properties of highly elongated brushes and the behavior of target molecules that bind to them. This could be achieved by selecting a brush shape and composition that produces an exclusion zone of the desired size and by using computational models that take into account the properties of the brush and the target molecule. A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph. Some properties of bounded distance graphs are generally easy to determine, for example their dimension will always be less than k+1. However, there are examples like the Petersen graph whose dimension values jump significantly, giving us reason to examine truncated dimensions of graphs more generally. Here we establish an upper and lower limit for the dimension of any graph when the distance limit is set to k, especially looking at even numbers k. Additionally, near its lower limit, a graph will always have a sub-set of vertices that provide the best identification with a number of vertices proportional to log(k). Besides distance capping, we also investigate a similar property where the vertices of a graph are identified using their second nearest neighbor distances, discussing some characteristics of graphs defined by their beta_k and gamma_2 dimensions. Some open questions related to these definitions are also raised here. Systematic methods for calculating both truncated dimensions are yet to be developed, so we present a new algorithm for calculating beta_k on finite graphs, building on existing approaches, and demonstrate its effectiveness with some examples, especially graph structures that give us insight into their dimension behavior when distances are capped. Lastly, this algorithm is used to investigate some general characteristics of graphs defined by their beta_k dimensions, especially how their dimension values increase as the distance limit increases, also exploring some relationships between different dimensions of the same graph, especially when the distance limit is two. Lastly, this definition is connected to some well-known graph properties and some new classes of graph attractors, and we discuss it in an abstract context as well. Finally, both theoretical analysis and computation using our algorithm are used to gather data and insights about both of these new graph properties.
