We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. Our analytical approach, involving the 
measurement of multiple PSF parameters, compared the light distribution of 
each target asteroid to that of its surrounding field stars. In contrast, our 
alternative method compared the spatial extent of the astronomical seeing 
(ASE) for each target asteroid and surrounding field stars. Both methods 
yielded a set of detection efficiency curves depending on binary separation, 
along with the ratio of the two binary components, and therefore allowed us 
to assess the capabilities of our analysis for identifying binary asteroids. 
Our results showed a $50\%$ detection efficiency for binary asteroids with 
solar reflection angles of 45 degrees, at binary separations up to 20 to 30 
kilometers, and with ASE values exceeding 5.5, 6.5, 7.5, and 8.5 for 4, 11, 
18, 36, and 50 kilometer diameter asteroids respectively. Ultimately, our 
analysis identified 15 potential wide binary asteroids, along with 7 known 
binary asteroids, from the analysis of over 12,000 images. Our research 
highlighted the value of combining survey data with high angular resolution, 
such as that produced by the Mauna Kea Infrared Telescope (MART), in order to 
confirm the wide binary nature of asteroids discovered through the Pan-STARRS1 
analysis. Lastly, five targets were recommended for observation with MART, 
namely 288 DC, 2003 CW11, 2011 QF48, 2011 YF3, and 2014 JN12, to confirm their 
wide binary status and gain insight into their formation and evolution. 
Generally, the detection of wide binary asteroids beyond 30 kilometers in 
separation remains a subject for further research and analysis. Ultimately, we 
believe our research provides a foundation for identifying a substantial 
portion of the estimated 2 million wide binary asteroids within the main asteroid belt. Systematic analysis of a wider range of survey data, coupled with the development of more sophisticated detection algorithms, will be crucial in achieving this goal. Additionally, our research highlights the importance of combining survey data with high angular resolution observations, such as those produced by the Mauna Kea Infrared Telescope

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org). To create
these tools, we employed Quasar and Vue.js web technologies to build engaging,
interactive viewers for visualizing galaxy spectra, SEDs, and diagnostic diagrams,
such as BPT diagrams generated from spectroscopic analysis. Leveraging client-side
processing via JavaScript minimizes server load, while maintaining seamless user
interactivity. Additionally, the adoption of modern web frameworks facilitates
extensive customization, making our visualization tools effortlessly integratable
into astronomical database websites and databases. Furthermore, this framework is
also compatible with Aladin Lite and other popular third-party web tools. By
open-sourcing these visualization utilities, we aim to contribute to the astral
community by providing customizable, reusable code that can be easily integrated
into astronomical databases and websites, and to present our methodology for
creating interactive data visualizers that can be employed alongside astronomical
data presented on the web. This code is now available through an GitHub repository
at https://github.com/astro-rcsed/rcsed-webtools, where users can access the API
docs at https://astro-rcsed.github.io/rcsed-webtools/api-documentation/. We are
currently expanding this framework to accommodate additional imaging and spectral
data visualizers, along with new analysis utilities, and we invite contributors
and collaborators to join this project by reaching out to the contact email at
rcsed@astro.queensu.ca. This project is supported by the National Science Foundation
Grant NSF ACI-1810230 for the Pico Formation and Disruption Network and by the Natural
Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada Discovery Grant for the
RCSED project. We are also grateful to the Centre for Research in Computational
Science and Engineering at Queen's University for providing computational resources
and technical support. Additionally, we would like to extend our appreciation
to the members of the astro-physics community at Queen's University for their input
and suggestions throughout this project. In conclusion, modern web visualization
tools, such as those employed in the rcsed2 database, now offer a more engaging
and interactive way to present complex astronomical data, along with spectroscopic
and imaging analysis utilities, thereby setting a new standard for astronomical
database websites and databases. This will help to better facilitate in-depth
analysis and interpretation of galaxy data

Research on magnetic anomalies in the region has enabled the reconstruction of ancient plate boundaries and movements. It is known that large igneous provinces in both Brazil and West Africa were created during the same period of rifting, which suggests the region experienced continental break-up with voluminous magmatism. However, the exact timing and duration of this process are subject to interpretation due to limited seismic data and the absence of distinctive oceanic magnetic anomalies in the region. A new study based on high-resolution seismic data and reflection correlation has allowed for a more precise definition of isochrons and the identification of key chronostratigraphic markers. As a result, the total duration of pre-break-up rifting in West Africa is estimated at 10-12 million years, with continental separation beginning around 126 million years ago. In contrast, the eastern margin of South America experienced a longer pre-break-up rifting period of around 20-22 million years, with separation occurring at 114 million years ago. The varying durations of pre-break-up rifting on either side of the developing Atlantic have significant implications for models of crustal extension and the associated magmatism, which suggest that pure shear played a more important role in West Africa than in Brazil. utilizes two primary components:  an information maximization objective and
a boundary-aware unsupervised learning objective.  The information
maximization objective is designed to reduce the representation learning

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal through conversation. We create the MasterMind system to excel in this role, combining two key components. Firstly, it utilizes a personalized, character-based dialogue model to tailor its interactions in a spontaneous and natural manner. This model is underpinned by a sophisticated theory-of-mind that enables it to anticipate the players' thoughts and behaviors, which, in turn, are driven by a sophisticated learning module inspired by Intentional Learning. We demonstrate the DungeonMaster's capabilities by having it guide not one, but up to four player characters through a fantasy adventure, showcasing the benefits of both its conversational prowess and its theory-of-mind abilities. These combined features allow the system to efficiently lead the players by balancing exploration and progress, outperforming a standard DungeonMaster by a substantial margin. Our evaluation data, along with the challenges and our solution, are now available for public perusal and replication. Moreover, we invite other researchers to participate in the G4C challenge by submitting their own DungeonMaster implementations for evaluation against our baseline performance. This challenge poses an intriguing question: Can a learning-based DungeonMaster surpass the standard, pre-programmed version even when the former is trained in an individualized setting but without the benefit of additional data? This question holds significance because it could serve as a benchmark for testing the potential of deep learning models in complex, real-world conversational scenarios. This challenge can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04378. Despite significant research on Lexical Semantic Change Detection, most approaches remain limited to standard model assessments. This study deviates from this focus, shifting towards change discovery - identifying previously unknown word meanings emerging over time within a comprehensive corpus vocabulary. By extensively fine-tuning both a type-based and a token-based methodology on German datasets, our work showcases their applicability in discovering new words with evolving meanings. Additionally, our proposed framework is designed for nearly full automation of both evaluation and discovery processes. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations. This study expands our knowledge on protein folding by demonstrating the existence of multiple folding pathways from natural states and highlights the significance of distinguishing between deep and shallow knots when analyzing these processes. Additionally, it demonstrates the usefulness of its statistical approach for comparing knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections and suggests potential applications for studying other complex biological processes. Furthermore, this research is available in the form of an online database that includes a tool for visually exploring the double-loop structures of proteins with shallow knots. This study provides valuable insights that can be used to improve the accuracy of protein folding predictions and folding dynamic simulations, particularly for proteins with trefoil knots. Additionally, it highlights the importance of considering the unique geometry of proteins with shallow knots in their natural state in order to make these predictions accurately. This study also offers a foundation for further research aimed at comparing the folding dynamics of proteins with shallow and deep knots as well as for investigating other important biological processes such as gene regulation and protein interactions that are influenced by a protein's three-dimensional structure. This research is supported by the National Science Foundation through the Research in Pair and Group Dynamics (RPGD) program and the online database is hosted by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI). This study is unique in that it combines the principles of topology and statistics to better understand complex biological processes and it provides valuable insights that can used to improve the accuracy of protein folding predictions and folding dynamic simulations, particularly for proteins with trefoil knots. This research is also notable for establishing an online database that includes a tool for visually exploring the double-loop structures of proteins with shallow knots and it highlights the importance of considering the unique geometry of proteins with shallow knots

To resolve the discrepancy known as the Hubble tension, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed. Although researchers agree on the existence of EDE, its properties remain unclear. By analyzing the Planck cosmic microwave background and the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's large-scale structure, we discovered varying results due to limitations of current constraints, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices. Employing an unbiased statistical analysis technique called a profile likelihood to assess EDE parameters, we determined a confidence interval of $f_\mathrm{EDE} = 0.072\pm 0.036$ ($68\%$ C.L.), providing a clearer picture of EDE and its potential solution to the Hubble tension. When combining the Hubble tension constraint with our new likelihood analysis, the EDE fraction is resolved and the Hubble tension is alleviated for the first time. This analysis highlights the significance of systematically evaluating current constraints and the necessity for more precise large-scale structure data, either from upcoming surveys like BOSS-5 or more comprehensive data from Euclid or SPT-ERIS, to either confirm or rule out EDE. These surveys will allow for a more precise solution to the Hubble tension and volume effects will become less influential in the future. Furthermore, we discovered that combining Planck and Baryon Acoustic Oscillation data leads to an unconstrained EDE fraction, however when combining these data with constraints on the primordial power spectrum, an EDE fraction below $0.046$ becomes ruled out at the $2\sigma$ level. Additionally, we found that profile likelihood and Bayesian methods yield comparable results for a flat prior on the EDE fraction, however the choice of prior has a more significant impact on the result than the method used. Building upon our previous research, we discovered a more robust estimate of the EDE density at matter-radiation equality, $\rho_\mathrm{EDE} / \rho_m \simeq 0.32\pm 0.16$ ($68\%$ C.L.), which provides a clearer understanding of the EDE component and may have a significant impact on model building. Furthermore, when combining this new constraint with the Hubble tension, the latter is alleviated for the first time. Finally, we discovered that the existing constraint on EDE has been overestimated due to limitations of current large-scale structure data, specifically volume effects that influence model parameter choices, resulting in an overestimation of the variance of the EDE fraction

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates the potential of utilizing single positive labels to generate high-quality multi-label samples, a problem the authors call single-to-multiple positive (S2MP) sampling.  A novel approach, multi-condition discriminator (MCD), is proposed to address this challenge.  MCD is positioned in front of a standard conditional GAN (CGAN) to sample diverse multi-label data from single positive labels, achieving this by generating probability distributions for each sample and corresponding target labels instead of fixed specific data and target combinations.  To train MCD effectively, a new multi-label sampling objective is developed that aligns with the standard cross-entropy loss used for single-label classification, allowing the network to be trained end-to-end.  Experimental results show that MCD's multi-label samples generated using single positive labels outperform those produced through random selection and match the accuracy of datasets with multiple labels, thereby validating its efficacy in real-world scenarios.  Code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/S2MP-sampling.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches and surpasses state-of-the-art baseline models by 10%. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates exceptional performance in real-world scenarios with unparalleled generalization capabilities, achieving a 12.5% boost in overall classification accuracy. It is available under the permissive MIT License and is currently the only comprehensive benchmark for wearable healthcare that incorporates code, data, and detailed guidelines at https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14342. This research is a collaborative effort between researchers from the University of Oulu and the University of Texas at San Antonio. This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive an explicit formula for the optimal control that switches between different modes at specific times, given certain conditions. We also establish a link between these conditions and the properties of the costs, which can result in significant reductions in complexity. Additionally, we show this formulation can be applied to a broader context, including costs with distinct levels in different time intervals. Finally, we provide a numerical example illustrating our findings. 

Finally, we consider a more general problem where the objective is to minimize costs subject to constraints on the number of times the system can switch between states, and derive an optimal solution by linking it to the problem with unrestricted switching. 

Both of these results can be interpreted through a resource allocation perspective, where the costs represent the rates at which a resource is consumed, and the constraints on switching represent the total amount of this resource available. 

One key consequence of these results is an implicit bound on the number of times the system can switch in a fixed time interval, obtained by scaling the results to a smaller time frame. 

Additionally, we show that when the costs are symmetric in the states, the optimal solution will switch between the same modes in the same order, even without additional structure. 

All of these solutions can be efficiently computed using a dynamic programming approach that is well-suited for problems with multiple switching times, even if some of these times are unknown in advance. 

One key aspect of this is a quasi-concave reformulation that allows for a significant expansion of known structures, such as concave and convex costs, and can lead to a substantial reduction in computational costs. 

However, even with this efficient computation, the optimal solution may not be feasible due to the underlying constraints, resulting in a need for a further adjustment that can also be efficiently computed. 

Finally, we show that when the costs are symmetric in the states and the system has multiple independent components, the optimal solution will switch between the same modes in the same order, even without additional structure, and that this structure is lost in a system with dependent components, even with symmetric costs. 

One key consequence of these results is an implicit bound on the number of times the system can switch in a fixed time interval, obtained by scaling the results to a smaller time frame, and that this bound holds for both independent and dependent components, as well as with and without structure.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. Consequently, it is essential to strike a balance between statistical and scientific expertise in modeling complex societal issues like epidemics. Ultimately, combining expertise from mathematics, statistics, and applied and pure sciences is essential to derive valuable insights from models that are critical for making informed decisions in the fight against pandemics. A call-to-action is issued for a more holistic approach to modeling that prioritizes the exploration of fundamental questions over the validation of established models. A brain tumor affects every age group and has the highest mortality rate.  MRI technology is commonly used for tumor detection and diagnosis by radiologists, who must accurately identify the tumor type and area for proper treatment planning.  However, interpreting MRI scans can be challenging and time-consuming for radiologists.  Building on advances in computer-aided diagnosis powered by deep learning, this study presents a multi-task attention guided network (MAG-Net) that can analyze MRI images to classify and segment brain tumors in coronal, axial, and sagittal planes.  The model was trained on the Figshare dataset containing 400 MRI images divided into three types (HGG, LGG, and Non-tumor) and was evaluated using metrics for segmentation and classification.  To enhance training and prevent overfitting, a data augmentation technique was applied, and a non-preemption strategy was employed for each task.  The proposed MAG-Net was compared to Baseline models (UNet and ResUNet) and State-of-the-art (SOA) models.  Experimental results showed improved performance in segmentation and classification when using the proposed MAG-Net model.  To validate the method's effectiveness, a comprehensive sensitivity analysis was conducted by simulating real-world applications.  The code for this research has been made available on GitHub, and the model has been deployed on Amazon SageMaker for brain tumor analysis.  Future directions for enhancing MRI-based tumor classification and segmentation are also discussed.

This method leverages the established capability of the SW3D-SLEVM scheme to be autodifferentiable, thereby enabling the use of advanced optimization techniques. In our proposed network, the shallow water equations are efficiently solved in three dimensions using an approximate 13.6-million-parameter representation, surpassing traditional numerical methods in speed while maintaining accuracy. Our research demonstrates exceptional promise, as the deep learning-based solution generator can be synthesized with initial and boundary conditions to produce solutions within a mere 0.25 milliseconds, amounting to a ~10,000-fold improvement over 1 second for the classical scheme, and showcasing potential applications in forecasting and simulation domains. Our model and associated data are freely accessible on the GitHub platform and the UCI Machine Learning Repository, respectively. We have observed exceptional performance preservation across diverse datasets, with only minimal data requirements, amounting to ~1000-condition samples for proper training. Our study has far-reaching implications, as the deep learning-based solution generator can be synthesized with historical and real-time data, enabling seamless integration in forecasting and simulation domains. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is conducted to evaluate how different factors affect solution convergence, including: the decomposition parameter in BDDC; three distinct AMG solver implementations (FenCSPO2, Pardiso, and Hypre); two different finite element codes (FENICS and in-house); three different types of heart muscle tissue tissue (Types I, III, and Arrhythmia); and various sizes of heart muscle tissue samples. By scaling up the problems to match real-world heart muscle tissue scales, an impressive fivefold improvement in convergence is observed with the BDDC algorithm when comparing small-scale to large-scale problems. However, further research is needed to fully understand how other factors influence solution convergence. An interesting finding from this study is that despite the significant improvement in convergence with larger domains, the time required to solve each iteration actually increases, highlighting a limitation with these scalable solvers. To address this, there is a need for more efficient iterative methods or solvers that can balance solution convergence with computational time. An equally striking improvement of up to fourfold with the BDDC algorithm is observed when comparing three-dimensional heart muscle tissue models to their two-dimensional counterparts. This study underlines the critical role that scalable multilevel preconditioners play in accurately modeling real-world heart muscle tissue mechanics by demonstrating that an essential feature of these models, fiber distribution, can significantly impact solution convergence. Ultimately, further exploration into the interaction between solver performance and heart muscle mechanics is recommended, along with potential areas for improving the accuracy of these models through the optimization of solver parameters. This study was conducted using a range of large-scale finite element simulations on up to 1024 processors at the National Institute for Computational Sciences (NICS) and the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC). Persuasive promotional videos are becoming increasingly influential in shaping consumer behavior and promoting social causes through various mediums such as e-commerce platforms and non-profit initiatives. Recent studies have uncovered the prevalence of gradient masking in purportedly robust adversarial defenses. Consequently, defense strategies based on this concept are considered ineffective and can be readily bypassed. Notably, research into quantifying the occurrence and magnitude of gradient masking across different networks remains limited. This study addresses this gap by exploring the mensurability of gradient masking as a multi-dimensional rather than a binary phenomenon. In addition, we introduce novel metrics designed to evaluate the presence of gradient masking in diverse neural networks. These proposed metrics not only offer computational advantages but also facilitate comparative assessments between models without necessitating elaborate tailor-made attacks. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the efficacy of these metrics in gauging the prevalence of gradient masking across different network configurations. The findings revealed that gradient masking exhibits network architecture-dependent behavior and tends to be more readily detected in smaller models and those with simpler architectures. The introduced metrics, along with comprehensive analysis and visualizations, are made available at https://github.com/soheli77/Measuring-Gradient-Masking for the benefit of the research community. Notably, one of the proposed metrics, the magnitude-based score, has been incorporated into the widely used FoolIQ evaluation framework with the designation "ms1". This study's contributions are particularly significant in the context of benchmarking FoolIH, the improved version of FoolIQ, which incorporates enhanced evaluation metrics. By providing a comprehensive evaluation framework that considers multiple dimensions of model behavior, FoolIH is poised to become a valuable resource for the community in identifying essential benchmarks for the assessment of intelligent systems. Furthermore, the incorporation of the ms1 metric in FoolIH underscores the importance of collaborative research between multiple independent parties, including the present authors, the creators of the FoolIQ suite, and our institution. This collaboration has resulted in the enhancement of the evaluation framework through the inclusion of the ms1 metric in FoolIH, which now serves as a benchmark against which the performance of the FoolIH framework will be evaluated. Additionally, the inclusion of the ms1 metric in FoolIH represents a significant step in recognizing the contributions of all parties involved in this collaboration. This concept, however, has not yet been implemented at the MHz frequencies common in ultrasound imaging due to difficulties in fabricating complex microstructures. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine and characterize the diffusion population's behavior under two main condition types: (1) independent and distinct diffusion characteristics for each individual, and (2) overlapping and diverse diffusion characteristics for the population as a whole. We demonstrate, theoretically and numerically, that even in the absence of direct relationships between individuals, their diverse characteristics can result in complex, non-Gaussian anomalies. Moreover, this diffusion phenomenon can be achieved where the population's spatial distribution as observed over time exhibits cubic growth in time. We further show, both theoretically and numerically, that even in cases of independent individuals with distinct characteristics, their collective behavior can lead to Gaussian, non-anomalous, and time-dependent diffusion profiles. Our research thus highlights the adequacy of time-dependent diffusion profiles in describing the spread of diverse individual entities. We refer to this as the 'diversity diffusion hypothesis'. It has implications for the dissemination of various individual entities in physics, biology, and finance, suggesting that a fractional Gaussian framework can effectively capture their complex diffusion behavior. We also demonstrate the 'diversity diffusion hypothesis' for time-dependent diffusion profiles in physics, specifically in the case of dispersion in a turbulent fluid, where we find that a fractional Lagrangian approach can accurately describe the diverse diffusion characteristics of individual particles by incorporating their varying lifetimes and mixing rates. We further show that in some cases of dispersion in a turbulent fluid, the diversity diffusion hypothesis can lead to a new definition of subdiffusion as an isolated phenomenon, rather than an anomalous diffusion type. We also explore strategies for parameter estimation and model selection, comparing two methods: a deterministic one based on the population's average characteristics, and a stochastic one based on the spread of individual realizations. We examine three scenarios for time-dependent diffusion profiles: early non-overslapping, late overlapping, and V-shaped profiles. We demonstrate the applicability of the diversity diffusion hypothesis to Lagrangian dispersion in turbulent flows and time-dependent diffusion profiles in physics, biology, and finance, including the spreading of susceptible and infected individuals in network models and SIR models, population spread in physics, the dispersal of phytoplankton in ocean flows, and wealth distribution in finance. This paper focuses on control systems characterized by differential inclusions that have bounded trajectories when the control input is restricted to a given control set with compact reachability set $\mathcal{Q}$. Given that $\mathcal{Q}$ is attractor-based for system trajectories and a compact set with asymptotic properties, we establish conditions under which there exists a locally defined, strict Lyapunov function associated with system trajectories and $\mathcal{Q}$. A recent study proposes a novel deep learning approach that utilizes generative adversarial networks to generate highly detailed turbulent velocity patterns from limited-resolution data across a range of Reynolds numbers. A specially designed multiscale model was utilized for high-resolution velocity reconstruction, with the assessment of its effectiveness being performed through direct numerical simulation data for turbulent flow with longitudinal obstacles at different Reynolds numbers. The assessment revealed that this deep learning framework accurately replicates high-resolution velocity statistics and multifunctional energy spectra from two distinct Reynolds numbers, specifically $320$ and $640$. Notably, this deep learning model successfully reconstructed turbulent velocity patterns even outside its initial training dataset, indicating its potential for super-resolution applications. Additionally, it was observed that two key factors contribute to the accurate reconstruction of turbulent velocity patterns: a sufficient number of high-resolution training samples and a sufficient distance between the training and prediction Reynolds numbers for satisfactory energy spectrum reconstruction. On the other hand, the proposed approach was found to be insensitive to minor differences in velocity statistics between two distinct Reynolds numbers, with the outcome being a deep learning model that effectively reconstructs turbulent velocity patterns via upscaling and super-resolution techniques. The accuracy of machine learning models heavily relies on their confidence calibration. Deep neural network-based classifiers have a common issue, however - they often provide predictions that seem overly certain but do not reflect the true likelihood of classification accuracy. This limitation is attributed to the inherent closed-world nature of traditional softmax formulation. As cross-entropy loss encourages models to classify inputs into a fixed number of pre-defined categories, this can result in overly confident predictions that fail to capture true uncertainty. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. This approach involves introducing an extra dimension to account for uncertainty and adds a loss function that learns from labeled data, thereby addressing the closed-world issue. Furthermore, this formulation is enhanced with an energy-based function to model the true data distribution in an open-world setting, enabling better uncertainty representation. A new loss function is defined, and AD-KAE, a deep architecture, is introduced to learn this distribution in the open world. Experimental results on confidence calibration, robustness, and transfer learning demonstrate the superiority of the proposed methods over existing baselines. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods that can adapt and expand their knowledge base naturally. In line with the principles of cumulative learning, we introduce Lifelong Learning (LL) as the preferred methodology and present LLExplorer, an exploration platform that incorporates this approach. To validate the efficacy of LL methods within this environment, we have developed various challenges featuring a range of tasks that learn from experience and emerge over time, requiring the learner to continuously discover and master new objectives alongside existing ones. Our results indicate that lifelong learning techniques consistently outperform their non-continual counterparts by overcoming the limitations imposed on them and proving that the environment can support a wide range of evaluation metrics in the field. Understanding business processes relies on process discovery methods, analyzing data trails to reveal underlying processes. As processes evolve over time, their models must adapt, otherwise they may inaccurately predict future behaviors. Our approach develops an algorithm to identify processes from event flows, even in dynamic environments, and provides a declarative framework for process monitoring and discovery. This algorithm uses a set of temporal logic formulas to capture event data relationships and declare process characteristics, such as start and end points. It discovers processes by determining the most constrained process fitting the data, using a parameter that controls complexity and preventing overfitting. Our implementation and tests demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency. Additionally, our approach and experiments show that processes can be accurately described with only essential attributes, even in scenarios with varying event densities, supporting the thesis that process discovery should consider attribute complexity in both data and processes. Our method and evaluation provide a foundation for further research into declarative process discovery and monitoring. Our code is available for review and reproduction of results. It can be used for process discovery, even in static settings, but is primarily designed for testing and refining methods for data quality issues that affect discovery algorithms. Our experiment data and process instances are available in SPARQL and CSV formats, stored in public query repositories and file repositories, respectively. Our research involves four event data sets with different characteristics and derived from diverse sources, including financial transactions, website click streams, email exchanges, and user activity logs. Our process models and assessments of their validity are supported by formal and informal analyses, including model checking and case studies. Our evaluation of discovered processes considers their executability, complexity, and alignment with initial process patterns, including prefixes and event sequences that indicate process starts and ends. Our code and results demonstrate that our approach delivers accurate process models, even in dynamic settings with varying event rates, but it may struggle with processes that have similar start and end points, due to limitations of our declarative process language. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. This processing system, called the Data Reduction System, will be responsible for delivering refined data to astronomers and uploading it to the Keck Observatory Archive. Optical systems that measure intensity in a particular mode are limited by the Rayleigh criterion by the number of modes squared, significantly limiting their capacity. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel bi-photon system that allows for the precise identification of mode states, even under intense laser illumination. Achieving this involves creating two entangled beams with a large number of modes and using one of these to enhance the measurement process. However, a significant challenge arises when trying to increase the resolution beyond the theoretical limit imposed by the entanglement's coherence length. To solve this issue, we suggest using a lens with a specific power that, although decreasing coherence, allows for an increased number of coherent measurements, effectively exceeding the Rayleigh criterion in proportion to the square root of the ratio of the system's intensity to its entropy. A functional experimental setup has been created using a source of entangled fiber optics and a binary phase plate, and has demonstrated the ability to distinguish up to 6x6 mode states, representing an exponential increase from the conventional limit. The novel approach presented here offers a viable strategy for enhancing optical communication systems that measure intensity in a particular mode, enabling them to process much more information than was previously possible. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. Specifically, it focuses on Shimura varieties and their connections to algebraic and analytic torus bundles. By drawing on both methods, we can gain a deeper understanding of the structures and properties of moduli spaces. The compilation presents existing research on this subject, covering chapters on integral structures in Hodge theory, torus bundles, and the Baily-Borel compactification, as well as an overview of current work and open problems. Integral structures in Hodge theory are the primary focus of Chapter 1, with an in-depth exploration of their existence, properties, and behavior under duality and symmetry. Chapter 2 delves into the world of torus bundles, examining their definitions, properties, and connections to Shimura varieties. Chapter 3 discusses the Baily-Borel compactification, with a focus on its construction, relationship to algebraic and geometric compactifications, and connections to the nonarchimedean Hermitian symmetric spaces that form the points of Shimura varieties. A significant amount of background material is included to ensure the document is self-contained, with a strong emphasis on the interplay between the algebraic, geometric, and analytic communities that has driven the advancement of our knowledge in this area over the past decade. This knowledge has been further solidified through a series of lectures and conferences supported by the Centre de Recerca Matem\`atica (CRM) and the University of Oxford. The resulting document is a comprehensive summary of the current state of research in this field, with contributions from various experts, including Jean-Pierre Labbé, Andres Navarro, Alberto Air\al, Eva M. Bayer, Andreas Malm, and Shou-Wu Zhang. This work is a product of the research project "Algebraic, geometric and analytic aspects of Hodge structures and moduli spaces" (CRM-2018/19, University of Oxford-2019/20). This document is available at https://www.math.uzh.ch/en/research/groups/alm-geom-grp.html. Additionally, all involved researchers have contributed to the development of enhanced online notes for this project, with the full collection accessible at the same URL. In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and understanding what causes them is crucial. This research focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where a predator with fast and slow reproduction rates targets two prey species, reproducing at respective speeds that are similarly dual-timed. By examining the model's behavior in a stable state and during a critical Slowing-Down Transition caused by the predator's slow population decline, the study aims to detect early warning signs of the sudden population change and analyze the transition's underlying mechanisms. The analysis of the model reveals the presence of a critical fluctuation in the prey populations just before the transition, which can be used as an early warning indicator. The study also finds that the fast-reproducing prey play a significant role in initiating the transition, the ratio of the fast-to-slow reproduction rates affects the critical fluctuation and the early warning sign, and the onset of the transition is influenced by a critical fluctuation in the fast-reproducing prey population and an asymptotic oscillation in the slow-reproducing prey population. The study's findings are supported by numerical solutions and confirmed by an asymptotic analysis. The study's results provide a framework for detecting early warning signs of sudden population changes and understanding the mechanisms underlying these changes in a wide range of ecosystem models. Recently, cache coherence protocols based on self-invalidation and self-downgrade have gained more recognition due to their minimalistic design, potential for increased performance efficiency, and reduced energy consumption. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. We also examine methods for repairing programs to prevent security breaches when the protocol causes memory instruction reordering and analyze how altering fence placements affects the outcome in cases of reordering leading to program termination or deadlock. Furthermore, we present a model for integrating our repair method into a compiler and investigate optimization strategies for existing programs via fence placement configuration parameters in our theoretical framework. Additionally, we establish the condition under which the image of $B^{H}$ on $[0,1]$ has a non-empty interior for Lebesgue measure. This condition is shown to be equivalent to $H$ exceeding $\frac{d}{2}$. We also demonstrate the existence of drifts resulting in the accumulation of measure zero on the boundary for Lebesgue measure within the image of $B^{H}$. Specifically, we find that our approach reliably reproduces both classical equilibrium points and chaotic regimes, as determined by calculating fractional occupation numbers at different microscopic configurations; these calculations reveal that quantum chaos can be identified by evaluating Jackiw-Kerman's parameter, which is linked to the fractional occupation numbers, in conjunction with our variational approach's ability to handle potential perturbations, as opposed to fixed mean-field approximations. Such understanding of quantum chaos within the H\'enon-Heiles model is made possible by our approach's ability to seamlessly connect classical and quantum regimes through a unified Hamiltonian framework. Through our study, we demonstrate that our approach aligns with standard mean-field theories when the trial functions are chosen appropriately, and we also demonstrate that our method for evaluating quantum chaos in the H\'enon-Heiles model can be applied more broadly to other Hamiltonian systems via a transformation of variables, rendering our approach a powerful analytical tool for exploring quantum chaos in complex potential landscapes. Furthermore, our findings provide a foundation for exploring both many-body phenomena and the relationship between quantum chaos and collective modes in complex potential systems. Through our research, we also demonstrate the utility of our approach in predicting the regimes of quantum chaos that have yet to be explored through experimental and numerical studies. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by identifying features in X-ray images that indicate a greater risk of complications.  However, the challenge lies in distinguishing between features that indicate a higher risk of death or severe illness and those that indicate a lower risk of the same.  In this research, we explore the hypothesis by focusing on identifying features in X-ray images that indicate patients who will die from COVID-19 rather than those who will survive.  Our experiments used the COVID-19 detection dataset from CSI with enhanced data by adding radiology reports that provide crucial information about patient outcomes.  We utilized classification without utilizing the reports and obtained a high accuracy rate of 97.08%.  Notably, we discovered that models performed poorly on a separate test dataset, indicating difficulty in generalizing to unseen data.  To overcome this limitation, we incorporated the radiology reports into feature learning.  Our results showed a significant improvement to 73.40% and importantly, uncovered 11 distinct regions in lung images that have a high correlation with patient outcomes as indicated by radiology reports.  Our analysis of these regions revealed patterns that could contribute to the understanding of COVID-19 complications and potentially other critical conditions. The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a functor when C is over a field k, specifically to the category of simplicial groups in Set_\omega obtained through iteration of the functor Simp_k -> Set_\omega induced by the classical universal bundle functor W_k. This enhanced universal bundle functor W still preserves the simplicial group structure, and we prove this result by demonstrating a equivalence between the category of simplicial groups in Set_\omega and the category of simplicial groups in C when C is defined as the simplicial sets represented by iterated simplicial W_k. Furthermore, we establish that this result extends to simplicial sets with composition laws in Set_\omega. Additionally, we provide an interpretation of the universal bundle functor in the context of categories as an equivalence between the category of simplicial groups in Set_\omega and the category of simplicial categories in Set_\omega induced by the functor that treats group operations as associative and unitary. This induced functor is proven to be fully faithful and essentially surjective, and we employ this to provide an alternate proof of the categorification of classifying spaces for finite groups. Lastly, we discuss how this result extends to the context of homotopy theory over a simplicial ring.

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. To address this issue, we proposed two key modifications. Firstly, we introduced a proposal distribution balancing technique, known as Balanced VRD, which adjusts the proposal distribution through a supplementary filtering process. By doing so, it reduces the impact of easily eliminable proposals. Secondly, we developed an advanced filter-based approach known as FilterVRD, which directly targets challenging proposals by incorporating a filter-based mechanism in place of the graph convolutional network (GCN). This results in a more balanced proposal distribution and reduced false positives. When tested on Visual Genome, our BalancedVRD method achieved a significant 8.9% mAP improvement. Furthermore, our FilterVRD method demonstrated outstanding performance on the VisKel dataset, achieving a remarkable 12.3% mAP improvement. When combining the two methods, we achieved a further 2.4% mAP improvement, indicating that our proposed techniques are highly effective in reducing false positives. System configurations and model parameters are provided in the supplementary materials. The code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/False-Positives-in-VRD. The comprehensive evaluation metrics for VRD are introduced in the supplementary materials. Due to the high qualitative standards of top-tier VRD conferences, we have chosen to present our work at CVPR, one of the premier computer vision conferences. The paper was submitted to CVPR 2023. One of the technique predecessors was initially proposed at ICLR 2020, named Easy-Hard Data Balancing, an earlier attempt at balancing difficult data. However, this method failed to deliver expected results in VRD. Consequently, we explored novel solutions, resulting in substantial improvements over the original methods. One of our proposed methods, FilterVRD, has shown outstanding performance on the VisKel dataset, an uncommon VRD dataset. As a result, we have submitted an extended version of this dataset to the MMLA 2023 workshop, available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.04398, alongside an evaluation of current state-of-the-art VRD models on the extended VisKel dataset, with the paper available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.04398. This study focuses on action recognition in scenarios with limited data and low-light conditions, common challenges in various surveillance applications. Notably, existing approaches often struggle with recognition in both low-light and real-world scenarios due to image degradation. To address this issue, our proposed method builds upon recent action recognition models while addressing two critical issues: (1) the impact of data quality on recognition and (2) the inherent differences between training and testing phases. Specifically, our method leverages the delta sampling technique to enhance data quality and mitigate overfitting in training, thereby enabling generalization to testing data. Moreover, our method employs a contrastive learning-based augmentation strategy to enhance the representation of dark action videos. Experimental evaluations on seven action recognition datasets with varying lighting conditions have demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed method. Notably, our method achieves exceptional performance compared to baseline models, especially under low-light conditions. To further validate the generalization of our method, we conducted comprehensive experiments on three real-world datasets under real-world scenarios, with surprising results showing that models trained in dark conditions consistently outperform those trained in bright conditions. Our method has achieved notable improvements over state-of-the-art models on multiple benchmark datasets, with source code available at https://github.com/zhengyuan-hu/R-BERT-ADA. For further inquiries, please contact the authors at zyhu@mmu.ac.uk or xiang.xu@mmu.ac.uk. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely captures Caxton C. Foster's pioneering ideas on parallel processing, incorporating the concepts of simultaneous parallel writes and the merging of output values – features commonly omitted in typical CAM applications like network routing. The resulting system allows a host computer to interface with the CAPP over USB/UART using a simple serial communication protocol, which has been effectively demonstrated with a Python-based driver. The system boasts an impressive 10 nanosecond lookup speed, outperforming even the fastest mainframe computers in literature. With a 1024-entry capacity and 32-bit word size, the system successfully passes rigorous test cases, including both random and ordered data scenarios, and has been successfully integrated into a larger project, a network processor, in a manner that works as expected. The design and associated challenges are discussed in detail, along with potential applications and the feasibility of scaling the design to larger CAM sizes. The design faces memory write-allon (MAW) challenges in both hardware and software, requiring a novel solution that redefines the standard CAM cell architecture, resulting in a working prototype that could serve as a foundation for building other complex hardware systems. The documentation provides guidelines for replicating the hardware using the SPARTAN-6 LX48 FPGA board but cautions that the design may not be compatible with other FPGA models due to the unique characteristics of the used FPGA model. The design and associated drivers are made available for public use and are suitable for inclusion in academic and corporate projects. We present new HST/WFC3 near-infrared F160W observations of a group of galaxies at $\chi = 2.72$ that were massive and quiescent in the early universe, and focus on a specific galaxy, GS-Maple-17, as its members change and shift towards us. This galaxy was once part of a pair with GS-Maple-18 but is now isolated and exhibits distinct characteristics - it has a highly asymmetrical disk and a central bulge that is likely composed of ancient stars. Unlike its sister galaxy, GS-Maple-17 shows no evidence of major mergers in its formation history and is not significantly affected by large-scale absorption or rescattering from the surrounding medium, allowing for a clear comparison of their structural and stellar properties. A detailed study using Chandra, HST, ALMA, and GMOS reveals that GS-Maple-17 is a highly asymmetrical galaxy with a large central bulge, a massive and compact core, and a mix of young and old star populations within its disk. A detailed analysis of the gas and stellar content in these two galaxies suggests a connection between the distribution of gas and the formation of their bulges and central star clusters. No studies on the periodicity of its solutions have been done previously, so we explore related issues by making some key assumptions about a given function, Q(y), which is periodic and has a minimum value at zero. We demonstrate that numerous "bubbling solutions" for this equation exist and are distinct when the given conditions are met in a certain manner. Additionally, we find that some of these solutions change over time in a cyclic way. This new approach enables us to prove the existing Guo-Qing Zhang paper's main theorem. Current cutting-edge neural code models excel at generating individual code segments but often struggle with producing coherent, functional code as a whole. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that leverages static program analysis for weak supervision. Our method employs machine learning to produce instructions based on a static program analysis phase, effectively bypassing the reliance on vast code datasets. We have tested this approach on two distinct code languages – C code and Neural Machine Code – and have observed remarkable results, with our models achieving superior code quality compared to state-of-the-art neural code generators while also demonstrating improved functional accuracy according to our rigorous human evaluations. Our research opens up exciting possibilities for the generation of complex code with a strong focus on functionality and coherence. We have also explored a new evaluation framework that assesses code quality based on both human and machine metrics, and have made significant strides towards developing a strong baseline for the neural code generation task. We have made our code and data available at https://github.com/ku89/neural-program-generation. Our work has further inspired a follow-up investigation that can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04378.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant event on November 7, 2004, linked to a powerful X2.0 solar flare. This event was not reported in daily solar records, which are typically released over 24 to 48 hours after the event and are based on data from satellites in orbit. As a result, it was classified as a weak flare at the time and didn't warrant further investigation. However, recordings of neutron decay protons, which are an indicator of neutrons in the sun's corona, revealed a significant increase of up to 10 times the normal level for several hours following the flare. This increase is consistent with the deployment of neutrons into the sun's corona as seen in previous large solar flares and coronal mass ejections. In this scenario, it is proposed that in addition to the detection of neutron decay protons, there may also be observable solar decay protons visible from the ground under certain conditions, particularly in relation to X-ray flares that have sufficient energy and are observed from relatively low altitudes. This finding is particularly relevant given that there are numerous ground-based observations of the sun that could be re-examined for evidence of such events. A simulation of the detection capabilities from ground-based observatories suggests that in addition to the November 2004 event, there may be other undetected solar neutron decay protons events that occurred before the advent of space-based satellites capable of detecting neutrons in the sun's corona. These events could provide valuable information on high-energy solar phenomena and the composition of neutrons in the sun's corona that has been released into the heliosphere. A review of daily solar records and radio blackbody spectra from the sun between 1965 and 2004 did not reveal any other instances of observable solar decay protons, suggesting that such events are rare and dependent on specific flare conditions. Real-time anomaly detection in continuous data streams presents difficulties for conventional and advanced methods due to shifting concepts and ongoing learning requirements. Existing approaches, such as using hash functions or nearest neighbors with fixed memory, can struggle to accommodate frequent fluctuations, remove smooth outliers, and adapt to deep neural network architectures. We introduce a new technique for continuous real-time anomaly detection based on quantum measurements, which can process infinite data streams at constant $O(1)$ update complexity and effectively estimate changing densities through random Fourier features and an exponential moving average. This approach was thoroughly evaluated by comparing it to 12 prominent algorithms for real-time anomaly detection on 9 diverse data streams. It consistently outperformed or matched the performance of every comparison method in all evaluations, demonstrating superior or equivalent performance in all experiments. All implementation details are available under an permissive open-source license at this link https://github.com/InQMAD Team/InQMAD. Due to its high performance and scalability, this method is particularly well-suited for applications involving high-speed data streams, such as streaming from sensors or log files, and high-performance computing environments like distributed systems and cloud platforms. Furthermore, it offers competitive or superior results in comparison to established methods for real-time anomaly detection while providing the most efficient update complexity among all evaluated techniques. This discovery was further validated by conducting comprehensive evaluations on both synthetic and real-world datasets in conjunction with the release of a new benchmark for continuous real-time anomaly detection, which is made available at this link https://github.com/InQMAD Team/InQMAD-baselines-and-benchmark. Additionally, the evaluation protocol, metrics, and source code for the evaluation are available at this link https://github.com/InQMAD Team/InQMAD-baselines-and-benchmark. This technique has been applied to detect anomalies in sensor data from an industrial robot by one of the sponsors, resulting in a working prototype available at this link https://github.com/InQMAD Team/InQMAD-in-industry. InQMAD has been successfully commercialized by one of the sponsors under the name "StreamInspector" which provides real-time anomaly detection for data streams and is available at this link https://streaminspector.com. Furthermore, the evaluation protocol, metrics, and source code for the evaluation have been incorporated into the StreamInspector software, along with additional features based on the results of the evaluation. A pivotal question arises when a court possesses information that an individual knows the passcode to a device. To answer this inquiry, we develop a novel approach to an established legal doctrine, drawing on precedents set by the case of Fisher v. US. Our overarching objective is to create a framework that clarifies whether any action not inherently communicative can be deemed 'testimonial' in nature. In turn, this framework would in turn define the scope of a court's power to compel a respondent to perform an action, such as decrypting a device. Using this framework, we would then determine the applicability of existing legal precedents to the situation at hand. Ultimately, we apply this framework to conclude that, in this scenario, the government's power to compel action not necessarily constitutively communicative is limited by the Fourth Amendment's protection against unreasonable searches and seizures. Consequently, we believe that, regardless of whether an individual's knowledge of a passcode can be deemed 'testimonial', it cannot be used as a basis to subject that individual to an unreasonable search. Therefore, we would rule that the government can compel the respondent to perform the requested action, but this decision would be made with consideration for Fourth Amendment protections rather than any arbitrary standard. In effect, we would establish that the court's power to compel action in this manner is essentially equivalent to their authority to direct a third-party actor to perform the same action, thus sidestepping any potential 'testimonial' implications. In the interest of advancing the ongoing legal discussion, we propose an alternative approach that prioritizes a more direct analysis of the situation at hand, drawing on the principles established in the case of Fisher v. US, without reliance on our proposed framework. Under this alternative framework, we would determine that the government can compel the respondent to perform the requested action, but only if the court's directive to that individual constitutes a search that the respondent has not consented to. This solution builds upon our previous algorithmic achievements, specifically leveraging the previously established quasi-Poisson property of such instances and extending the applicability of our method to incorporate non-uniform weight values. Our implementation takes advantage of the symmetry present in the instance to achieve more efficient computational performance, resulting in a PTAS that is directly applicable to a broad category of CSPs, including but not limited to, graph coloring, unique satisfiability, and Max-Cut, even when the underlying variables are assigned non-standard weight values. The effectiveness of this solution is illustrated through a demonstration of its application to several prominent CSP benchmarks. The algorithmic technique we employed relies heavily on the algorithmic framework introduced by Kolmogorov in 2006. The ability to deliver a PTAS is guaranteed by a method that involves an iterative process of locally exchanging neighboring variable assignments with the potential for a significant improvement in cost, albeit with the limitation that such exchanges are constrained to adhere to a general rule known as the '4-line property'. The algorithmic solution for each individual variable involves identifying and selecting the most favorable exchange opportunity from a defined set of candidates, with this selection often being achievable in practice through basic comparison operations. The implementation of this algorithm for each variable is a critical component towards the overall solution of the CSP. The algorithmic solution for the entire CSP is then obtained by an iterative process of iteratively solving for each individual variable through this exchange-based algorithm, with this process being repeated until a designated stopping criterion is met. The ability to deliver a PTAS for any given variable relies on the definition of a suitable neighborhood that is used to identify potential exchange candidates, with this neighborhood being defined as all possible variable assignments within a limited range of the current value, with this range being specifically tailored to achieve a balance between being sufficiently large enough to capture a significant portion of the instance's quasi-Poisson structure and being small enough to ensure that the resulting exchange-based algorithm converges in a polynomial-time frame. The algorithmic solution for each variable is then guaranteed to converge to a value that is representative of the instance's quasi-Poisson structure and is therefore amenable to approximation. Advancements in machine learning and signal processing have generated substantial interest in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), which excel at solving complex, engineering-driven problems. Nonetheless, employing such networks for critical life-altering decisions demands a deeper understanding of their decision-making processes. Unfortunately, most artificial neural networks, including DNNs, function as opaque systems, hindering insight into their internal workings. Although some research has initiated the quest to illuminate their behavior, the field of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) remains underdeveloped. This study aims to offer a comprehensive overview of not only the attempt to interpret the inner workings of DNNs but also the visual representation of their capabilities and methodology. In the subsequent sections, we will delve into the diverse techniques employed to grasp the behavior of artificial neural networks, visualize their functionality, and facilitate the design of more effective and transparent networks. Finally, we will discuss the scope of research in this domain, along with the challenges and potential future directions for researchers and practitioners within the XAI community. In addition, we will make available a representative compilation of methods employed to analyze the behavior of artificial neural networks, which can be accessed at https://github.com/ghaffari/DeepNeuralNetworks.git. This survey seeks to contribute meaningfully to the XAI community by providing a thorough exploration of the subject matter. Nonetheless, it is essential to acknowledge the speed at which research in this domain progresses, and as such, future editions of this survey will be necessary to capture the most up-to-date developments. Furthermore, we would like to extend our gratitude to the researchers whose work has contributed to this survey and to the editors and reviewers of the ICICS Conference for their valuable feedback. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we would expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that any internal mixing patterns do not indicate y$^\dagger$ values greater than 0.8, and confirmed that any internal heat distribution discrepancies are not significant enough to be detected. We also established that any spin-down due to a convective core is not noticeable until at least 10 K in temperature difference. We considered two possible scenarios to explain the observed rotation pattern: one involves hiding a planetary body that the star has ingested, and the other posits newly discovered angular momentum transport processes. We based our estimates on both scenarios and found the following: for the planetary engulfment scenario, stars similar to 9267654 must swallow at least 0.8 Jupiter bodies every 10 days; for the new angular momentum transport mechanism, we derived equations that can be applied universally to any given core radius and rotation period, and found that 9267654's rotation pattern occurs at a critical boundary where its core radius falls within the transition zone between two distinct angular momentum transport regimes. This discovery opens up the possibility of investigating similar scenarios in other stars. Additionally, we proposed potential markers for identifying stars that exhibit the 9267654 rotation pattern, and confirmed KIC 10466702 and KOI-813002836 as two such stars based on their light curves and rotation periods. Further research is required to validate these findings through additional constraints and more precise measurements of key parameters. Moreover, future studies should delve into the underlying physics of angular momentum transport processes and potentially hide planetary bodies within stars, and consider how these processes might influence and shape the evolution of massive stars in greater detail. Ultimately, a deeper comprehension of these processes will provide valuable insights into the evolution and behavior of rotating massive stars throughout their life cycles. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation creates a substantial obstacle for the current methods in detecting false news on unexpected events. Furthermore, the fact that newly emerging events necessitate building a new model from scratch or retraining the existing one, which is often expensive, time-consuming, and impractical in real-world settings, adds to the magnitude of this challenge. In addition, given the restricted capacity of models to generalize across domains, the necessity of conducting separate training for each event arises. In light of these difficulties, we propose a novel Fake News Detection system suitable for real-world applications, capable of processing multiple data types, such as text, images, and graphs, and leverages a Compose Neural Process model that addresses the generalization issue across different events by generating a specific model for each event through targeted Compose Neural Process modules. This approach enables our system to detect false news on unexpected events with limited labeled data. Experimental evaluations on two diverse datasets with newly emerging events demonstrate the superiority of our proposed system over existing methods. Moreover, a practical application of our system to Twitter datasets reveals its effectiveness in real-world settings. Source code is available at https://github.com/soheli77/MFNPD. Two new datasets, namely COVID-19 and Climate Change datasets are available at https://github.com/soheli77/MFNPD/tree/main/datasets. Finally, a preliminary evaluation of our system on climate change datasets is presented at https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.00831. This work is a significant advancement in the field of multi-modal fake news detection, particularly on unexpected events, and is a vital step towards creating a robust system for real-world applications. It is also an important contribution to the community by introducing novel techniques and a new framework for multi-modal neural networks in the context of fake news detection. This paper investigates the age of information (AoI) in a discrete-time status updating system that employs the Ber/G/1/1 queue. We demonstrate that utilizing a two-dimensional state vector which simultaneously monitors AoI and packet age enables derivation of the stationary AoI distribution via analysis of a constructed stochastic process.
