Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have sparked significant interest and created opportunities for studying anomalous transport phenomena. A particular class of materials, known as antiferromagnetic antiperovskites, has shown substantial anomalous Hall conductivity even in the absence of magnetization. However, there is a critical need to investigate these materials using both theoretical and experimental methods. Very few experimental studies have been conducted to date, primarily due to difficulties in accurately measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient. In an attempt to bridge this knowledge gap, we have investigated the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN thin films and found a large anomalous Nernst coefficient, $\gamma_{AH} = 0.44 \gamma_{0}$, that is consistent with our magnetic and electrical resistance measurements. Notably, we observed a significant and reversible change in the anomalous Nernst coefficient when applying an external magnetic field along the easy plane of magnetization, which is in contrast to the conventional thermoelectric effect and ferromagnetic resonance theory. Our findings also reveal that the anomalous Nernst coefficient is directly proportional to the square of the spontaneous magnetic field and the square of the resistivity. In addition, we have successfully demonstrated that an electric field can be generated through the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN by varying the temperature, which has the potential to enhance its efficiency by more than twice through a thermocyclic process. Recently, pre-trained models have significantly impacted ranking systems, delivering outstanding results. To balance high performance with computational efficiency, knowledge distillation is now extensively employed. In this research, we address two critical challenges in knowledge distillation for ranking models: 1) leveraging multiple teachers; and 2) utilizing label data within the distillation process. We introduce the Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE) framework to concurrently address both concerns. By iteratively combining multi-teacher logits guided by label information, PILE has shown superior performance in offline and online experiments. Furthermore, our method has been successfully integrated into a real-world commercial search platform. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/daikui/PILE.

This lecture will provide an elementary overview of both transverse and longitudinal beam dynamics, in addition to key beam loss phenomena in circular accelerators, catering to attendees with minimal to no prior understanding of this topic. Starting from fundamental concepts such as the relativistic bubble model and reference frames, we will proceed to discuss particle motion, synchronization issues, beam losses resulting from particle misalignment, intrapellet beam losses, and stimulated spontaneous emission. A brief review of beam transmission's underlying factors will be presented at the conclusion. Furthermore, hands-on exercises are designed to engage students with key concepts through interactive beam simulations using the MAD-X software. Introduction to the software, beam simulation tasks, and a discussion on beam optimization using results from the exercises will also be covered. Lastly, an overview of the beam operation challenges in circular machines is presented as a final topic. This lecture is an expansion of Beam Dynamics (Physics) and (Engineering) courses but is designed to be self-contained. Nevertheless, participants with a basic understanding of particle physics and electromagnetism will be at an advantage. Due to the extensive nature of this topic, certain details are omitted and covered in the provided supplementary material. This includes elements from high-energy physics, electromagnetic field derivation, and the derivation of beam transfer matrices. Although knowledge of these concepts is not a prerequisite, having some familiarity with them will be beneficial, especially with beam transfer matrices. Consequently, this lecture serves as an introductory primer on beam dynamics and related loss phenomena in circular accelerators for accelerator engineering students and provides essential foundation on this topic for the presented case studies of circular machines, linear machines and Free Electron Lasers. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing more comprehensive and intricate data sets. However, analyzing and interpreting such vast amounts of data have become a limiting factor for further breakthroughs. To overcome this challenge, it is essential to integrate data collection with machine learning algorithms in real-time, enabling simultaneous high-speed acquisition and in-depth analysis, filtering out relevant information as data is generated. This combined approach opens up possibilities for real-time, remote experiment monitoring and control via high-speed data transmission at large-scale user facilities, like national labs and synchrotrons. This integrated system also addresses user training and expertise requirements by automating and standardizing data collection and analysis processes, reducing barriers for new users and eliminating the risk of data loss due to user schedule conflicts. As a result, materials research can now be more data-driven, with a focus on comprehensive and systematic approaches, and can take advantage of cloud-based analytics and machine learning platforms for further scaling and refinement. This paper presents an example of this integrated system at the National Institute of Standards and Technology Center for High School Research, where machine learning algorithms accelerate and refine data collection at the Soft Condensed Matter Scattering beamline at the NIST-NRC electron microscope, a remotely operated facility with real-time data analysis. This system is based on a custom-built web interface that provides secure, multi-user access and management for scheduling, data storage, and analytics, leveraging cloud services for scalability and robustness. This has resulted in accelerated materials research at the institution, with studies on protein aggregation, bacterial biofilms, and graphene overlaid with silicon, among others, along with educational outreach programs and student training in experimental design, data collection, and machine learning. This approach has significantly increased throughput and efficiency at user facilities, making them more accessible and integral to the research community. As a result, there is a growing need for similar facilities to adopt this integrated approach to remain relevant in materials research. This paper will be of interest to user facility directors, researchers, and machine learning engineers, as well as anyone involved in operating and managing large-scale research infrastructure. This work has been recognized with the 2020 Office of Naval Research Award for Outstanding Research and Development, the 2020 Materials Research Society Award for Advances in Research and Development, and the 2021 NIST Director's Award for Excellence in Science, Technology, Engineering and Math Education. This research is ongoing at the NIST Center for High School

A promising technique known as quantum annealing has been proposed for efficiently solving combinatorial optimization problems embedded in the Ising Hamiltonian's ground state. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form enables researchers to find the target ground state. Including non-stoquastic terms in the driver Hamiltonian is thought to enhance QA's performance, but a major challenge lies in decoherence hindering this process. Surprisingly, our study reveals that including anti-ferromagnetic interactions within the Hamiltonian results in catastrophic QA failure even with infinitely long annealing periods. This critical issue can be overcome by introducing controlled decoherence, which, surprisingly, results in precise avoidance of catastrophic failure in exchange for slightly diminished success probabilities. Notably, the probability of success exhibits an intriguing, albeit complex, relationship with two opposing forces: the destructive impact of anti-ferromagnetic interactions and the salvaging effect of decoherence. This intricate connection can be understood through a simple, yet insightful, classification based on decoherence's relative magnitude in comparison to driver-problem transformation time. This groundbreaking finding may significantly contribute to the development of robust quantum annealing algorithms by providing a useful analytical framework that can facilitate the identification of solutions in complex spin systems. Furthermore, our research paves the way for a thorough examination of the general properties of driver Hamiltonians that can withstand the destructive impact of anti-feromatic interactions and ensure successful outcome even in the presence of destructive interactions, critical for broadening the application of quantum annealing to diverse scenarios, including those involving multiple-body interactions, in addition to decoherence's complex interplay with Hamiltonian's structure. In addition, our study discloses the crucial role that decoherence plays in the evaluation of a successful quantum annealing, a notion that is mathematically defined and quantified through a successful probability expression that is derived from a combination of quantum adiabatic, driver-problem transformation, and decoherence-induced tunneling, along with new understanding of quantum chaos that arises from the interplay between driver-problem transformation and decoherence, which can be monitored through a novel decoherence-induced level-recurrence time that is directly linked to the half-life of entanglement and revealed through an analysis of symmetry-based operator algebra. This essay explores the development of the Kapteyn Astronomical Laboratory from 1921 to 1957, during the tenure of director Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, who succeeded the lab's founder, Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn. When van Rhijn took over, the lab was working to implement Kapteyn's Selected Areas Plan. However, van Rhijn's contributions were marred by his limited success in realizing Kapteyn's vision due to his personal struggles with health and mental resilience, as well as the constraints of operating in the turbulent scientific landscape of the Netherlands during the Nazi occupation and early post-war period. Despite these challenges, van Rhijn maintained the lab's focus on the Selected Areas Plan, making notable adjustments and enhancements until his own retirement in 1957. Under his direction, the lab produced a comprehensive catalog of over 150,000 stars, along with numerous other significant contributions. Upon his departure, the lab entered a period of transformation under its new leader, Hendrik Christoffel van Hamme, who would go on to make substantial changes to the lab's goals and operations, shifting its attention away from the Selected Areas Plan. Van Rhijn's legacy in this period is marked by his unwavering commitment to upholding the core principles and goals established by Kapteyn, even as he navigated the significant scientific and personal obstacles he faced. His story serves as an inspiring example of an individual's unrelenting pursuit of a complex, ambitious goal over the course of nearly four decades. Ultimately, his journey provides valuable insights into the development of modern astronomy and the enduring legacy of its pioneers. Van Rhijn's life and work offer a compelling case study for the value of perseverance, the importance of supporting the mental and physical well-being of researchers, and the critical role that individual visionaries play in shaping the course of scientific history. His story also serves as a reminder that even in the face of the most trying circumstances, a robust scientific community is capable of withstanding the tempests of the outside world, allowing its most dedicated members to leave a lasting impact that can be appreciated long after their retirement. Van Rhijn's contributions to the development of modern astronomy, coupled with his remarkable life story, make him an ideal subject for a biography that will resonate with readers from a broad spectrum of the scientific community and general historical enthusiasts. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules, the learning process is efficiently decoupled for both CNNs and RNNs. This investigation explores the impact of remote learning during the COVID pandemic on various student demographics, focusing on underperforming students who struggled to stay on track with academic progress. Unlike previous studies on remote learning, this research leverages detailed, subject-specific data to examine performance in multiple subjects, using a unique measure that indicates students' ability to progress to the next grade level. Our analysis employs a rigorous method to account for biases and confounding variables, applying propensity score matching and instrumental variables to ensure the validity of our results. Our key findings show that, overall, remote learning increased the likelihood of students failing to stay on track by 12.8 percentage points. However, significant disparities emerged across different student subgroups, with certain demographics experiencing notably greater difficulties as a result of remote learning. For instance, students from lower-income families, those with English language barriers, and those who already faced challenges in a particular subject faced a significant increase in the likelihood of falling behind by at least 15 percentage points, indicating a substantial gap of up to 5.3 percentage points compared to their counterparts. In contrast, some student subgroups demonstrated a marginally lower likelihood of failing to stay on track due to remote learning, although the overall decline in on-track rates during the pandemic was still evident for these groups as well as for those with no apparent negative impact. To mitigate the adverse effects of remote learning, we recommend targeted interventions tailored to the specific needs of underperforming students in each subject area, in addition to exploring alternative learning solutions such as blended models that combine remote and in-person instruction. Furthermore, we suggest that policymakers and educators consider the heterogeneous impact of remote learning as an opportunity to identify areas where learning outcomes can be improved, potentially leading to long-term benefits even after the pandemic has ended. Our analysis highlights the value of examining the heterogeneous effects of remote learning on performance in specific subjects, as well as the importance of accounting for confounding variables when analyzing the effects of remote learning on staying on track during the pandemic. Our results also emphasize the need for future research to explore the varied effects of remote learning on different student subgroups in various subjects and learning settings. Our data and analysis code are available by contacting the authors. Our study provides a foundation for investigating the long-term effects of remote learning on performance in specific subjects, in addition to examining the effects of subsequent learning on those who fell behind during the pandemic. Our findings suggest that some student subgroups experienced persistent difficulties with staying on track in certain subjects after the pandemic, while others were able to recover and make progress

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations due to their poor spatial resolution. Our research involved the use of high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) sensors directly implanted on the motor cortices of the brain in five subjects who were able to walk on a treadmill at varying speeds. Our findings show that both the on-foot and walking state conditions could be distinguished with 95% accuracy and walking speed rates could be predicted with a margin of error at 0.25 km/hour when using a linear model and 0.5 km/hour with a polynomial model. Our high spatial resolution and high temporal frequency recordings provide new insights into the brain signals associated with walking and suggest that non-invasive EEG could potentially recover walking ability in individuals with spinal cord injuries in the future. Furthermore, the high precision of our step rate predictions could facilitate the development of a closed-loop BCI system that could automatically adjust its stimulation in response to the state of the subject being recorded, leading to faster and more precise predictions in the future. Additionally, our research indicates that the brain signals associated with walking on foot are significantly different from those recorded during walking on different surfaces with full body weight support, suggesting that recovering walking ability on different terrains may be feasible with this BCI system. Leveraging our breakthroughs, our research team plan to conduct further studies that explore the decoding of brain signals associated with reaching and the simultaneous recovery of walking and upper limb function in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Such advancements in BCI technology could potentially enable the recovery of a higher level of functional mobility in these individuals in the future. To achieve this, we propose establishing a new non-invasive EEG-based BCI platform that combines our previously described ECoG-based walking BCI study and a recent study led by Dr. Zelalko at UC Berkeley involving the recovery of upper limb function using a robotic arm. This new system will allow us to conduct high precision recordings of the brain signals associated with both walking and reaching on a treadmill and will provide us with the opportunity to explore the recovery of mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries due to thoracic or lumbar spinal cord injuries in the future. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. To address this limitation, we present a novel approach called Deep Dynamic Effective Connectivity Estimation, which leverages a state transition model to capture the evolution of connectivity patterns. This model enables the learning of a dynamic graph representation at each moment in time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DDECE in classification tasks by utilizing a trained model to interpret the temporal graph, rather than individual time series. Notably, we focus on uncovering effective, rather than actual, connectivity in brain networks using EEG data. The results show that our approach outperforms alternative methods and delivers performance on par with fully supervised methods while reducing the required number of samples. Notwithstanding the creation of numerous network generation tools, a shortage of discourse and comparison among these tools persists. To address this disparity, we undertake a comparative analysis of a wide assortment of phylogenetic network generators by evaluating and contrasting the topological characteristics of the generated networks. Our research covers 13 distinct network generators, 5 of which produce loopless networks, and we examine a broad range of phylogenetic tree sizes. Our findings reveal that several generators produce a significant proportion of loops in their generated networks, which could have implications for the interpretation of Bayesian phylogenetic analysis. Our study also reveals that some network generators produce an excessively high frequency of specific reticulate patterns, which could result from an inherent design predisposition. Our research provides a thorough assessment of the topological characteristics of phylogenetic network generators, which can serve as a foundation for further exploration of these processes and potential improvements to their design. Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat or capturing prey, which they achieve through various methods of locomotion including crawling, flying, slithering, swimming and bipedalism. This report describes a novel method to automatically identify these forms of locomotion in videos, a task complicated by similarities between different movements and the presence of distracting background visuals. To overcome these challenges, our approach involves extracting local and global features from each video to determine its underlying locomotion pattern. To accomplish this, a comprehensive database consisting of 4500 annotated video segments, spanning 18 species and 8 types of locomotion, has been developed through extensive crowdsourcing. Experimental results show that our proposed algorithm is highly accurate in detecting locomotion patterns and outperforms existing methods, also demonstrating substantial improvements in speed and scalability. A key aspect of this research is providing a standardized framework for identifying biological locomotion in videos, which is particularly useful in biological monitoring and habitat preservation efforts. A key finding of this research is the creation of a distinct sound signature for each species's movement, which is independent of visual analysis and holds promise for low-light or nocturnal animal monitoring. The developed database and detection algorithm are both made publicly available for future use and integration with additional data and methods. The widespread use of matrix inversion in various applications such as linear systems, least-squares, and optimization motivates the development of efficient iterative methods for matrix inversion. By leveraging sparse matrix storage and employing basic operations like addition, subtraction, and element-wise multiplication, fast iterative matrix inversion (FIMI) has achieved remarkable performance, especially when utilizing GPU acceleration. To build upon this success, the FIMI algorithm has been enhanced to employ higher-order formulas, such as Nystrom and product integration, to increase its efficiency and scalability. This work explores the development of higher-order formulas for GPU matrix inversion by deriving a general framework that results in simpler and more versatile iterative schemes. A set of higher-order formulas, including their extensions to higher-order sparse formats, are presented alongside their computational costs. Through extensive experiments on CPU and GPU platforms, the proposed algorithms have demonstrated significant speedups and memory reductions, with some achieving speeds up to 5 times and memory reductions of up to 95% over the conventional FIMI method. Notably, the highest performance improvement was observed with a CPU implementation using a low-precision variant of the method for an image denoising application. Furthermore, the proposed algorithms have shown a notable increase in efficiency over alternative GPU-based methods, including those employing bfloat16 precision, with an observed speedup of up to 1.5 times over the current state-of-the-art fast matrix inversion library, Mumps v5.2, for a range of benchmark problems. The enhanced algorithms have been made available through an updated Mumps library, Mumps v6.0, alongside an evaluation of the scalability of the proposed methods on a growing set of large-scale sparse matrix inversion problems. The results indicate a promising future for the proposed algorithms in tackling even larger-scale problems efficiently. A new quasi-score linearity test has been developed for assessing linearity in continuous and count-based network autoregressive models. The test's asymptotic distribution is analyzed under various scenarios, including fixed and increasing network dimensions, null hypotheses, and specific alternative hypotheses. Key findings indicate that when model parameters are identifiable, the test's distribution converges to the chi-square and noncentral chi-square forms. Notably, the results are robust to parameters at their space boundaries. For non-identifiable parameters, an alternative test has been proposed, along with an established asymptotic distribution for a fixed network dimension. Given the challenges of tabulating test critical values, an empirical approach is implemented for p-value calculation. This includes the use of feasible bounds and bootstrap approximations. The theoretical framework is supported by consistency and asymptotic normality findings for the quasi maximum likelihood estimator, under specific conditions. A simulation study and empirical analysis provide further insight into the test's performance, exposing potential biases influenced by network sparsity, model parameters, and sample size. The results highlight the test's efficiency and accuracy in assessing linearity for network autoregressive models. The developed tests hold promise for linearity evaluation, offering a valuable solution for a critical theoretical issue in network autoregressive models. The study concludes by outlining potential research extensions for time-series and panel network autoregressive models. The supplementary materials include the technical proofs for the test's asymptotic distribution, estimation and test implementations, and further simulation and empirical analysis results. Recent breakthroughs in declarative networks and related work have demonstrated the capability of differentiating the solution mappings of continuous parametrized optimization problems. This has the potential to embed mathematical optimization problems within trainable end-to-end models. By providing an alternative expression for computing derivatives, this differentiability enables significant reductions in memory requirements, obviating the need for unrolling optimization procedures during backward passes. However, this typically requires the computationally expensive inversion of large Hessian matrices. In this research, we examine two specific applications - robust vector pooling and optimal transport - to illustrate how problem structures can be leveraged to achieve more efficient computations during backward passes, reducing both memory and processing requirements. The concepts developed here can serve as a guiding framework for enhancing the computational performance of innovative declarative network components. Our models not only offer superior performance but also achieve this through the exploitation of problem-specific knowledge, in contrast to alternative methods that rely on universal memory-efficient backward passes. The declared differentiability of our models permits the use of universally accepted optimization frameworks, ensuring their validity and enabling reproducibility. The code for these models has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ethan-james-wright/declarative-networks. The novel computational advancements presented here can also be applied to other optimal transport models that employ a similar declarative network framework. One such model is the convex optimal transport model proposed by Salnikov et al. (2020), which can be used as a classifier. Our research demonstrates that this model can be used as a basis for declarative networks that incorporate features such as robust pooling and semi-synchronous optimization. However, our experiments indicate that these problem structures can reduce efficiency, necessitating the use of explicit optimization in backward passes. Nonetheless, our results show that the optimal transport model can be used as a highly interpretable classifier with a feature size similar to that of a support vector machine. One such experiment involved using the MNIST dataset, which yielded a classification accuracy of 0.93 using a simple linear feature set. In contrast to this, our experiments involving the CMU Panoptic Dataset achieved a 25% reduction in energy expenditure when comparing a model with and without the Hessian inversion, respectively. This discrepancy highlights the significance of problem structure on computational performance. In conclusion, our research underscores the value of examining problem structures in innovative declarative network components to derive computational savings. Although the models presented here perform optimally due to the explicit inclusion of problem structures, this research lays the groundwork for exploring alternative methods that bypass optimization in backward passes

With consideration of this complexity, our goal is to develop a multi-faceted framework for modeling cellular spreading and locomotion, taking into account the movement of proteins across lipid membranes. The unique combination of decentralization, redundancy, and pseudo-anonymity in public blockchain platforms has made them appealing for cryptocurrency adoption. However, these same features have enabled cybercriminals to exploit vulnerabilities in blockchain technology and deceive users through social engineering to execute malicious plans. Existing methods for identifying malicious actors typically rely on transaction history from specific wallet addresses, but often neglect the underlying money trails. In contrast, we propose an innovative approach centered on money trail analysis, incorporating new features to detect suspicious activities within cryptocurrency blockchains. Specifically, we investigate the cyclic behavior present in temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, focusing on uncovering hidden patterns. By applying our methods to the Ethereum blockchain, we reveal distinct cyclic patterns indicative of malicious activities such as gambling, phishing, and money laundering, as well as identify two specific temporal cyclic transactions. Notably, we observed a user who engaged in phishing, using the funds to participate in a gambling activity, which was subsequently used for a laundering operation. Our analysis on the Ethereum blockchain spanning from block 1 to 7.5 million demonstrates the presence of at least 154 unique temporal transaction graphs, emphasizing the vast diversity present in cyclic transactions within a large-scale blockchain. With our proposed approach, we provide an explicit example of a temporal transaction graph related to a phishing attack, which was previously unknown to law enforcement agencies and security experts. Our study paves the way for further exploration into the temporal transaction graphs within a blockchain, providing a theoretical framework that can be applied across different cryptocurrency blockchains. Additionally, we outline an initial design for a practical implementation of our approach, along with a discussion on potential security issues and potential solutions. Our research on the Ethereum blockchain has generated valuable insights, which can be applied to other cryptocurrency blockchains, such as Bitcoin and Hyperledger Fabric. In conclusion, our study on the Ethereum blockchain has demonstrated the presence of temporal transaction graphs, which can provide a basis for identifying malicious activities through money trail analysis. Furthermore, we have made our research findings available to law enforcement agencies and security experts, which can be used as a starting point for further investigation. In the future, we plan to explore additional features within the temporal transaction graphs, such as community behavior and graph dynamics, which can provide even more comprehensive knowledge on the cyclic transactions within a blockchain. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a decoder environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied. We developed two decoder architectures - based on reinforcement learning and neural networks - that were tested on data simulated for the SiQEC system, showing significant improvements over traditional minimum-cut flow methods. Our research demonstrates the viability of reinforcement learning methods for real-world quantum decoding applications. We also offer an open-source framework for quantitative evaluations of quantum decoding systems, known as QDecoLearn, alongside the code for training recurrent neural network decoders, trained on data for the SiQEC system, which can be found at https://github.com/QuantumMachineLearning/QDecoLearn. We anticipate this work to contribute to the development of robust quantum systems by providing a framework for evaluating the tolerance of quantum decoding systems to various forms of errors and poor observations, crucial components for real-world quantum computing applications. We've investigated a method for quantum metrology using entangled light through a two-cavity setup, where we compare the effectiveness of periodic measurement and quantum reinforcement techniques. Our study shows that applying quantum reinforcement allows us to achieve a level of accuracy significantly better than periodic measurement, yielding a level of precision improved by a factor of $N^{4/3}$ over periodic measurement with $N$ rounds of measurement. We've also analyzed the ideal quantum gain, finding it reaches a $N^{5/3}$ increase with quantum reinforcement. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these advantages in precision and quantum gain can be attained using realistic parameters from current experimental setups. Quantum reinforcement offers significant advantages in precision and gain, indicating it has substantial potential to enhance metrological performance in optical systems. To further explore this method's effectiveness, we simulate quantum reinforcement in a three-dimensionally entangled light configuration, demonstrating that this approach's advantages in precision and gain can be attained in such complex systems as described in section 4.2.2. We propose a feasible experiment setup for implementing quantum reinforcement in a two-cavity setup using linear optics, phase modulation, and a beam splitter, offering a viable path for experimental verification of our findings. This proposal involves manipulating $10^{-20}\, \text{J}$-scale amounts of light, making it theoretically achievable with present-day technology. We anticipate that quantum reinforcement has broad applications in optical systems, providing significant boosts to precision and gain, potentially yielding substantial breakthroughs in various metrological applications. We believe that exploring this method further will reveal even more ways it can be optimized for different systems and scenarios. We are also investigating how quantum reinforcement can be applied to systems with interactions between light and matter, looking into the potential for it to provide significant increases in precision and gain in such systems as described in section 4.2.3. We anticipate that quantum reinforcement will offer significant advantages in optical systems over periodic measurement, particularly in cases with large gain, and that these advantages can be more substantially increased with negative feedback control, yielding a level of precision improved by a factor of $N^{7/3}$ and quantum gain increased by a factor of $N^{8/3}$ with $N$ rounds of measurement. We plan to explore this further, looking into the potential for quantum reinforcement to provide significant breakthroughs in optical systems, and to experimentally verify its effectiveness in optical systems. We anticipate that this method will offer substantial increases in precision and gain in optical systems, potentially yielding major breakthroughs in various metrological applications

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions at similar multiplicity levels. Hadrons with high $p_T$ are significantly suppressed in Au$+$Au collisions, and this suppression is more pronounced for hadrons associated with high-$p_T$ direct photons, indicating that the medium exerts greater forces on particles moving in the same direction as the rest of the system. The dependence of this suppression on centralities and the $p_T$ of directly photons remains consistent with other experiments. These results provide further evidence for medium-matter interactions and the importance of in-medium $k_T$ broadening, and have helped quantify the coupling between medium particles and direct photons, showing that this interaction is sensitive to frequency and is influenced by final-state hadron interactions as particles exit the medium. These findings also indicate that quarks and gluons exhibit similar interaction widths with the medium, and that the ratio of $2$-particle $p_T$ correlations to single-particle $p_T$ distributions is independent of direct photon $p_T$, supporting the concept of an average in-medium $k_T$ and its relation to medium properties rather than direct photon properties. These results are influenced by final-state hadron interactions as particles exit the medium, and further research is needed to fully comprehend the medium's properties. Consequently, these data have insufficient information to draw a distinction between different models predicting medium properties such as viscosity, elasticity, and surface tension. These findings are based on a more detailed analysis involving a broader range of hadron types, centralities, and direct photon $p_T$ than previously reported. Additionally, this study presents an upgraded version of the hadron $p_T$ spectrum extraction, along with a more precise calculation of hadron $p_T$ shift in relation to the $p_T$ of the associated direct photon. This study provides a detailed explanation for the suppression of hadron production in heavy-ion collisions and the characteristics of hadron production in $p$$+$$p$ collisions, and these results are available on arXiv under the reference arXiv:2201.07201 [nucl-ex]. Cloud-based HPC deployments can provide significant cost savings, but they also introduce network latency that can impact application performance and scalability. To assess the effect of network variability on HPC applications in the cloud, we conducted a comprehensive study involving 12 widely used benchmarks and 5 test networks with different levels of latency and message transfer times. This work presents an extreme degree of freedom gain analysis for an interference network with K users, relying on optimal and binary (on/off) power control. We show that the extremal GDoF gain of binary power control, as described by YZ in 2017, is linear with respect to GDoF (kbar in notation), whereas the extremal GDoF gain of optimal power control is proportional to the square root of kbar, with a coefficient equal to twice the square root of kbar, for any K greater than 2 users. Furthermore, this gain of optimal power control over binary power control expands in proportion to the square root of K. Notably, this indicates that the improved performance achievable by optimal power control, as opposed to binary power control, becomes significantly more substantial with an increase in K. This finding is validated through numerical examples with networks containing up to 10 users, providing a gain of at least 2 in the square root of kbar for all scenarios examined. It is worth mentioning that a 2019 study by AY and YZ proposed a sub-threshold of kbar of 3/5 in extremal GDoF gain for optimal power control as compared to binary power control, displaying a 4 to 1 ratio in support of our more general proof of a square root relationship between kbar and the extremal GDoF gain in question. A critical component of our proof is the introduction of a new metric known as generalized throughput, along with its corresponding characterization under both optimal and binary power control. A key aspect of this characterization is an information-theoretic upper bound on generalized throughput, as well as a new code construction that provides a generalized throughput result. A generic application of this code construction across all pairs of users forms the basis for our proof of the extremal GDoF gain for optimal power control. A separate code construction is then designed to address the specific scenario in question, as well as an associated upper bound on generalized throughput. A general approach to decoding is also presented across all receiver-user pairs, as well as a technique for handling edge cases in certain instances. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, existing methods can be inefficient for large-scale simulations that incorporate numerous particles. Existing methods require integrating the equations of motion for granular materials at a rate determined by the collision time, regardless of the time step used for integrating the fluid flow equations. As a result, these methods can be computationally expensive for simulations involving many particles. To address this challenge, we developed a multiple-time-step integration algorithm that allows for distinct time steps for integrating the equations of motion for granular materials and fluid flows. Only every n-th time step, where n represents the ratio of the two time steps, the algorithm fully integrates the equations of motion for granular materials, including integrating the collision integral over n time steps. When n is much larger than the collision time of the particles, this method can determine the average collision time and use it to select appropriate interaction models for particles during the time steps that are not fully integrated. To verify the method, we simulated three test cases: sedimentation of single particles, sedimentation of multiple particles and settling of elastically colliding particles. The method successfully matched the results obtained with the conventional method and settled the issue of the double-time-step algorithm's failure case. Additionally, we found that our method can significantly reduce computational costs for simulations involving numerous particles by offering up to a 50-fold improvement in computational efficiency for the case of elastically colliding particles. The proposed algorithm demonstrates potential for significantly reducing the computational expenses associated with large-scale simulations involving numerous particles and could be an essential component for the development of advanced simulation tools that can efficiently simulate a wide range of industrial applications involving the motion of individual particles. Furthermore, the new algorithm can also be applied to other discrete-time integration algorithms that handle particle collisions. A significant challenge in developing legged robots for real-world applications involves their ability to function in environments with soft, yielding ground. This research focuses on creating a one-legged robot that can jump on ground that deforms like sand or mud. To control the robot, we've developed a mathematical model predicting its movement and behavior in such environments. To validate the model, we performed a virtual simulation, making adjustments to optimize the robot's performance. These optimizations helped the robot achieve stable, repeated hops on the soft ground, a task it initially struggled with. Our findings show that a small change in the robot's design can have a significant impact on its ability to hop on soft ground. By applying this knowledge, we were able to create a one-legged robot capable of hopping on soft ground in real life. This research could also provide insights for developing control systems for multi-legged robots to help them navigate soft, yielding ground. This work is an extension of a previous study presented at the 2019 Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS) conference. Despite its importance, negation poses significant challenges to modern natural language processing systems. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. Conformance checking focuses on comparing modeled process behavior to observed process behavior from actual event data. A recent technique, called alignments, identifies and measures deviations between process executions and predefined reference models, pinpointing the discrepancies in process traces. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although molecular cations generally exhibit stronger and longer wavelength electronic emission than their neutral counterparts, comprehensive spectral models are hindered by existing limitations in data availability. This paper addresses this challenge by reviewing the current state of molecular cation spectra, with a focus on those containing oxygen as a critical component. A comprehensive database of 116 lines across 67 different cations, including 23 with oxygen in at least one molecule, is presented. The challenge of representing a positive entity as a sum of squared components dates back centuries to notable mathematicians Bachet and Lagrange. Though successful methods exist for certain types of structures (such as integers or polynomial equations with rational coefficients), the task remains an open question for numerous other positive entities. This research introduces a new approach for achieving this representation, applicable to any element in either a finite field of non-negative integers or a rational field of polynomials, that is formally defined over a set of integers with a specific algebraic property. This property, known as being 'quadratic-integers factorable', ensures all elements within the defined set can be represented as the sum of squared components. This new approach is a composite of two key methods: one for fields with a finite number of elements, and another for fields of rational polynomials. Within the former category, our method involves an exploration of all possible combinations of components, whereas within the latter category, our method relies on an innovative application of the Hermite Normal Form that is both efficient and scalable. Through this research, numerous previously unrepresented positive integers and rational polynomials can now be expressed as the sum of squared components, providing evidence that all elements defined by quadratic-integers factorable orders can be represented in this manner. This breakthrough raises the question whether this representation can be achieved through a more fundamental property of these definitions, potentially expanding the scope of this solution to a broader class of structures beyond those with quadratic-integers factorable orders. This research also introduces an open problem related to the solution of systems of Diophantine equations, where a proposed method could be used to achieve this representation. This proposed solution method is shown to be equivalent to an existing method but is more straightforward and easier to comprehend. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning from heterogeneous and non-interisible data on a complex network with individual nodes being privately owned. Existing random walk methods typically require the graph to be fully observed and learned model updates are usually performed in a centralized manner, limiting their potential. This paper proposes a novel random walk approach, where agents based on local optimization and gradient information perform independent updates in parallel, and then embark on a random walk on the underlying graph to share their updated model parameters with the central server. The server then combines the received information with the current model and shares it with the agents at the next time step. Theoretical analysis along with simulations confirm the efficacy of this walk-based approach in convergence, and it shows the proposed method outperforms existing random walk methods by a significant margin in terms of convergence speed in various network settings. This method is particularly suitable for learning models from non-interisible, heterogeneous data in the presence of budget constraints, and is applicable to a wide range of graphs, including those with dynamically changing node degrees. Its key advantages include reduced communication, lower computation requirements, and the ability to handle a wide range of graph topologies. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/parag-ghosh/walk4fl. This approach is further demonstrated in a real-world experiment involving the classification of remote-sensing images using a distributed dataset based on geographical boundaries. This framework is also compared with FedAvg, and found that the proposed approach converges in half the number of iterations with an improvement in accuracy of up to 15%. This method is currently being explored for potential applications in the areas of multi-agent reinforcement learning, and in the context of an emerging new paradigm called Artificial Intelligence Graph. This new framework is also discussed in the context of potential solutions to several open research challenges in the area of graph-based FL. This includes the challenge of developing efficient and robust algorithms for learning models in the presence of a large number of attacks from selfish and malicious agents. Another challenge addressed in this paper is the design of efficient and robust algorithms for learning models in the presence of a large number of attacks from selfish and malicious agents, and solutions to these challenges are also discussed. This is the extended version of an earlier presented paper, and is currently being considered for presentation at IEEE ICME 2023 in Melbourne, Australia. Three-dimensional rotating turbulence, once believed to be stable due to rotation, has been observed to support highly active and dynamic fluid motion. Certain observations suggest that this phenomenon is driven by an interplay between stable shear layers and unstable core regions. The former resist changes and maintain their stability through energetic exchanges with the latter. The latter's dynamics are highly active, with energy freely transferred between scales. This has led researchers to investigate the turbulent transfer of energy within these regions. Recent studies using direct numerical simulations have measured the spectral energy distribution within these regions and have found a specific power law at high frequencies, characteristic of an inertial wave turbulence. This particular power law is distinct from that of a Kolmogorov spectrum, which is observed in non-rotating turbulent fluids, but surprisingly this spectrum exhibits the same power law as its non-rotating counterpart, with a similar exponent but a different scale that is directly linked to the scale of the energy-containing eddies. This new understanding provides a new basis for estimating the transfer of energy within these regions and has shown that the triple product that drives this transfer is conserved within these eddies, a finding that is consistent with previous observations of the locality of the energy transfer in these regions. This has significant implications for the broader field of turbulence research and suggests that similar phenomena may be observable in magnetohydrodynamic turbulence driven by Alfv\'en waves. These findings and this new perspective on turbulence are expected to be influential in shaping future research in this field.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crimes results in savings of $1.40 for every dollar spent on mental health treatment.  However, there is room for further research into the specific effectiveness and costs of mental health treatments to better understand its return on investment.  An examination of North Carolina's current laws and practices following the analysis's period showed that the state's legislation became more restrictive regarding mental health treatment for offenders in 2011.  An analysis of court decisions from 2011 to 2015 revealed that the effect of mental health treatment on future crimes has been downward trend over time with no clear explanation for this decline.  Overall, the research supports the expansion of mental health treatment for individuals within the criminal justice system to decrease their likelihood of returning to the justice system in the future.  Furthermore, there is a need for more detailed data on mental health treatment's cost and effectiveness to evaluate and improve existing and future policies. This enhancement includes upgrading the Level 1 trigger based on calorimeter data to utilize finer details of the data with a same-speed approach. A key component of this system is the Full Digital Calorimeter Trigger (FDCT), responsible for systemizing and speeding up calorimeter data for the Level 1 trigger decision. These 3D VLSI hybrids integrate 32 ATLAS readout chips that receive and process data from the calorimeter system with a 400 Mbit/s throughput. Each hybrid also features four XAUI links for high-speed communication with the ATLAS Global Trigger System using a 3.2 Gbit/s bandwidth. These hybrids also feature a 64-bit 2-stage pipeline for the calculation of maximum and minimum values, along with an 8-bit 1-stage pipeline for the calculation of mean values. These integrated processors are complemented by a 64-bit 2-stage pipeline for the calculation of sum values. It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. This work extends and generalizes previous research on estimation under a complex sampling design and it provides an efficient method for obtaining consistent estimators in scenarios where the efficiency of the standard estimator is unknown.

Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Furthermore, we provide an alternative, more intuitive proof of this aspect of $P$ being surjective when $M$ is not compact. This is then followed by an examination of its implications to the topic of manifold embeddings and overdetermined boundary value problems. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. Moreover, a comprehensive simulation framework is provided to facilitate reproducible experiments. Simulation results demonstrate the convergence of the FedBuff algorithm even with unbounded gradients in realistic scenarios. A practical application involving IoT devices in a smart city environment further showcases the algorithm's effectiveness and efficiency in real-world settings. Theoretical and experimental findings show that the FedBuff algorithm can achieve a high quality optimization within a reasonable latency in multiple scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/author-name/FedBuff-PA. The supplementary materials are available at https://www.dropbox.com/sh/author-name/author-folder?dl=0. The paper's official publication is awaited.

Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed as a solution to overcome such issues in certain scenarios. Several studies suggest that domain knowledge can be effectively transferred from one dataset to another with minimal displacement, either through matching existing domains or combining them. On the other hand, cross-lingual transfer learning offers a way to leverage knowledge across languages, with English serving as the primary baseline. Nonetheless, when it comes to low-resource languages, there is often a scarcity of data in multiple domains and languages. To tackle this challenge, we propose a two-tier transfer learning approach. In the first tier, we transfer knowledge between similar domains within the same language using matching networks. In the second tier, we utilize this knowledge to make cross-lingual transfers. We tested this approach on four low-resource languages - Arabic, Hindi, Sinhala, and Urdu - using a dataset with eight different domains. The results showed significant improvements over non-transfer learning, with an average reduction of 11.6% word error rate. The findings also revealed that the two-tier transfer learning approach outperformed single-tier baseline models in every case, suggesting that the proposed method is an effective solution for multi-domain and cross-lingual low-resource speech recognition tasks. The code and models are available at https://github.com/seyed-gh/ctf-xl-asr-transfer. The word error rate reductions of our approach in comparison to non-transfer learning and single-tier transfer learning are available in the supplementary materials at http://seyedgh.com/files/ctf-xl-asr-transfer-suppl.html. The technique has been showcased on the Sinhala dataset in the paper's accompanying video at http://seyedgh.com/files/ctf-xl-asr-transfer-video.mp4. The video is also available on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q5Q5Qf5G6Qo. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface of support, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. This effect is caused by the ongoing competition between two speed factors: the rate at which the particles reassemble, which is influenced by forces like viscosity and surface tension, and the rate at which neighboring particles move apart due to the expansion of the surrounding fluid. This balance also determines how the cracks within the raft form and shift as it is being stretched. It is notable that all changes in this system occur gradually and are therefore predictable, in contrast to the sudden, unpredictable behavior often seen in breaking materials like glass. This distinction is linked to the technical difference between material breakdown and material failure, which we differentiate based on the rate at which changes occur. Because all changes in this system occur gradually, it is theoretically possible to prevent material failure by actively controlling this rate at which sub-critical cracks within the system mature. This concept could be applied broadly to other situations where sub-critical cracks have the potential to cause significant failure in a few seconds, as seen in the emulsion raft example, where the same principles could be used to prevent a much larger type of fracture. This idea could be used to prevent other sudden, unpredictable failures like sandcastles falling down, the sudden spreading of droplets when they are placed on highly expanded rafts, and even large-scale geological events like big earthquakes triggered by small ones, where the same principles could be applied to prevent a much larger type of fracture. It is also possible to control the rate at which cracks within the system mature by applying an external force that counteracts the expansion of the surrounding fluid, as seen in the case of droplets on highly expanded rafts, where this technique could be used to prevent a much larger type of fracture, or in cases where the same principles apply, big earthquakes triggered by small ones, where the same principles could be applied to prevent a much larger type of fracture. This paper explores the concept of sorting networks consisting of comparators with more than two input values. We focus on the interplay between three parameters: the number of inputs, the number of outputs, and the depth of the network. Our model is relevant to the sorting process used in streaming applications, where data is periodically buffered and sorted before being sent out to the next stage.

We investigated sorting networks with comparators of arbitrary size, where a single comparator can compare n inputs and produce n outputs. We established a lower bound for sorting networks with comparators of size n, demonstrating that as the number of inputs increases beyond n^2, the required sorting network has a depth of at least n, regardless of the number of outputs, and that this bound is achievable for specific values of n.

However, the situation becomes more complex when comparators of different size are considered. We proved that any sorting network with comparators of size n for inputs of n^2 can be simulated by a network using comparators of size n^2 for inputs of n, with a depth of n. This simulation is achievable in a sorting network with a depth of n when comparators of size n can sort inputs of n^2. Interestingly, this result implies that the n-comparator class can sort n^2 inputs in a network of depth n, a result we prove using a recursive approach. This approach is also shown to produce optimal networks for certain input sizes. Furthermore, this result is shown to be nearly optimal in a different context. Finally, we investigated constant-depth networks, demonstrating that any sorting network with a depth of d can sort inputs of d^2, and that this property holds for comparators of arbitrary size. This property is shown to be optimal in a different context. This research provides a comprehensive exploration of the parameters of sorting networks with comparators of arbitrary size. Although comparators of size 2 are essentially the standard sorting network comparator, our results are nonetheless relevant to that setting due to their general applicability. Our results are applicable to any comparator size and are therefore universally applicable, regardless of comparator size. Our results are presented in a universally applicable manner, with all conclusions extending to any comparator size. Our research offers a universal framework for the study of sorting networks with comparators of arbitrary size, providing a framework for the study of any comparator size. Our results provide a comprehensive exploration of the parameters of sorting networks with comparators of arbitrary size, with a focus on constant-depth networks. Our research provides a comprehensive exploration of the parameters of sorting networks

We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. Two new exact solutions are derived in the Einstein theory, with one representing a two-fluid star directly from a single-fluid solution, while the other is constructed from a previously identified universal relation. A numerical scheme is established to solve the anisotropic TOV equations in the context of Brans-Dicke theory, where the character of gravity influences the equation of state, resulting in new solutions within the Einstein and scalar-dominated gravitational fields limits. Three new exact solutions in General Relativity can support stellar configurations in the Einstein and Brans-Dicke theories, with two of these solutions exhibiting stability in both theories, while the Brans-Dicke theory allows for stars with stable, stable-to-unstable, or unstable boundary conditions depending on the specific value of the gravitational coupling constant. Galactic mergers under real cosmic conditions are evaluated for their interaction with magnetic fields in a fully comprehensive, high-resolution simulation without magnetic field influence. Comparing the outcomes to similar simulations that account for magnetic fields reveals their substantial impact on galaxy mergers, influencing the shape and structure of both gas and stellar discs in an individual galaxy during the process of merging. Generally, magnetic fields restrict the extent to which galaxy pairs are able to distort each other, limiting extension beyond 3 times their original diameter. In contrast, mergers without magnetic fields show neater, more circular patterns and less disrupted systems generally. The way magnetic fields are wound during proximity without merging is significantly affected, with enhanced density seen in both gas and stellar components, alongside developed spiral patterns, particularly visible in stellar components. These changes are often retained in a certain period after the merge. The changes mentioned above are more noticeable in stronger magnetic field scenarios. The distortion of galaxy shapes and structures due to magnetic fields may provide a viable explanation for existing observational data on nearby galaxy pairs, particularly those with distorted light patterns indicating spiral patterns. Further study on individual galaxy components, such as supermassive black holes and star-forming enhancements, is worth exploring in follow-up simulations of galaxy mergers. Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT images into Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Critical COVID-19 grades. To achieve this, we proposed a cutting-edge infection-aware 3D classification network called the Contrastive Mixup Classification network. This innovative approach was designed to remedy two common issues: the limited training data and the variations in CT scan quality. To address these challenges, we employed a data augmentation technique called Simulated Vessel Extraction (SVE) to create high-quality training data and incorporated an infection-aware model. This infection-aware model was particularly effective at extracting valuable information from low-quality scans. To prevent the overfitting of our model to the training data, we utilized two techniques: a data augmentation technique and a contrastive loss function. To further enhance our model's performance, we employed two metric-based ranking methods. Our infection-aware network achieved remarkable results, outperforming the baseline model by a significant margin and ranking 6th overall in the competition with a score of 0.3466. Notably, our model's performance was particularly impressive on the test set, earning us the 4th place in the final ranking. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyuan-yi/CMCNet. Our model's excellent performance provides a foundation for future advancements in COVID-19 severity detection, and we believe it offers valuable insights for tackling other classification challenges in medical image analysis. To build upon these results, we are open to collaborating with other researchers and the COVID-19 community to address the outstanding issues in COVID-19 severity detection and to explore new research avenues. To facilitate such progress, we have submitted an extension of this work to a top-tier conference, and we look forward to presenting it at the conference. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus on producing consistent output for various test sets with minimal editing, primarily due to the difficulty of obtaining annotated data. To address this challenge, we reframe the issue as a domain adaptation problem, taking into account the fact that source and target domains share common underlying structures. Since acquiring data for multiple domains at once is still a challenge, we investigate few-shot domain adaptation, aiming to adapt to new domains with only a limited amount of labeled data. In particular, we explore whether it is feasible to learn a general framework that can facilitate adaptation to new domains with minimal annotation, drawing inspiration from meta-learning theory. Experimental results on the VTB corpus demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over a strong baseline, with an average improvement of 6.3 in F-scores across 10 new domains with only 256 labeled data in each domain. Moreover, we discover that our proposed method achieves a significantly larger gain in F-scores for domains with more severe errors, showcasing its potential in correcting a wide range of grammatical errors. Furthermore, we find that pre-training our proposed model on a large corpus leads to a 10.5 gain in F-scores on unseen domains, underscoring the model's ability to capture underlying structural similarities across domains with diverse data. Source code is available at https://github.com/ruotianeng/FSDA-GEC.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of the single-crystal, hexagonal GdInO3 through an integrated approach that combined experimental and theoretical analysis. A centered honeycomb structure comprising triangular and honeycomb sublattices was formed by two inequivalent Gd3+ ions. The results from direct current susceptibility and specific heat measurements indicate two transitions into antiferromagnetic states at 2.3 K and 1.02 K. Additionally, the analysis of isothermal magnetization revealed a unique 1/3 magnetization plateau, and the comparison with the model of a frustrated system on a honeycomb lattice yielded comparable energies for the 120° and canted states. A notable increase in the entropy was also detected in the GdInO3 system below the lower transition temperature, demonstrating a non-monotonous behavior in the magnetic system. The study suggests that the lower transition at 1.02 K originates from the competition between the 120° and canted states in the hexagonal system. Conversely, the higher transition at 2.3 K is thought to result from the ground state of the triangular sublattice. A Néel-Bose-Jordan model was proposed to describe the two-level system, yielding a well-defined free energy and various thermodynamic properties that were calculated in the study. These findings contribute to our current understanding of the intricate physics governing the centered honeycomb system and suggest that further research is needed to clarify the intricate balance of interactions within this lattice configuration. Moreover, the results indicate that the model of a frustrated system on a honeycomb lattice holds significance, warranting its application to other antiferromagnetic centered honeycomb materials. A comparison of the calculated and measured values of the magnetic properties of GdInO3 validates the study's findings and provides a comprehensive framework for investigating other materials with similar properties. In our research, we diverge from the standard practice in unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) of employing a direct one-to-one correlation ('mapping') between source and target domains. Instead, we utilize stochastic translations to account for the inherent ambiguities in domain transformations. This strategy enables us to achieve better results by generating various outputs based on a single source image, thereby utilizing both accurate translations and data augmentation to handle visual variations, producing reliable target labels through the averaging of source predictions across multiple transformed versions of a single target image, and training and aggregating diverse target networks by regulating the degree of stochasticity in translations. Notably, our findings demonstrate notable improvements over strong recent UDA methods exhibiting mapping behaviors, with achievements including top-ranking performance in the CVPR 2019 UDA Challenge and exceptional performance in severalfurther evaluation metrics. For classification tasks, we employ a straightforward stochastic translation approach in which a single source image is transformed into multiple target images with the same label. This method is analogous to utilizing data augmentation in the source domain. However, due to the difficulty of accurately capturing source domain transformations, we use a transformation that over-represent the source domain. In contrast, for segmentation tasks, we employ an indirect translation approach, transforming a single target image into multiple source-domain images with the same label and then combining the masks of these images. This method is akin to utilizing super-resolution techniques in the target domain. In both cases, our method achieves superior performance when compared to strong recent UDA baselines, with improvements of 1.3% and 2.5% in accuracy and mIoU, respectively. This study explores how uncertainty about chance influencing job success and earnings impacts redistribution policies in a society with varying levels of inequality. We examined three scenarios: one based on a realistic economic model, another with an abstract framework for job achievement, and a third with abstract utility functions. In all scenarios, we measured inequality using the Gini coefficient and inequality of opportunity using the coefficient of variation of chance outcomes and earnings. Our key finding is that inequality of opportunity declines with increased chance influence on job success and earnings in all three scenarios, supporting the theoretical concept of inequality of opportunity. Our data suggests that inequality also decreases with greater chance influence on job success and earnings in all three scenarios, although it reaches a plateau in the realistic model and the abstract framework for job achievement. We found that a larger range of income inequality leads to greater redistribution in the realistic model and the abstract framework for job achievement, but surprisingly, smaller increases in inequality of opportunity lead to greater income inequality in the abstract framework for job achievement, resulting in no optimal income range that leads to the greatest redistribution in this scenario. In the scenario based on utility functions and described as "normal" or "pro-social," we observed income inequality and inequality of opportunity within ranges of 0.4 to 0.7 for both metrics. This equivalence allows us to adapt and generalize a 2005 proof by Hasset-Landsberg and Cotterill to prove the isomorphism between quantum $K$-rings of these varieties and a specific ring constructed from the fundamental representations of the Lie algebra $gl_n$.
