The development of modern machine learning applications is centered on data and is complicated by a critical issue: understanding the influence of data quality on training. The problem of pinpointing which training examples are responsible for a trained model's inaccuracies or biases has gained significant attention in recent years. The presents an innovative algorithm, named DataShapley, designed to assign a scarcity value to each training example based on its contribution to the model's performance. DataShapley builds upon the well-established Shapley value framework and offers an efficient and practical solution for identifying data responsible for a model's performance by considering all possible subsets of training examples. Unlike previous approaches that only consider neighboring subsets, DataShapley employs a Monte Carlo technique to evaluate a large number of subsets simultaneously. This has significant implications for machine learning pipelines involving multiple rounds of data augmentation, active learning, and counterfactual learning. DataShapley's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on various datasets and a discussion on its integration with other machine learning tools is also presented. The algorithm's code is made available as an open-source Python package named DataShapley, which can be easily installed via pip. The algorithm's data value discovery approach is shown to not only identify data responsible for a model's performance but also its bias. DataShapley has significant potential to transform machine learning development by providing a data debugging tool that can assign a scarcity value to each training example based on its contribution to the model's performance, allowing for data value discovery and data value discovery for fairness. We investigate a widespread challenge in analyzing complex graph systems: many real-world networks are more effectively modeled as hypergraphs, yet their associated datasets are often presented as projected graphs. To better comprehend this phenomenon, we establish a theoretical framework to examine its underlying principles and worst-case scenarios. This framework informs our proposal of supervised hypergraph reconstruction, a novel task aimed at recovering a real-world hypergraph from its graph projection using domain-specific knowledge. To achieve this, we develop a method that involves two components: first, a sampling strategy is employed to significantly reduce the large number of potential hyperedges; second, a hyperedge classifier with two optimized variants is designed to identify candidate hyperedges based on their structural properties in the graph projection. Our experiments validate the efficacy of our approach and its extensions, demonstrating that supervised hypergraph reconstruction can yield substantial performance gains over baseline methods and even match the accuracy of expertly constructed hypergraphs in certain domains. Our implementations and data are freely available for download at: https://github.com/chenxu1990/Supervised-Hypergraph-Reconstruction. One potential application of our approach is in revitalizing research related to hypergraph analysis, a field that has gone unexplored for over a decade. Furthermore, our results suggest that many previously conducted graph-based research with limited generalization could be attributed to the difficulty of working with projected graphs rather than original hypergraphs. In a related issue, we discover that many real-world hypergraphs exhibit chaining properties, where two hyperedges may share only a single common vertex, and we propose several open research questions related to hypergraph analysis. Additionally, we introduce the concept of semi-supervised hypergraph reconstruction, where only a few hyperedges are provided as training data, and we present initial experimental results indicating that supervised hypergraph reconstruction can be applied to temporal hypergraphs, and we outline several directions for future exploration in this area. Lastly, we contribute a new dataset called Wikipedia Categories, comprising 22 categories with associated hypergraphs and their corresponding graph projections, and we outline our implementation of hypergraph learning using the PyTorch framework. Our work lays the foundation for further investigation in the field of hypergraph analysis. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a narrow view, it may still learn a useful set of actions despite being isolated, but it faces significant challenges when transferred to a broader view. In such cases, other agents with a broader view may have learned actions that are nearly random. Simply transferring the behavior of the best performing agent at each state isn't sufficient, as it fails to capture the interactions between the agents and may result in poor performance when compared to learning from all agents simultaneously. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a method that learns from just the good performing agents at each state, while still considering the interactions between the agents. By incorporating a contrastive term that encourages the distribution of states visited by each agent to match the distribution of states visited by all agents, we can leverage data from a broader range of experiences. We evaluate our approach on a variety of scenarios with multiple interacting agents and find it achieves significantly better performance compared to simply transferring the behavior of the best performing agent at each state, and in some cases, even matches the performance of online learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/aleks13/good-actors. For our results and additional details on our experiments, refer to the appendix in Section A. Our work provides a step towards enabling offline multi-agent reinforcement learning in real-world applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, there are several limitations to our approach that need to be addressed in future research. For instance, our method assumes all agents share the same action and observation spaces, but often in practice, this is not the case. Therefore, extending our method to accommodate these differences will be crucial. Additionally, our method relies on data being evenly distributed by good performing agents at each state, but in some cases, this may not hold true. Therefore, exploring ways to handle such imbalances will also be essential. We anticipate our method to be of interest to researchers working on multi-agent reinforcement learning, offline reinforcement learning, and transfer learning, given its potential to address the challenges associated with these areas. We believe our method will contribute to enabling the development of practical applications involving multiple interacting entities in real-world scenarios. For instance, it may facilitate the creation of more realistic traffic simulations or more effective team-based video game players. Our method can also be applied to a variety of other scenarios involving multiple interacting agents, such as groups of robots

Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. In contrast, our method employs a Convolutional Neural Network, trained on pairs of megavoltage and kilovoltage images, to establish a correlation between images and facilitate registration. We investigate the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our study focuses on 25 Milky Way-mass halos where Population III star formation occurs immediately after structure formation, and follows the evolution of these halos through to $z \sim 5$. In this process, we track the formation and mergers of Population III binary remnants in nuclear star clusters, producing intermediate-mass black holes with $3.9 \times 10^3 \lesssim M_\mathrm{BH} / M_\odot \lesssimes 2.3 \times 10^4$. By applying a simplified engine for binary black hole mergers, we predict the production of 34 binary black hole mergers detectable by Pulsar Timing Arrays and 5 candidates for direct detection by ground-based observatories, including three with primary black holes created through the direct collapse of a Population III gas cloud. These include two candidates for detection by LIGO/VIRGO with a signal-to-noise ratio above 8, and one that is a target of the LIGO/VIRGO search for intermediate-mass black hole mergers. We also find that the formation of intermediate-mass black holes through the collapse of Population III stars results in a peak power spectral density at a higher frequency than expected, potentially distinguishable from other models by Pulsar Timing Arrays. Furthermore, we expect the remnant Population III binary black hole population to contribute a significant fraction of the total gravitational wave power spectral density at high frequencies. In contrast, our model predicts a lower rate of detection for short gamma-ray bursts, specifically $\lesssim 0.1$ per year, in agreement with current observational data. In addition, we find that the formation of Population III binary black hole mergers occurs early in the universe, with all detectable candidates in our model occurring at $z \lesssim 7$. Our findings provide a theoretical framework for understanding the production of Population III binary black hole mergers and their detectable products in the universe. Consequently, detection of these events has the potential to offer valuable insights into the early universe and its underlying physics. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the significance of continuing to explore this fundamental period in the universe through gravitational wave astronomy. The primary objective of the Gravitational wave high-energy Electromagnetic Counterpart All-sky Monitor (GECAM) is to observe various Gamma-Ray Bursts (GRB) that arise from binary black hole or neutron star mergers, or other extreme astrophysical events, which can also generate gravitational waves. To ensure the performance of GECAM and its scientific value, a portable Gamma-Ray Burst simulator has been developed for testing and validation purposes. This burst simulator, which operates within the energy and spectral bandwidth of GECAM, can simulate different types of GRBs and associated phenomena such as cosmic-ray showers and transient events resulting from binary collisions, and will be utilized to simulate multi-band data in conjunction with the GECAM team, in addition to providing calibration sources for GECAM. The design, technical specifications, and test results of this simulator are discussed in this paper. With a power supply system that comprises a direct current-direct current-direct current (DC-DC-DC) converter and a high-voltage direct current-decay resistor, the simulator can generate high-voltage pulses required for its operation. The technical specifications of this simulator, which comprises a photoelectric detector and an 8-inch by 1-inch straw tube, are characterized by an energy range of 0.1-1000 MeV, a count rate of 10^4 counts per second, and a signal duration that can be adjusted between 10 microseconds and several seconds. Moreover, the data obtained from the engineering tests of this simulator demonstrate its capability to simulate bursts that can be detected by GECAM, and provide necessary validation and calibration

Significant advancements in NLP have been observed in the last decade thanks to neural models and substantial labeled datasets. However, NLP models are often hindered by a critical limitation: the need for extensive data. This issue is exacerbated in domains with limited resources, where the risk of overfitting and accuracy fluctuations under new conditions is particularly pronounced. One promising approach to address these challenges is data augmentation, which involves creating new labeled data to supplement existing resources. This survey delves into an in-depth examination of data augmentation in NLP under low-data conditions, focusing on prominent methods like token-level augmentations, such as word substitution, and system-level augmentations, including generative models like T5 and BART. We also explore metrics used to evaluate these methods as well as experiments conducted under low-label settings. Notably, our study reveals that different evaluation metrics often yield conflicting results and can be influenced by model size. These findings are supported by numerous experiments conducted under low-label settings for NLP tasks. We also explore the interplay between two crucial factors: labeling and augmentation quality. We provide empirical support for the concept that labeling high-quality augmented data is crucial, regardless of the augmentation technique used. This insight has implications for future research aimed at enhancing NLP data under low-label settings through augmentation. We conclude by outlining potential avenues for future research in this domain. System-level augmentations have been met with skepticism in the NLP community due to their high cost. In contrast, token-level augmentations have been widely adopted because they are relatively inexpensive. However, our analysis reveals that system-level augmentations can be more effective in certain scenarios. We provide empirical evidence that supports the idea that labeling high-quality augmented data is critical, regardless of the augmentation technique used. This discovery has far-reaching implications for future research aimed at enhancing NLP data under low-label settings through augmentation. We also offer a theoretical framework that could facilitate the design of more cost-effective data augmentation systems in the future. This framework involves modeling the relationship between labeling and augmentation quality as a non-linear curve. We based our analysis on multiple NLP datasets. We anticipate that this framework could be useful to other research communities that involve modeling complex, data-driven relationships between multiple variables. However, further research is required to validate this model and assess its generalizability to other datasets and scenarios. We hope that this survey and our associated findings will be beneficial to other researchers working in the data augmentation for NLP under low-label settings. This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation in $\mathbb{R}^3$, outside a compact convex obstacle, under the condition $u_{tt}+ \Delta u - (|u|^p) x^{-2\beta}=0$, with initial data given as $u_0$ and $u_1$. We demonstrate that if $p$ and $\beta$ satisfy $p> \frac{4}{3}$ and $\beta \in [0,1)$, and the energy of the solution is bounded, then the solution will inevitably collapse within a finite time period. Additionally, under the stricter condition $p> \frac{5}{3}$ and $\beta$ equaling $1$, and given that the solution's energy remains finite, we conclude that the solution will collapse within a finite time period. These conclusions are applicable regardless of the obstacle's size and shape. We achieve this proof by first constructing a transformation that alters the equation to a form in which one variable is eliminated, and then establishing a connection between this modified equation and a self-repulsive Schrödinger equation in a higher-dimensional space, before ultimately deriving the desired collapse results from this established connection, along with an associated existence and uniqueness theorem for the modified equation. This methodology builds upon and expands previous research in [CN, CV, LL]. 

Keywords: nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation, blow-up solutions, exterior domain, obstacles, supercritical NLS.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers. This analogy is extended to varieties defined over non-zero finite fields and incorporates algebraic and geometric multistability. Moreover, we demonstrate the compatibility of such reductions with various geometric constructions, including affine cones, monomial subvarieties, and toric varieties. Our framework is based on a novel reduction framework called Local Uniform Reductions (LURs), which encompasses a broad range of geometric and algebraic settings. LURs are proven to be stable under multiple operations, such as discrete valuation rings, composite varieties, and constructions over LURs. Our results are particularly relevant to constructing varieties with desired local characteristic-zero properties using their positive-characteristic analogs, which is a key aspect of the DR-POET framework for software security. LURs provide an essential abstraction for developing the DR-POET compiler, an event-driven, position-independent, and thread-safe C compiler, that transforms programs written in a higher-level language based on LURs into optimized binary code for microcontrollers. Our results ensure the security and performance of the compiled software, which is critical for the development of the Raccoon Trail Game. Our findings also contribute to the development of the DR-POET compiler, specifically its use of homomorphism-invariant subfields, which is an application of LURs in the DR-POET framework. Our results, in turn, rely on a novel extension of the Artin-Schreier theorem to partial characteristic-zero, semi-parametric definitions, which is a key ingredient in the construction of the Raccoon Trail Game. Our results, in conjunction with our earlier work on the rational function fields, provide a complete solution to the DR-POET problem statement, which asks for the classification of local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric definitions corresponding to polynomial varieties defined over finite fields and their positive-characteristic reductions. Our results demonstrate that such definitions are equivalent to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers and provide a foundation for the development of the DR-POET compiler, an event-driven, position-independent, and thread-safe C compiler, that transforms programs written in a higher-level language based on LURs into optimized binary code for microcontrollers. Our ISD and GGA studies confirm that V$_2$O$_3$ surfaces undergo a metal-insulator transition based on termination, agreeing with experimental findings. We attribute this phenomenon to distinct electronic configurations resulting from different surface oxygen coverages, which are influenced by the size of the isolated islands and the distance between adjacent layers. In particular, our results show that two-layer slabs and certain single-layer configurations exhibit itinerant behavior due to sufficient electronic interaction between layers, whereas isolated island surfaces and certain single-layer setups become insulating because of reduced interlayer connection. Notably, our data also indicate that specific single-layer structures, exhibiting metallicity, can switch to the metal-insulator transition when adjusting the height of the islands. This suggests that V$_2$O$_3$ surface electronic structure can be manipulated by adjusting the height of the islands, offering potential for flexible electronic properties in device applications. We propose that suitable single-layer constructions with metallicity can serve as models for identifying suitable materials for realizing the metal-insulator transition in low-dimensional systems. Furthermore, our results suggest that V$_2$O$_3$ surfaces providing optimal electronic properties can be achieved through suitable adjustment of oxygen coverage rather than layer thickness. This finding holds implications for experimental research, indicating that achieving desired electronic structures might require careful consideration of oxygen exposure during deposition, in addition to controlling layer thickness. Ultimately, our results highlight the value of theoretical investigation in understanding the results of experimental research, the challenges encountered, and the new insights obtained from re-examining the data with new eyes. Additionally, our study underscores the significance of surface termination in determining the electronic structure and metal-insulator transition properties in V$_2$O$_3$ ultrathin films. Collective electron correlation plays a crucial role in determining the surface termination-dependent metal-insulator transition, as evidenced by comparisons between GGA and ISD results for two-layer V$_2$O$_3$ models, which show that distinct free and bound electron configurations contribute to this transition. Our results also demonstrate the influence of distinct surface terminations on the electronic structure and metal-insulator transition properties, as illustrated by the analysis of single and double layer V$_2$O$_3$ models, which exhibit itinerant and insulating behavior due to varying degrees of interlayer connection. Our study has implications for the design of materials with itinerant and bound electron configurations, as well as the understanding of surface termination effects on electronic structures and metal-insulator transitions in 4d and 5d transition metal oxides

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. A crucial aspect is the strength of interaction between the incident light and the target system, as it determines scattering intensity and serves as the basis for spectroscopic signals. When this interaction is weak, techniques like scattering, absorption, or emission spectroscopies are applicable. In contrast, our research focuses on situations where the x-ray scatterers strongly interact with electrons in atoms or molecules, leading to the creation of excited states or electron jets with known properties. By measuring the intensity of scattered x-rays at specific angles under these conditions, we can reverse engineer the incident x-ray field. This knowledge allows for the extraction of information about target nuclei through the scattering of soft x-rays, a process we call nuclear phase retrieval spectroscopy. This new framework offers possibilities for ab initio studies or those using theoretical models, thereby uncovering details about nuclei in atoms or molecules that cannot be accessed via other means. As a demonstration of its capabilities, we used x-ray electron protein scattering (XEPs) to estimate the half-life of watermarked tryptophan within α-lactalbumin. XEPs represents an advanced form of X-ray scattering that leverages genetic code modifications and tailored molecular constructs to attach N-terminal markers like tryptophan or tyrosine to proteins. These markers have inherent half-lives that can be determined via XEPs, enabling the noninvasive tracking of protein aging. In a broader context, nuclear phase retrieval spectroscopy provides a means to control and measure the strength of light-matter interaction in strong interaction regimes, a feature that can be incorporated into existing x-ray spectroscopic techniques to extract additional details about the target system's atomic, molecular, or nuclear components. In the specific case of XEPs, it facilitates the measurement of key decay parameters in proteins and other biomolecules marked with radioactive half-life tags. As such, this research has the potential to contribute to various applications, including the development of novel x-ray-based biological clocks, halflife tagging, and x-ray-induced luminescence, among others. By linking quantum error correcting codes to models of disordered classical statistical mechanics and examining the phase diagram of these models, researchers have found a valuable tool for studying how these codes resist errors under various noise conditions. This study expands this mapping to account for realistic faulty quantum circuits when implementing code operations, adding in circuit-specific errors in addition to quantum error noise. When coupled with the standard quantum error correction paradigm of continuous feedback control, this simulation considers independent control of both the system's dynamics and its classical hybrid measurement process. When applying this framework to study the quantum Shor code, researchers found that small modifications to standard circuit architectures can significantly increase the fundamental error thresholds of this code from approximately 10.51% classical noise alone to as low as 15.03% when including circuit errors under strong laser tuning, or as low as 12.45% under weak laser noise, without the need for feedback learning procedures. These findings suggest that realistic faulty quantum circuits and learning-controlled implementations can hold significant promise for improving the performance of quantum computing systems. Furthermore, this framework based on classical disordered statistical mechanics models can be applied to investigate other quantum error correcting codes.

These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Our proposed method uses traditional hybrid-dimensional techniques to model conductive fractures and a more recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach for blocking fractures in their respective spatial dimensions. This new method shows the same major advantages of hybrid-dimensional methods, including an easily computable pressure solution and a measurable flux. Additionally, our approach is compatible with the mass lumping scheme, enabling stable and predictable implementations even with simple explicit time stepping methods. Our method is also proven to be stable and its performance is demonstrated through various numerical experiments. This includes comparisons with established solutions for specific types of fractures as well as novel configurations, highlighting the method's potential for further exploration and potential applications in modeling dual-porosity fluids in the absence of mass transfer across fractures. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can be an effective tool to assess and compare alternative theories by measuring the likelihood of observed data under each model. However, the reliability of Bayes factor estimates depends on the degree of model fit, with larger factors obtained for novel data that confirms previous findings and significantly higher factors for opposing outcomes or those with minimal similarity to the data. Given the variability in the psychology data, it is not uncommon to see Bayes factor ranges of 10 to 1000 in studies that compare model performance. A crucial consideration for researchers is to ensure they are not drawing conclusions based on preliminary results with high variability but rather on those derived from re-analyses using re-sampled data sets, which are independently evaluated by researchers for consistency. To achieve this, we propose a method where we re-sample the data sets used for model evaluation, a process we refer to as the 'posterior predictive similarity test'. A key aspect of this approach is the development of an unbiased similarity test for comparing data sets, along with a data visualisation tool that enables a more intuitive understanding of results. Furthermore, we demonstrate the stability of results derived from this analysis by comparing them to traditional Bayes factor estimates for several cognitive psychology studies. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences and can greatly benefit various natural language processing tasks including sentence semantic role labeling and sentence classification. Despite their utility, automated analysis of these indicators is generally inaccurate due to their diverse nature and the lack of corresponding lexical representations. To address this challenge, a novel approach called DiscSense has been developed to provide a comprehensive semantic characterization of discourse markers. This approach combines multiple strategies to derive lexical representations for each indicator based on their part-of-speech categories, the structures of prepositions, and the entities they relate to, as well as the syntactic patterns they define. To validate DiscSense, a comprehensive dataset containing 25 discourse indicators has been created and used in various experiments, including the enhancement of semantic role labeling and the classification of sentences with these indicators, resulting in significant improvements over existing approaches and the baseline models. The developed system and the DiscSense Framework along with the proposed dataset are both made available for public access. Due to the wide-ranging applications of discourse indicators in NLP systems, the characterization of each indicator is crucial, as evidenced by the results showing that the semantic analysis of these indicators contributes substantially to the enhancement of NLP models. To ensure the reliability of the characterization of each indicator, a systematic evaluation has been conducted to verify the accuracy of the derived representations and the corresponding representations of the indicators' parts, as well as the predictions of the DiscSense system, showing that the characterization of each indicator is unique and robust in response to varying input data. To facilitate the characterization of previously unknown indicators, a set of rules has been established based on the structure of the prepositions, the defined entities and the part-of-speech categories of the indicators, as well as their frequencies of use, allowing the characterization of 9 previously unanalyzed indicators using this framework. The proposed DiscSense system and the characterized discourse indicators, along with the DiscSense Framework and the discourse indicator dataset, are both made available for public access. Our findings indicate that increasing temperature leads to a reduction in the intensity of visible and infrared light interacting with the center, as well as a decrease in desired ODMR peaks due to crystal damage at higher temperatures.  We develop a mathematical model to describe the decline in visible light intensity and observe that it is in line with a nitrogen-vacancy diamond (NV-diamond) application standard.  We discovered that the main spin resonance in ODMR remains responsive to temperatures up to 1200 K, but the effectiveness of vacuum conditions is crucial in this range of temperatures due to the risk of heating-induced diamond damage at high temperatures.  We also observe changes in ODMR frequencies with temperature, but are unsure of their cause and suggest further research is needed. This presents an insurmountable challenge to modeling brain function accurately. A new algorithm developed for two-layer networks overcomes this hurdle by doing away with explicit error calculation and backpropagation altogether. This algorithm remarkably translates to a neural network that closely mimics the brain's connectivity pattern and learning processes, and experiments show it rivals the performance of backpropagation across various datasets. A key feature of this algorithm is the emergence of local supervision within specific neural ensemble nodes, suggesting it could provide a foundation for developing more sophisticated models of the brain's learning mechanisms. A mathematical analysis of this algorithm's properties is also presented, and it is further observed that it is insensitive to the choice of optimization method. This algorithm's potential to enhance our understanding of how the brain learns and adapts is also discussed. A new implementation of the Hartree-Fock (HF) method has been developed to efficiently achieve robust convergence for well-behaved central potentials. The method converts HF equations into a generalized eigenvalue problem by using a B-spline basis in a finite-size box and incrementally increases the strength of electron-electron interactions. The accuracy and performance of this implementation were verified through a series of benchmark tests involving s-, p-, d-, f-, g-, and h-atoms, up to bismuth, and certain model potentials. The results showed that the number of basis functions required for convergence is directly proportional to angular momentum and linearly proportional to nuclear charge in a simple manner. The new implementation was applied to the electron gas, and its potential was examined at various densities. The results for energy and magnetic moment from the HF approach matched well with Monte Carlo simulation findings, and the potential derived from HF was used to explain the nonlinearity observed in the electron gas's spin susceptibility vs density plot. The new method can also be used to study electron systems confined within finite volumes or in clusters with arbitrary central potentials by easily switching to an atomic basis. These capabilities make the new implementation suitable for the investigation of nonuniform electron gases in atoms, clusters, and electron gases subject to arbitrary central potentials using the B-spline basis HF method. This notion was initially proposed by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, who conjectured that every simple, relatively small bipartite graph could be colored using only a limited number of colors, specifically in relation to its maximum degree and specific subgraph constraints. This paper presents a counterexample to a strengthened version of that conjecture, specifically focusing on a 3-degree bipartite graph and providing it in a cubic form. This counterexample is particularly interesting because all of its equitable royal families are composed of small, identical components, a property that is not generally true for larger subgraphs. We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, in contrast to "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. To investigate this, we observed the movement of evaporating droplets as they interacted with different air temperatures and humidity levels. Our findings reveal that, regardless of weather conditions, spherical droplets travel up to 4.5 meters in 30 seconds to 2 minutes. However, their size reduces to 0.1 millimeters by the time they reach this distance in that time frame, limiting the viral load they can carry over longer distances. The risk of infection within this 4.5-meter range is further shown to be influenced by air temperature and humidity, which affect how quickly droplets evaporate and settle in the air. For example, warmer air accelerates viral decay and increases the spread of virus-carrying droplets, while humid air hinders the evaporation of larger droplets that can carry more viral load. These discoveries imply that increased humidity may increase infection risk within close range, whereas warmer air has the opposite effect, and evaporation patterns are weather-condition-independent. Unfortunately, a significant shortcoming in various semantic tasks, including dialogue state tracking, is the presence of erroneous labels in training data. To address this challenge, a prominent approach is to develop robust models capable of distinguishing between accurate and inaccurate labels during training. To tackle this problem, we propose an innovative framework called ASSIST, which incorporates a pre-trained dialogue language model and employs a label noise-aware training strategy to enhance the model's performance when faced with uncertain or inaccurate labels. Notably, our method introduces two key innovations: first, a technique for estimating the uncertainty of individual labels based on their counterparts, and second, a modified training scheme that leverages a mixture of label smoothing and posterior sampling to mitigate the impact of noisy labels. Our experimental evaluations on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset demonstrate that our proposed framework achieves superior performance compared to baseline models and mitigates the influence of assumed label noise. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. To address this, the project proposes a modified version of the epidemiological model, incorporating two new factors: a simplified climate change aspect and a specific mechanism for modeling population movements. Despite some difficulties in predicting Santiago's rioting patterns, this project successfully simulated the disturbances' temporal progression and demonstrated the model's potential for use in analyzing and forecasting disorders in other cities. The proposed model also exhibits mathematically stable properties and is suitable for analytical predictions in more straightforward scenarios. To validate the model, a numerical method was developed to estimate its parameters based on Santiago's rioting data from the third day of disturbances. This estimated model then accurately replicated the observed temporal progression of disorders in a satisfactory manner. To further assess the model's validity, a method was devised to assess its uncertainty and fitness. The model's variables and parameters undergo significant changes when the disorders' distribution is modeled for different areas within Santiago, and interestingly, some of these variables exhibit notable correlations with the city's infrastructure and certain environmental aspects. Notably, the model reveals a crucial aspect of Santiago's that may contribute to the observed distribution of riots, which is the presence of a significant park at the city's main square. This project's findings and model provide a valuable starting point for further research aimed at refining the model and exploring its applications in examining and forecasting disorders in other cities. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing AI models but, due to data confidentiality, safety standards, or exclusive ownership, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite their willingness to contribute. To overcome this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking into account the constraints of federated learning, such as data remaining on local devices and limited communication. To demonstrate the feasibility of FedSA, we conducted an experiment called the FedSA Challenge, where 13 participating teachers from six distinct institutions contributed their datasets and trained models for six different projects. By employing a selective aggregation method that simulates a careful evaluation process in a controlled environment, we successfully created a robust student model, surpassing the performance of 50% of the contributing teacher models. This study employs a motivic perspective to examine twisted algebraic $K$-theory.
For a variety over a zero-characteristic field and an Azumaya algebra over it, the paper defines motivic twisted $K$-theory spaces and shows they are motivically invariant.
It also demonstrates that these twisted $K$-theory spaces are related to motivic cohomology sheaves and establishes connections between twisted $K$-theory and motivic cohomology.
The paper can be seen as extending basic properties of twisted $K$-theory from the smooth homotopy theory setting to a broader context of the motivic homotopy theory setting. 
Building on these extensions, the paper proves the twisted version of Geisser's theorem about the comparison between twisted $K$-theory and motivic cohomology and also identifies the twisted version of motivic cohomology with the slice filtration of motivic homotopy theory's zero-characteristic slice theory.

This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant differences in Venus and Earth's evolutionary paths, certain atmospheric processes have remained relatively constant, offering a high degree of stability. These processes include atmospheric loss due to solar winds, mass exchange between the atmosphere and surface through volcanism and surface chemical reactions, and temperature fluctuations that affect water vapor and carbonate species. Volcanic activity has played a crucial role in atmosphere-surface interactions and has been influenced by tectonic activity and the cooling interior. The cooling interior, in turn, has influenced the rate of volcanic activity and atmospheric loss. This cycle of interactions has been self-regulating, with increased volcanic activity and associated cooling of the surface leading to a stronger hydrostatic circulation and atmospheric loss. This, in turn, has resulted in a hotter and more active surface, followed by increased chemical weathering and silicate gas production, and ultimately, a stronger atmospheric sink, reinstating the cycle. This analysis highlights the complex interconnections between Venus's interior and exterior and the atmospheric processes that have governed its evolution and are still at work today. It also emphasizes the difficulty of accurately modeling Venus's atmospheric evolution due to the interplay of various processes and the limited scope of current research. This work does, however, provide a framework for assessing the atmospheric evolution of other terrestrial planets and offers a framework for studying the interconnections between interior and exterior processes on these planets. It also highlights the necessity for a holistic approach to studying planetary evolution and composition, along with the importance of interdisciplinary research in planetary science and geology. It is clear that the atmospheric evolution of Venus has been governed by a complex interplay of endogenous and exogenous processes, and understanding this interplay is essential for a comprehensive understanding of this planet's evolution and composition. By employing time and space resolved measurements, reaction nanoscopy reveals the droplet's surface and interior chemical reactions over time. Building on the success of tensor network methods, we explored the converse problem - decomposing a given state into a tensor network with minimal depth. We based our approach on the broad framework of operator growth in quantum systems and established a new decomposition framework that leverages local measurements to combine operators in a network representing a given state. We applied this framework to both classical and quantum scenarios, demonstrating its relevance to both unitary circuits and graph neural networks. Notably, our framework enables the evaluation of any observable in the decomposed circuit, making it a more versatile tool than direct decomposition methods. We specifically considered two scenarios: first, when the tensor network has a known form, such as a matrix product state, and second, when the state is represented by a unitary circuit. We developed an iterative algorithm to decompose matrix product states into shallow quantum circuits, demonstrating an exponential reduction in circuit depth for certain systems by comparing our decomposition to the native tensor network representation. Our results showed that the graph neural network approximation of physical systems has a fundamental limit determined by the system's entanglement properties and that certain systems can achieve an exponential reduction in circuit depth through our decomposition method, exceeding the efficiency of current quantum algorithms by orders of magnitude. Our findings also revealed a non-trivial relationship between the approximated and actual physical systems as evidenced by the issue encountered in decomposing the FTVYY model, which highlights the challenge of accurately capturing the spectral properties of certain systems using GNNs. Our research provides a new framework for evaluating the practical applications of tensor network algorithms in quantum computing and machine learning and has significant implications for the further development of efficient quantum algorithms. We believe that our contribution will inspire a new wave of research in quantum computing and machine learning focused on the inverse problem of preparing a given state and the study of operator growth in quantum systems. The success of cancer diagnosis and treatment is heavily reliant on histopathology reports that are generated from comprehensive assessments of tissue samples. However, this process is resource-intensive and subject to human error. One potential solution involves using machine learning on histopathology images, but this requires these complex images to be represented in a way that is amenable to model training. We believe that a hierarchical graph representation can capture the spatial relationships and tissue patterns present in these images, and we present evidence for this through two separate applications. Firstly, we demonstrated the ability to detect invasive areas within breast tissue samples that are stained with H&E. Secondly, we classified different regions of prostate glands based on their functional status, using images that are stained with H&E. In both cases, our proposed method outperformed existing approaches and achieved accurate results according to expert pathologists. Our method is also transparent and its components are easily interpretable by domain experts. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghanejad/hgr. One notable aspect of this work is that it paves the way for the integration of machine learning with digital pathology, a field that is already experiencing significant advancements in areas such as tumor segmentation, and we are confident that our proposed method will contribute to this progress. One potential extension to this work is the integration of machine learning with clinicopathologic correlations that take into account the underlying biology of cancer, and we are exploring ways to incorporate this dimension into our method. One possible direction for this involves incorporating biological processes into the graph topology, and we are investigating various ways to design the nodes and edges within this structure in a way that is informed by the underlying biology of cancer, and we are in the process of testing this approach using prostate adenocarcinoma, a type of cancer that is characterized by the formation of glandular structures. One notable aspect of this cancer is that it is treatable if detected early, and one potential solution to this involves the development of computational methods that can accurately detect these structures within digital pathology images, and we are confident that our proposed method will contribute to this goal. One notable aspect of this work is that it is an extension to our earlier work that was presented at the MICCAI 2020 Pathology conference, and we are grateful for the feedback that we received from the community that encouraged us to explore this direction further. One possible direction for this involves the development of computational models that can accurately detect the underlying biological structures within digital pathology images, and we are confident that our proposed method will contribute to this goal.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields. A key point process that fits this description is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is widely employed due to its intuitive and tractable properties. However, exact likelihood estimation is impractical due to the intractable residual process, leading to a need for alternative methods. A recent study developed an efficient yet systematic way to create estimators for the nonlinear Hawkes process by linking the residual compensation measures, resulting in a system of compound Hawkes processes that can be resolved through a flexible and tractable approach. Within this framework, various estimator forms were identified that vary in parameters such as memory length, intensity, and node connectivity, enabling a systematic exploration of their properties and a framework for their systematic construction. Our research extends the framework by introducing a Bayesian method for estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process, which produces a distribution of estimators rather than a single value. This method utilizes a Laplace prior for the intensity parameters and an inverse-gamma prior for the memory kernel, leading to a computationally tractable form of posterior distribution. By comparing our method with established estimation techniques, we found that it offers improved accuracy in estimating the intensity parameters and memory kernel, especially in scenarios with limited or real-world dataset observations. This research provides a foundation for exploring alternative Bayesian configurations and developing more efficient estimation techniques for the nonlinear Hawkes process, ultimately leading to its broader adoption in complex event dynamics modeling. Our study is further illustrated by analyzing a sample neuronal activity dataset, which reveals distinct event types with different characteristics and dynamics. This finding is verified through additional independent analysis, underscoring the reliability of our method in discovering unique event types and their underlying structures. Our research code is available under the GNU General Public License, which enables free usage, modification, and distribution. This license aims to promote the advancement of estimation methods for nonlinear Hawkes processes through community-driven development. In line with this vision, we invite researchers to collaborate with us in further improving and refining our method, as well as exploring novel applications for nonlinear Hawkes processes in complex event dynamics modeling. Our research is a product of our ongoing collaboration with the Brain Research through Advancing Interventional Neurological research, supported by multiple universities and research institutions. Our research code is hosted on GitHub under the BAYHAWKE project, which is an open-source C++ library for computing compound Hawkes processes and their Bayesian estimation method. This project is released under the permissive MIT License

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate conservation capabilities, which remain flawless when accurately integrated, maintaining machine-precise levels of total mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum conservation. Notably, this property becomes particularly valuable in complex, high-energy astrophysical events such as neutron star mergers. Although the inclusion of gravity in such scenarios poses significant computational challenges, a recent implementation of the fast multipole method has made it feasible to preserve system-scale properties, such as total linear and angular momentum, through the use of particle cross-talk cut-offs that ensure precise conservation of system mass, energy, and linear/angular momentum in all simulated NSM candidates to date. This work builds upon that finding, providing a detailed mathematical justification for the conservation of angular momentum within the smooth particle hydrodynamics framework when fast multipole method gravity is accurately integrated. Furthermore, this study confirms the previously observed particle talk cutoff-independent behavior of total linear and angular momentum conservation in all simulated neutron star merger candidates to date. No specific new simulation results are presented in this work; rather, it aims to make available the explicit mathematical justification in an appropriate context. This is particularly relevant given the recent growth in number of researchers working on simulations of neutron star mergers. This study is a theoretical analysis of the underlying mechanics of the smooth particle hydrodynamics method, providing a mathematical justification for the conservation of angular momentum from the perspective of the author's hydrodynamics group. This study is an extension of the author's previous work presented at the 2019 APS April Meeting in Denver, Colorado. Leveraging this justification, this study has been submitted to the Journal of Computational Physics in May 2019 but has since been on review extension. Consequently, this new research on the convergence of many-body problems has become the primary focus for the author's research group. As such, this study has been re-submitted to the Journal of Computational Physics in January 2020 with a significant revision that incorporates a novel approach that significantly improves the convergence of many-body problems, leading to the dramatic acceleration of many existing and future first-principle smoothed particle hydrodynamics simulations of neutron star mergers and other many-body problems. Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have reached optimal performance in medical image segmentation, the process is hindered by a large number of required annotations for training. Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) techniques have potential in addressing this issue by effectively utilizing both labeled and unlabeled medical image data. Specifically, our proposed Contrastive Semi-Supervised Learning (CSL) method leverages SSL's capacity for efficient use of unlabeled data in conjunction with a Segmentation-Contrastive Learning (SCL) technique that learns from unrelated anatomical structures to facilitate domain adaptation at batch-level. As a result, our method is capable of segmenting new images by leveraging a small labeled dataset and a large unlabeled dataset as well as domain adaptation across similar anatomical structures. We applied our proposed method to two benchmark segmentation datasets, namely the Vertebral Artery (VA) and the Right Ventricle (RV). For the VA dataset, we investigated the challenge of segmenting the VA by leveraging experience and knowledge gained from the segmentation of the nearby Cervical Carotid Artery (CCA) while for the RV dataset, we explored the challenge of segmenting it by leveraging knowledge from the Left Ventricle (LV). Compared to the baseline model, our proposed CSL method delivered a 12.5% boost in VA dataset, a 11.5% boost in RV dataset and a 10% average boost across all datasets. Furthermore, our method demonstrated robust performance on datasets with limited unlabeled data, outperforming other SSL techniques by a significant margin of 15.6% on the VA dataset, 14.1% on the RV dataset and 13.5% on the RV dataset with only 32 unlabeled data per batch. Our proposed method's capacity for domain adaptation across similar anatomical structures holds promise and paves the way for further exploration and expansion in the domain of medical image analysis. Additionally, our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/CSL. Moreover, Pre-trained models on VA and RV datasets can be found at https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/CSL/tree/main/trained-models. Moreover, our paper's metric details and contrastive learning threshold's selection details can be found in the supplementary materials available at https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Q0Q5Q1Q5Q1Q5Q1Q5Q1Q5Q1Q5Q1Q5Q1Q5Q1

We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for code rates less than half, there is a diverse class of rank metric codes capable of accurately decoding any symmetric error, even those of maximal rank. Moreover, this code class includes, as a subset, the family of Gabidulin codes with rates less than half. Secondly, we propose a method for correcting symmetric errors of up to n-k rank, which can be applied for code rates greater than half, thereby extending the effective use of this type of decoding in higher rate scenarios. Both of these conclusions contribute to a better understanding of the fundamental properties of rank metric codes and their relationship with error matrices, and can serve as a basis for further research into decoding of rank metric codes, especially in scenarios where certain error matrices have known properties. As an example of this research's practical value, we demonstrate an improved decoding approach for Gabidulin codes with rates greater than half, which can take advantage of a code's structure to provide superior error correction performance than the standard bubble sort algorithm. This research builds upon our prior findings presented at the IEEE Information Theory Workshop 2019, where we first reported on the existence of high-rate Gabidulin codes with a limited number of correctable symmetric errors, and proposed a more efficient decoding algorithm than the state-of-the-art method by van der Hem and Kotter, which corrects up to (n-k)^2 errors. This new decoding algorithm enables the correction of all symmetric errors of up to n-k rank for high-rate Gabidulin codes, which can be viewed as a special instance of a more comprehensive conclusion drawn from our new analysis presented in this paper. Building upon recent work by Faulkner et al., we obtained a general holomorphic and anti-holomorphic spinning AdS$_3$ OPE block expression in terms of CFT$_2$ mirror image reflection of the conformal block. This new expression is derived from combining the conformal bootstrap equation and Einstein gravity's Weyl anomaly, leading to a key relation that connecting AdS$_3$ OPE blocks to their CFT$_2$ reflected counterparts, commonly referred to as "mirror blocks". A detailed analysis of "mirror blocks" was conducted at both generic and low-generic points. Notably, we found that the generic "mirror block" formulation aligns with the form predicted by the "holomorphic dual" description of gravity, as proposed by Hammergaard et al. Moreover, we identified a novel, non-trivial "entanglement central charge" sub-component within the "generic mirror block" framework, revealing its relationship with the full "mirror block" and an intriguing "central charge" matrix that determines its properties. When considering low-generic points, we obtained a more explicit, detailed understanding of "mirror blocks", showing their connection to "semi-holonomic" dispersion relations and an associated "dispersion matrix", as well as a new "entanglement dispersion matrix" concept. A discussion on the implications of our findings for the holographic principle in AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ is also presented. Ultimately, we demonstrate our general "mirror block" framework by successfully applying it to a specific instance involving a spinning 4-point block, as well as a discussion on possible future directions for research. Additionally, an open-source Mathematica notebook is made available alongside this manuscript to facilitate reproducible computational research. This supplement includes the underlying symbolic computations that derive the "mirror block" formula, as well as a detailed "implementation guide" for users to explore and customize the "mirror block" framework in accordance with their specific needs and research objectives. System specifics and environment setups can be found within the provided header at the beginning of the code. In line with the spirit of open-source community-driven initiatives, this notebook is designed to be fully editable and updatable by both the author and external contributors. Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however a significant challenge lies ahead. Delensing, a process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, the next generation experiments will need alternative methods. We propose a new approach, using a neural network to reconstruct the lensed CMB and then subtracting this from the observed CMB, effectively delensing it. We simulate this method on a dataset resembling what will be obtained by the CMB-S4 experiment and evaluate its performance under various conditions, specifically when the primordial signal is strong. The results show this method is highly effective even at high $r$ values and outperforms the quadratic estimator in a high signal-to-noise scenario. We also examine the impact of several variables on delensing efficiency and find that in certain situations the efficiency can be quite high, potentially over 80\% when the primordial signal is weak, but may be limited by noise in the dataset. We believe this method is viable for the next generation experiments and could be further improved in the future. We have made the code for this project publicly available. We discuss potential ways to improve this method further, specifically by training the model on realistic datasets and using other machine learning methods. We also consider the computational resources required for this method and how it may be implemented in the future, including the potential for using the model in real-time when analyzing the CMB data. We have explored applying this method to other machine learning estimators for $r$ and found it could be useful in those cases as well. We discuss some limitations of this method, specifically that it may not be as effective when the primordial signal is localized to certain regions of the sky and that it may be limited by certain assumptions in the simulation of the dataset. We consider some future experiments that could test the validity of this method and provide guidelines for optimizing the training of the model, specifically by controlling the level of noise in the dataset and the level to which the model generalizes to other conditions. We have made some recommendations for the parameters that should be considered in delensing analysis and have identified some areas that need further improvement in machine learning estimators for $r$. In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. We also present a simplified explanation for the computability of Pontrjagin classes within such manifolds, utilising basic geometric and topological properties. Building on this understanding, we then present an analytical representation for the Pontrjagin classes of any differentiable manifold, using a distinctive kind of combinatorial manifold that is topologically equivalent to the original manifold. This analytical expression for the Pontrjagin classes enables us to verify the Gelfand-MacPherson conjecture, which previously related the computability of Pontrjagin classes to the singularities within a manifold, but was known to have some limitations. Our validation of this conjecture covers all situations, including those with singularities and those of manifolds with boundaries, and it demonstrates the accuracy of the combinatorial approach in calculating Pontrjagin classes for any differentiable manifold. Our work offers a significant expansion of the original Gelfand-MacPherson framework, as well as a powerful verification of the conjecture, but it falls short of supporting the original broader interpretation of their method, which involves integrating the concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds as a new geometric framework. Instead, in the context of our work, a combinatorial differentiable manifold solely represents a discrete reflection of a manifold's topological characteristics, and our results, in effect, validate the effectiveness of this discrete reflection in capturing the fundamental properties of the underlying manifold. Ultimately, our findings validate the core principles of the Gelfand-MacPherson approach, but they do not address the broader implications of their method. Our work is primarily an analytical representation of a combinatorial differentiable manifold as a discrete reflection of a manifold's topological characteristics, and it is under this interpretation that our results provide a clear affirmation of the original conjecture of Gelfand and MacPherson. We explore the connection between the original method of Gelfand and MacPherson and modern approaches to studying manifolds, as well as the extension of the original conjecture to include Gauss-Manin connections, but this part of our discussion is primarily anecdotal in nature. Our work is an analytical representation of a combinatorial differentiable manifold

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 463 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a remarkably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar SNe. Observations during the plateau and decline phases were compared to well-known SNe, with SN~2020jfo exhibiting faster photometric and spectroscopic declines. A combination of metallicity effects and low pre-explosion masses from the H$\beta$ spectroscopic indicators are offered as possible explanations for its low luminosity. A lack of hydrogen and clear H$\alpha$ absorption in its plateau phase spectra led to SN~2020jfo being compared to other SNe displaying similar features, with possible analogues including 1999em and 2011dh at later stages. A key similarity with SN~1999em was observed in its nebular phase spectra, which showed unique O~II and N~II spectral lines typically seen in SNe with higher pre-explosion nitrogen enrichment. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a new arrangement called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE system consisting of 9 segments can effectively reduce the number of necessary image sensors by a factor of nearly 10 while maintaining the same detection efficiency and only slightly increasing the system's total area. This concept can be an economical solution for providing wide coverage with high sensitivity in X-ray monitors, especially when combined with a trigger system that identifies interesting events and allows for further in-depth analysis with higher-resolution imaging. Furthermore, MuLE optics can also be an innovative solution for the challenging problem of managing large numbers of LE units in such wide-field X-ray monitors. If each LE unit is assigned a unique pattern of rotation angle, MuLE can uniquely determine the corresponding angle and thus the corresponding unit, making it possible to employ a much larger number of LE units than the previously possible with a single sensor. This new arrangement can be employed with both direct and back-illuminated image sensors, and its effectiveness has been verified through both simulations and observations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. Ultimately, when the simulation parameters were modified further, models trained on density information alone failed to predict halo masses accurately, demonstrating the importance of velocity field effects on the halo collapse, particularly in certain mass scales. These findings highlight the significance of velocity field influence on the formation of dark matter halos and suggest future large-scale structure reconstruction projects should consider incorporating velocity field information for a more accurate understanding of cosmic structure. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the utility of deep learning as a powerful tool for exploring complex phenomena in cosmological simulations. This research is ongoing, with new models being trained on velocity field information combined with density information at multiple stages of dark matter simulations. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Partial-Label Supervention Learning, offers a more cost-effective way to train models by only labeling specific fields in each document, rather than annotating every detail. Compared to traditional full-label supervision, this method has been shown to achieve similar levels of accuracy using significantly less labeled data - a significant reduction of up to 90%. For example, for an invoices dataset with 1,000 examples, only 40 would need to be fully labeled under PLSL, in place of the 400 required under full-label supervision. We believe this method to be highly relevant to current trends in document automation, such as Structured Prediction, and have successfully applied it to three diverse datasets covering invoices, product catalogs and driver licenses, using popular models such as Vision-Linux and Tesseract. Our code and results are available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/main/PartialLabelSupervisionLearning. With the vast amounts of documents that need to be processed, any method that can make the labeling process more efficient could potentially have a major impact, and we are confident that our approach will contribute to advancements in this area. Although the models we used are quite sophisticated, the method itself is quite general, and we are exploring the possibility of applying it to other domains that involve extracting data from images and documents. One possible extension to this method is combining it with another technique, known as Masked Augmentation for Structural Prediction, that generates artificial labels for fields that are difficult to annotate, by using a model's predictions and then refining them with additional information. We are also looking at ways to make the method more efficient and any improvements we make will be incorporated into an updated version of the paper, which will also include results from a larger dataset, namely 5,000 examples, and from other datasets such as medical records and technical manuals, and will be posted on arXiv.org. The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of mergers involving compact objects, including neutron stars or black holes. However, the joint electromagnetic and gravitational wave observatory remains underutilized due to limited low-frequency sensitivity in gravitational wave detectors. This restriction is primarily caused by the existing approach to signal detection, which relies on a fixed waveform template and a method called matched filtering. This traditional method excludes a wide range of potential mergers with large orbital eccentricities, thus limiting the detection capacity and hindering the identification of these events in the electromagnetic spectrum. This project introduces a novel method that employs convolutional neural networks to detect and classify gravitational wave signals directly in the time domain, without relying on predetermined waveforms. This innovative method has been put into practice by training a network with a diverse set of merged waveforms featuring various levels of eccentricity, resulting in the detection of 92% of simulated binary black hole mergers with zero false positives and a 95% accuracy rate in the classification of such events. When applied to realistic noise from the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, the network demonstrated the ability to identify 90% of binary black hole merges and 80% of neutron star-black hole merges with large orbital eccentricities that were previously undetected using the matched filtering method. By enhancing the detection capacity of these events, this deep learning approach has the potential to facilitate multi-messenger observations and contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the behavior of compact binary systems in dynamical environments, in addition to providing valuable insights into the formation and merger history of such systems. Furthermore, this novel method has the capability to identify specific features within merging binaries, such as large orbital eccentricities, the presence of massive objects like stellar-mass magnets or intermediate-mass binaries, or even the unique characteristics of neutron star mergers with late-little Big Rip cosmological scenarios. This discovery of merging binaries with unique features and large orbital eccentricities offers promising avenues for electromagnetic follow-up observations and serves as a stepping stone for future gravitational wave detectors like the laser interferometer of the Deci-Hertz Interferometer of Notable Events. This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two different fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the underlying equation's structure, we can divide the problem into manageable components, explicitly solve each part, and consequently derive a comprehensive solution despite the discontinuities. We also utilize numerical modeling to illustrate the efficacy of less frequent switching in minimizing costs for both scenarios. Key findings include the optimal solution being in sync with the underlying wave-like structure in both cases, and the prevalence of just one switch in the fastest time solution at a cost of $1^2$ for both scenarios when the scallop starts from one of its extreme positions. We validate our analytical solutions by matching them with numerical solutions obtained from a scallop model, and we explore potential extensions of our analysis to other types of oscillators. We find that the optimal solution for time-optimal and minimum energy problems in both scenarios is $\frac{3T}{4}$ and $\frac{5T}{4}$ respectively, where $T$ is the period of the swimmer's wave-like structure. We observe this optimal solution is achieved when the swimmer is at one of its extreme positions. We also find that the cost of switching is $1^2$ for both time-optimal and minimum energy problems. We validate our results by comparing our solutions with solutions obtained from a numerical model. We show that the cost of switching is low enough that solutions obtained when allowing for switching are similar to solutions obtained when not allowing for switching, and that solutions obtained when allowing for two switches are similar to solutions obtained when only allowing for one switch.
