Buchholz established a practical approach to understanding massless two-dimensional scattering theories. Within this approach, we've demonstrated that a given theory is completely characterized by its asymptotic algebra and scattering matrix under specific conditions. By applying a procedure grounded in von Neumann algebras, we've derived multiple families of interacting wedge-local nets, one of which is closely related to Buchholz-Lechner-Summers' chiral CFT deformation. We've also successfully constructed a family of wedge-local nets in 2d, based on integrable representations of su(2)$_k$ and loop groups, in a manner that aligns with Buchholz' theoretical frameworks for solvable and scattering theories. Ultimately, our construction, which is under specific deformed and representation theoretic conditions, can be summarized as follows: given any positive, hermitian matrix $E$, we can define a wedge-local net represented as U$_E$(G)$_w$, where U is a unitary representation, G is a loop group or Virasoro algebra, and $w$ denotes a wedge-local version of these algebras. This construction, which encompasses multiple instances of interacting wedge-local nets, demonstrates that many of Buchholz' theoretical frameworks for scattering and solvable theories are universally applicable. Notably, we've proven that both our constructed nets and Buchholz' standard examples fall under the classification of Longo-Witten endomorphisms, which form a strictly positive, compact and crossing unitary category. This categorial description can be viewed as a representation of the scattering theory's fundamental properties. On the other hand, given any positive, hermitian matrix $E$, we've established that there exists a category ${\cal D}_E$ which defines a family of interacting wedge-local nets U$_E$(G)$_w$. This approach allows us to demonstrate the existence of multiple family instances of interacting wedge-local nets in a straightforward manner, which would be extremely challenging, if not impossible, to derive directly using the original Buchholz-Lechner-Summers approach. This new understanding provides a powerful framework for both constructing and proving the existence of interacting wedge-local nets in 2d. This framework can be applied to any positive, hermitian matrix $E$, and as such, it represents a significant breakthrough in the field of wedge-local nets. Furthermore, this new understanding offers a clear and concise proof that both our constructed nets and Buchholz' standard examples fall under the classification of Longo-Witten endomorphisms

Implementing 5G antennas across a region is crucial for delivering 5G connectivity. Yet, little attention has been given to assessing 5G cellular tower exposure among children and occupants of sensitive locations, including schools and medical facilities. To address this, a systematic approach is outlined to numerically evaluate downlink 5G exposure among children, teenagers, schools, and medical centers, also applicable to pre-5G scenarios. This method is experimentally validated and applied to two real-world use cases - a children's playground and a hospital. Our results reveal that in some scenarios, 4G/5G exposure around towers can exceed recommended limits up to 7 times for all considered settings, yet decreasing with distance from the tower. Underage individuals and locations with higher occupancy rates tend to receive relatively higher exposures in proportion to area rather than height. Interestingly, in one examined case, the ratio of 5G to 4G exposure was found to be 3.3 times. To facilitate further investigation, the developed approach is designed for user extension and flexibility. Furthermore, considering the vast investment in 5G infrastructure, it is essential to balance the roll-out with exposure concerns, potentially benefiting from optimized placement methods, potentially leading to better exposure-performance trade-offs. In conclusion, the outlined approach offers a versatile means for evaluating 4G/5G exposure around towers and can be a useful tool for researchers, policymakers, and industry stakeholders. By applying these methods, we arrived at a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. This new closure model features the same Hamiltonian Dysthe equation we derived, and we validated its accuracy by comparing it with our two-layer model, demonstrating that they predict identical results, further justifying the validity of our Hamiltonian formulation and transformation techniques. In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here. Furthermore, an extension of the Stokes formula is demonstrated for forms with variable degree. This is achieved by demonstrating that an iterated application of the modified Stokes formula can be utilized to derive the desired outcome for differential forms of arbitrary degree. This strategy is applicable because of the arrangement of the spaces in question, namely F-space type F^m_n, particularly near points where forms with singularities are defined. It is shown that forms can be transformed into a suitable form utilizing a differential operator, and this enables the use of the modified Stokes formula for forms of degree one. This process can be repeated to derive the modified Stokes formula for forms within the specified class on locally convex spaces with a particular topology. This topology is introduced in conjunction with recent research regarding surface layer operators and the Denjoy-Kneser existence theorem for differential equations within locally convex spaces. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing and counteracting false news has become increasingly vital. To combat the high operational costs associated with human-led fact-checking, this study leverages automatic text summarization to filter out central information from news articles, enabling more efficient detection of false news. Specifically, this research develops and evaluates a novel false news-detection framework, which utilizes Bidirectional LSTM with Word Embedding and Ontology-based Semantic Role Labeling to identify crucial information in news articles. Our experiments reveal that the proposed framework achieves impressive performance, surpassing existing methods and serving as a solid foundation for further research aimed at differentiating true and false news. Moreover, this study paves the way for exploring the connection between text summarization and false news detection. This evaluation guide is appended as Section 5 in this document. Leveraging the proposed framework, a real-world application centered on false news detection has been launched and is currently accessible via https://fake-news-detection.com/. This application is an extension of the developed model and is designed for both expert fact-checkers and laymen. The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have more intense X-ray spectra. In order to explore the link between a Cataclysmic Variable's synchronization status and its X-ray emission pattern, we conducted a comparison between standard and asynchronous polars using their entire sample set, discovering a possible association between harder spectra and the former, albeit without conclusive statistical evidence. Another possible correlation with spin period was also identified, suggesting that it might have a more pronounced impact on the X-ray properties of polars than their accretion pattern. Eight out of ten asynchronous polars and three out of four standard polars with known spin periods were included in this study's sample. The remaining polars were excluded due to their spin periods being too short or unknown, which could have introduced an unfair bias since short spin periods are uncommon in polars. All sources' X-ray data were analyzed in three energy bands: soft, medium and hard, through spectrally integrated counts as well as hardness ratios. As a control for any potential biases related to the target selection, a hard X-ray selected sample was also examined, with similar findings. This research was conducted using data from two large X-ray surveys, ROXTE's All-Sky X-ray Survey and XMM-Newton's Serendipity Survey, which were combined with additional data from the Swift All-Sky Survey. Systematic corrections for any potential biases related to the target selection were also applied, resulting in a more representative sample of polars. A similar analysis of hard and soft X-ray spectra was conducted through X-ray spectral fitting using the latest version of the model for a polar, which took into account both the target's spin period and its orbital period. The findings of this research provide a basis for further studies aimed at validating the theoretical model describing the X-ray emission of asynchronous polars and identifying potential targets for such studies. This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100. Although the partitioned approach faces stability issues due to the relatively low accuracy of the reduction methods for this benchmark, the monolithic approach successfully yields desirable results with both types of RB implementations. Notably, the monolithic approach in our setting encounters difficulties in resolving the boundary layer in the fluid domain, leading to an excessively thick boundary layer, with a magnitude of $O(10^{-1})$, in comparison to the very thin boundary layer in the range of $O(10^{-3})$. This issue is more pronounced in the partitioned approach due to its higher stability requirements. To address this challenge, we explored an alternative formulation that transforms the fluid problem into a non-dimensional form with a different rescaling, resulting in a more manageable boundary layer, with a magnitude of $O(10^{-2})$. This improvement, however, does not yet fully integrate with either of the two FSI methods employed in our setting. Therefore, we cannot provide a comprehensive comparison involving the recently developed more stable reduced fluid formulation. Moreover, both monolithic and partitioned approaches rely on a finite volume method, and as such, do not align with the standard RB basis generation and extension techniques. Consequently, a new approach is necessary to generate the basis, involving the direct use of a snapshot method for both fluid and solid modes. This method does not follow the standard RB dimensionality reduction framework. This project's objective is to explore the possibility of integrating the RB methods with the two mentioned FSI approaches, but it does not aim to develop novel reduction methods for either the fluid or the solid component of the FSI problems. This project focuses on a specific test case, characterized by a relatively low fluid Reynolds number of 100, and does not extend to higher Reynolds numbers. This project's results indicate that the monolithic approach, solving the fluid and solid problems simultaneously, yields desirable outcomes with the RB method for a fluid Reynolds number of 100.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect this minuscule magnetic field by exploiting the magnetic flux gradient generated around a superconducting cylinder. As atoms pass through the interferometer, they are susceptible to the influence of this flux gradient, resulting in a shift in the phase of their interference pattern that is proportional to the expelled magnetic flux. By optimizing the experimental setup, it becomes possible to surpass the capability of magnetic field-sensitive materials like Ni and Cu. For example, we have demonstrated the sensitivity to measure magnetic fields as low as $10^{-14}$ $\text{Tm}$, which is a record-breaking achievement to date. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model that incorporates these elements. We specifically analyze the condition where the gap between the areas is minimal and focus on gap-plasmons there. Our study reveals that, in the absence of a gap, a quantum hydrodynamics model predicts two cloaked modes of propagation – one electric and one magnetic – which arise due to the unique relationship between electric and magnetic fields in this regime. Contrary to our findings, a standard hydrodynamics model fails to accurately describe this phenomenon even in the limit of vanishing gaps. Notably, the spillover effect contributes significantly to the propagation of the magnetic mode, while nonlocality has a negligible impact compared to this influence. The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. For a single Mn adatom, our model failed to replicate the observed spectral structure; however, this discrepancy may be attributed to the presence of a surface state on Nb(110). Further analysis of isolated Mn sites revealed that the BCS pairing is not uniform and only present in the outermost layer. Moreover, in an isolated Mn site, the superconducting gap is reduced from its native 1.1 mV to approximately 0.7 mV due to the strong magnetic moment, with the YSR state then residing within this reduced gap. For a separated pair of Mn sites, our calculations showed that the spin of one Mn site interacts with two superconducting gaps from the adjacent sites, resulting in two YSR states located within the reduced and unchanged gaps. For a close proximity of these sites, the YSR states hybridize and the spectral structure exhibits a more complex appearance. Furthermore, when placing the two Mn sites at a greater distance from each other, the spectral structure regains its double peak shape. In contrast to the results for a close proximity of these sites, the splitting of the YSR states was found to be significantly smaller than the distance between the peaks, demonstrating the effect of inter-site tunneling. In the case of a chain-like arrangement of Mn sites, our model produced a more complex spectral structure with multiple peak assignments, with the most prominent ones located at the binding energies of approximately 3.1 and 4.3 mV, with the latter corresponding to a peak that hybridizes with a quasi-bound state located within the superconducting gap. Our theoretical framework offers a comprehensive understanding of the YSR states in Nb(110) induced by the presence of magnetic impurities and provides a clear peak assignment for the spectral structure observed in tunnel spectroscopy. Additionally, this study highlights the significance of taking into account the unique orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for an accurate analysis of the YSR states in Nb(110). Furthermore, the outcomes of this research may also be applicable to other superconducting materials with a robust exciton

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks with fewer input pixel coordinates. By integrating the Fourier transformation, FourierMask achieves instance segmentation masks with a simplified network architecture compared to combining an implicit network with a mask refinement network. Our experiments demonstrate that FourierMask can produce accurate instance segmentation masks and outperforms the baseline architecture on the COCO dataset, achieving 61.5% AP, and also excels in frequency-aware evaluation metrics. Furthermore, FourierMask shows consistent AP improvement when evaluated on smaller instances and achieves 36.9 AP on CRAFT. The code is available at https://github.com/leopeng88/FourierMask. Since implicit functions facilitate vectorized operations, FourierMask's mask generation time drops to 0.0005 seconds per pixel with a 3080Ti GPU, enabling real-time instance segmentation. Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imagery are limited to analysis of the most transparent portions of clouds. This study utilizes solar radiation measurements from the MISR instrument to derive an unprecedented level of detail in the analysis of opaque convective clouds, spanning from optically thick cores to fully clear skies outside of cloud boundaries. Using a statistical approach to locate and extract information from intermediate optically thicknesses between these endpoints, researchers have mapped out the "veiled core" of clouds, revealing a key threshold for cloud water content that remains hidden from passive satellite retrievals. Data from the MODIS instrument, used in conjunction with the derived values from MISR, shows a significant improvement in the accuracy of water content retrievals for these clouds, with a mean absolute error decreased by approximately half. Additionally, a new parameter called the "clearance angle" is introduced to describe the point at which scattering patterns from cloud boundaries and optically thick cores separate, offering potential uses in cloud validation, assessment of cloud retrievals and adaptation of algorithms for other satellite systems. Further analysis of these results and subsequent water content calculations from the MODIS instrument and aircraft measurements show a positive correlation, with some scatter due in part to uncertainties in the derivation of cloud tomography and potential discrepancies between in situ measurements and the corresponding satellite-derived water content values. Future applications of this approach to cloud analysis using cloud tomography could provide valuable insights into the behavior of clouds across their full depth and extent. With the advent of high spatial resolution passive and active satellite systems such as the future GEO-PIR and GEO-CLAS systems, this technique could be utilized to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of cloud processes and properties, enabling better assessment of cloud processes and improved validation and calibration of cloud retrievals. Due to its versatility, this approach can be applied across different cloud types both in the atmosphere over oceans and over land. Consequently, it has the potential to become an essential tool for the future generation of satellite systems, providing a more detailed and clearer view of clouds from space. Furthermore, this technique can also be employed to validate and calibrate cloud retrievals using active and passive systems such as the future active and passive cloud radar and lidar systems on board aircraft and to derive cloud tomography from aircraft measurements using radiation budget and scattering matrices in conjunction with cloud tomography software such as the MISR and MODIS cloud processing system. We investigated how a laser pulse with a changing frequency impacts its passage through a sub-wavelength target and the acceleration of ions. Our findings show that a laser pulse with frequency variation can cause a relativistic self-induced transparency effect by synchronizing the movement of electrons with a specific "breathing" mode of the plasma, resulting in the creation of a highly charged, stationary plasma layer and enabling the acceleration of ions through a large potential difference. This effect is observable in the spectral variation of the laser pulse and can be manipulated by controlling its frequency variation and the composition of the target. Our research demonstrates the possibility of achieving ion acceleration through a laser pulse with frequency variation and suggests the potential for further optimization of ion acceleration in high-density plasmas through the choice of target materials. We propose an "optimal transparency" regime characterized by a specific ratio of the frequency variation and central frequency of the laser pulse, which could provide a useful guideline for the design of chirped laser pulses in ion acceleration experiments. The potential of this "optimal transparency" regime was validated through particle-in-cell simulations, which showed that it can result in the successful acceleration of protons and heavier ions to high energies and provided insight into the relationship between the frequency variation and the acceleration of ions. Building on our previous work, we have conducted additional particle-in-cell simulations to investigate the limitations of this technique and the effects of varying the intensity and duration of the laser pulse as well as the thickness of the target. These experiments showed that the optimal transparency regime can be achieved with a wide range of laser pulse characteristics and target thicknesses and that it can produce high-energy protons and heavier ions regardless of the specific conditions used. However, it was also found that the maximum energy achieved through this technique can be limited by the intensity of the laser pulse due to the occurrence of laser pulse defragmentation at high intensities. As a result of this limitation, the optimal transparency regime may only be attainable with lower-intensity laser pulses. Further research into the mechanisms governing this technique and the development of more sophisticated simulations will be necessary to fully understand its potential and any limitations it may impose. Building on our previous research, we have conducted additional simulations to investigate how this technique can be used to accelerate heavier ions to high energies. Our results show that the optimal transparency regime can result in the successful acceleration of heavier ions like aluminum and gold to high energies, but the maximum energy achieved through this technique may be limited by the charge of the ion due to the occurrence of laser pulse defragmentation at high intensities

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Our findings also include a general upper bound for structures with at least 3 nodes, reaching a critical density of 1/2, and an infinite graph theorem that connects upper density problems to Ramsey numbers. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between prestellar and protostellar mass functions.  The Dragon infrared dark cloud, located at a distance of 2.7 kpc, is one of the youngest and most distant samples in this study's database.  The analysis encompasses 14 protostellar and 41 starless cores within this cloud, with 5 protostellar and 11 starless cores exhibiting signs of outflow, with the remaining located in regions with molecular outflow precluding detection due to sensitivity limitations.  The mass of each core or outflow precursor was calculated through a combination of the dust continuum and line observations, with an adopted temperature of 10 K and no evidence of temperature variations among protostellar, starless cores, or outflows.  The analysis also accounted for the effects of temperature on mass determinations, but no such influence was detected.  In addition, mass determinations were found to be insensitive to the adopted temperature within a certain range.  A log-normal distribution was used to model the mass of protostellar and starless cores, with a median mass of 8.3 $\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$ for protostellar cores and 4.5 $\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$ for starless cores.  A comparison of the two distributions revealed a mass difference of 3.8 $\pm$ 1.5 $\mathcal{M}_{\odot}$, with no overlap between them.  Protostellar cores were found to have greater mass than their starless counterparts even when considering mass functions for individual outflows, with no evidence of massive prestellar cores.  The discovery of core growth with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation is highlighted, with further research needed to explore the effect of this finding on the established correlation between prestellar and protostellar mass functions.

We investigated the surface properties of various materials as they interact with different stages of liquid foam dissolution. Despite its buoyancy, a foam cube can penetrate deeply into a container filled with a viscous liquid, indicating that viscous forces are insufficient to explain this phenomenon. By comparing the surface characteristics of two types of materials - one with a smooth, curved surface and another with an irregular surface - we made an interesting discovery. The former requires a much more significant curvature to exhibit similar behavior to the latter, suggesting that surface roughness plays a crucial role in its interaction with liquid foams. To further understand this relationship, we developed a theoretical model that describes the frictional forces at play when a material with an irregular surface meets a liquid foam. Our calculations showed that this model accurately predicts the observed frictional forces in experiments involving both smooth and rough surfaces. When a material with an irregular surface is immersed in a viscous liquid, similar to those that make up a liquid foam, its interaction with the surface can be comparable to that of a curved surface that is twice as curved. This is because the irregularities on the surface of this material act as channels that allow the liquid to flow over the surface curves, mimicking the behavior of a smoother, more highly-curved surface. When these channels become filled with a thicker non-Newtonian liquid, as is the case with a more advanced stage of foam, the relationship between the surface and the liquid changes, resulting in a weaker connection between them. This leads to an increase in the frictional forces when a less dense layer of this liquid is replaced by a denser layer, causing the friction to almost instantly shift to match the new layer's curvature. This phenomenon of surface roughness playing a crucial role in the interaction between liquid foams and certain materials has significant implications for the development of novel medical treatments and cosmetic products that can effectively remove dead skin cells by taking advantage of the unique properties of surface roughness in relation to liquid foams. Furthermore, our discovery of frictional forces being influenced by the stage of foam dissolution may also provide a basis for a more in-depth examination of surface characteristics across a broader range of materials and substances. Additionally, the model we developed for understanding the frictional forces in these interactions could be a useful starting point for exploring other complex phenomena in physics. In the case of liquid foams, the stage of dissolution appears to be a critical factor in the frictional forces at play, and further research into this aspect could be a valuable contribution to both scientific and academic communities. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Notably, our method achieves the best performance among all attention methods while requiring no additional parameters. System implementations are also significantly simplified, resulting in substantial speed-ups. Look-ahead attention's effectiveness can be attributed to its ability to learn a strong target-to-target representation, facilitating the generation of not only adjacent but also distant target words. We make our model code and data scripts publicly available at https://github.com/ruotianeng/laa. Moreover, an analysis of our method's strengths is provided through the application of pre-trained multilingual models, whereas some theoretical aspects are discussed through the lens of pre-trained transformer models. Look-ahead attention's simple yet powerful design allows it to be readily integratable with other attention methods, including teacher-student attention, and even simple baseline architectures. We also explore the practical implications of our discovery, specifically that target word generation is similar to that of source sentence generation, with the only difference being the direction of the attention mechanism. Building upon this insight, we design an innovative reverse look-ahead attention mechanism that focuses on predicting previous source word parts to generate target words, resulting in another substantial performance gain, amounting to a 0.6-1.0 Characer Error Rate (CER) improvement, for the WMT English-to-Chinese translation task. We further experiment with other attention methods in this setting, discovering some that perform notably better than state-of-the-art baselines by up to 3.4 CER points. Look-ahead attention's simplicity and strength make it an appealing research topic, with numerous interesting issues yet to be explored with its application to other machine translation generation tasks like summarization and dialog generation. Look-ahead attention's unique characteristics, such as its ability to model distant target word relationships, necessitates a novel metric, namely the target word similarity metric, to be designed in the future. Current monitoring methods rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data, but they often come with limitations of high costs, restricted coverage areas, or unreliable data due to low user participation rates. In this study, a framework for detecting urban road issues using a network of rideshare vehicles in optimal sensing locations is presented. This framework utilizes mixed-integer linear programming to determine the most effective locations for data collection, thereby maximizing the detection of road issues under certain constraints such as reduced travel distances and limited observation periods. This unexpected characteristic, which we term "sensitivity disparity," is an unaddressed issue that could have critical implications for individuals in similar situations and warrants further investigation. The associated persistence probability $p(t,x)$ measures the likelihood that the walk remains above a specific level over time. Our study confirms the universal exponent $\phi(x,t) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\pi} \arccos(x) + o(1)$ as $t$ approaches infinity, as initially hypothesized by Bouchittte-Gallagher. Additionally, we demonstrate that $\phi(x,t)$ characterizes the persistence probability and determines the distribution of the number of crossings within time $t$. The estimated value of $\phi(x,t)$ may provide insights into more complex models, such as directed polymers in random media and certain types of interface models, for which similar persistence problems can be formulated. In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies. A stability switch and Hopf bifurcation periodic solution occurrence are identified through the Bogdanov-Takens normal form and by satisfying the Huang-Meltzer theorem, respectively, at a critical parameter value of $r=1$. A stability switch and the emergence of periodic solutions is observed in the model's behavior when the nematode production rate is below, at, and above the critical value, respectively. A comparison between time series graphs for model parameters set at and above the critical value reveals that the model exhibits periodic solution behavior when the nematode production rate is higher than the critical value, which indicates that the model's periodic solution provides a more effective approach to managing pests through continuous nematode release. An interesting phenomenon, where the model's periodic solution inhibits the population of target insects, is observed when the nematode production rate is set at and above the critical value, which further confirms the model's ability to manage pests more effectively. A numerical simulation and case study for the model's periodic solution, where the model's parameters are set at and above the critical value, reveal that the model's population of target insects can be managed at very low levels through continuous nematode release, which further confirms the model's ability to manage pests more effectively. A discussion on the potential applications and implications of the model's results, as well as its potential extensions, is also presented. In conclusion, this research provides a theoretical and numerical analysis of a microbial pesticide model, which exhibits a more effective approach to managing pests through continuous nematode release, and highlights the potential benefits of this approach over conventional chemical pesticides. Furthermore, this research provides a framework for investigating the potential benefits of continuous release of entomopathogenic nemematodes in pest management, which can be applied to other microbial pesticide models, such as the model presented in reference [25]. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel nucleus detection framework called W-Net, which is comprised of two distinct components. Initially, a background removal module with a closing filter is employed to eliminate time-consuming manual mask creation and accelerate training by reducing unnecessary computation. This module is followed by a closing filter that removes fragmented nuclei and facilitates smooth, closed-shaped ones. Building upon this foundation, we further develop this background removal module, refining it into a fully automatic system called Four-Net, which is designed for nucleus extraction in cytology images. By leveraging both quantitative and qualitative evaluation metrics, we demonstrate W-Net's/ Four-Net's efficacy and practical applications in nucleus detection. Additionally, a comprehensive analysis of experimental outcomes is provided to illustrate W-Net/Four-Net's performance in comparison to existing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, Four-Net is introduced for the first time in this paper, where detection speed is significantly enhanced by exceeding human visual perception standards. Furthermore, experiments conducted on publicly available datasets validate W-Net's/ Four-Net's superiority over baseline and renowned nucleus segmentation networks. As such, W-Net/Four-Net is poised to make a significant contribution to the field of nucleus detection and pave the way for its clinical applications. Nonetheless, network complexity and substantial required training data remain significant challenges that necessitate further exploration and innovative solutions. Systematic evaluation of publicly available datasets is also crucial for unbiased assessment and generalization capabilities. In the context of cytology, evaluation of detection results against ground truth masks is critical in order to ensure accurate nucleus annotation. As such, W-Net/Four-Net is specifically designed for detection of single cells in cytology images. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. This concept is mathematically formalized, and a complementary objective is defined to identify and eliminate such interference. It is proven that an optimal combination of the original and this additional objective yields a simplified version with no negative impact on the desired outcome, thus facilitating reinforcement learning despite external state and reward variables. This solution is demonstrated on a hypothetical scenario and a robotic arm control system. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction that is settled on a public ledger. To ensure these contracts are secure and effective, a robust verification process is necessary. This paper presents HELMHOLTZ, a sophisticated contract verifier built from the ground up using refinement types. It not only checks the soundness of contracts but also identifies potential errors and provides user-friendly feedback to aid developers in fixing issues. HELMHOLTZ is specifically designed for Tezos smart contracts and utilizes dependent types to achieve a high level of precision in the verification process. Our approach is general and can be applied across various contract types. To demonstrate the effectiveness of HELMHOLTZ, we have developed a working prototype and successfully verified several high-performance contracts that are currently deployed on the Tezos network. Our verification tool has been designed to be efficient and scalable for real-world applications, verifying contracts with up to 10 million lines of code in a reasonable timeframe. Our approach is general and can be applied across various contract types. GCNNs can be seen as an extension of traditional neural networks, combining convolutional structures with recursive operations to process data on graph domains. This work focuses on exploring the fundamental understanding of GCNNs through a matched filtering approach, considering the non-stationary nature of data in such domains requiring state-space models to describe their evolution. Leveraging state estimation techniques, particularly measurement modeling, we analyze the structure of GCNN layers, revealing their compatibility with traditional filtering methods. This analysis provides a data-driven interpretation of GCNN operations, demonstrating how learning in GCNNs is equivalent to estimating latent variables in a state-space model. This knowledge can be used to enhance the performance of GCNNs through optimal filter design, a technique that learns a graph that maximizes the accuracy of signal estimation in a probabilistic framework. A demonstration of this approach in practice is shown in experiments conducted on synthetic and real-world datasets, resulting in improved estimation results when using optimally designed graphs in comparison to GCNNs and other baseline methods. Furthermore, this work facilitates a discussion on a potential match between machine learning methods and traditional signal processing techniques, such as matched filtering and maximum a posteriori estimation, along with an exploration of an optimisation problem for building a graph that maximises the estimation performance of a state-space model, such as the extended Kalman filter, through a deep learning framework. A initial examination of a method for constructing a graph that achieves optimal results in the estimation of a state-space model is also presented, along with an exploration of an association between machine learning methods and signal processing techniques like matched filtering and maximum a posteriori estimation, together with a discussion on a formulation for optimising the performance of the estimation of a state-space model, such as the EKF, via a deep learning framework. A preliminary exploration of an approach to building a graph that yields the best outcomes in the estimation of a state-space model, such as the EKF, is also included. Elastography, an advancing medical technology, allows the internal mapping of mechanical properties within the human body for better disease diagnosis and treatment planning. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies heavily on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate and scanning velocity in ultrasound scans. Several factors contribute to this disparity including the transmission of pressure waves, reception of backscattered signals, and ultrasound scanning itself. To address these limitations and improve lateral displacement estimation, a new approach called Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) has been proposed. In VSSA, multiple transmitted pulses with varying central frequencies are combined to enhance beamforming. By joining these frequency sets, VSSA achieves better lateral resolution and larger scanning velocities without the need for beamforming at each transmission frequency. Furthermore, VSSA leverages the unique properties of ultrasound to boost lateral displacement estimation by utilizing received data from all transmitted pulses. This proposed method has been implemented and tested on tissue-mimicking phantoms and real tissue with positive results. Compared to conventional synthetic aperture techniques, VSSA exhibits enhanced lateral displacement estimation and outperforms existing methods. To facilitate widespread adoption of VSSA, a comprehensive software framework has been developed and made available for research communities. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. We demonstrate this idea through examples, including solutions to reachability problems for binary trees and stacks, by creating logical pseudocodes and mapping them back into natural deduction proofs. This reconstruction process allows us to rederive the original proofs, proving correctness and obtaining actual runs of the algorithms. We also explore how cuts in natural deduction can be located and quantified in the corresponding logical pseudocodes, providing insight into how the equivalence between algorithms and proofs can be expressed quantitatively. The concept of Boolean Ramsey numbers for sets of posets was initially explored in relation to Boolean lattices and posets obtained from chains with minimal elements combined into a V-shaped structure. A key aspect of this study is identifying the minimum number 'n' required to divide a Boolean lattice of height'm' into exact copies of V-shaped posets, where each copy contains unique elements. Our research focuses on determining these Boolean Ramsey numbers for V-shaped posets in general cases and certain specific cases when the height of the posets reaches 4 or more. Additionally, this study provides upper and lower bounds for these Boolean Ramsey numbers and confirms their equivalence in most instances. However, in some instances, the proposed upper and lower bounds differ, indicating the necessity for further analysis to determine the optimal value 'n'. Furthermore, this research also establishes a connection between Boolean Ramsey numbers and certain enumerative properties presented in the form of generating functions, which could serve as a valuable reference for any subsequent studies. Our findings have been validated through extensive computational testing, utilizing a custom-built algorithm to calculate the required numbers 'n' for each V-shaped poset and each Boolean lattice of a given height, ensuring the accuracy of our results up to the cutting knowledge date of March 2023. We introduce a novel hierarchical framework for resolving large-scale stochastic pursuit-evasion games that involve multiple evaders. Our hierarchy divides the game into two levels: a macro-level where agents make broad decisions based on approximate value functions, and a micro-level where agents optimize their actions to maximize these approximate values. By leveraging convex optimization at the micro-level and dynamic programming at the macro-level, we derive an efficient algorithm that produces locally optimal solutions for each level. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to a significant urban pursuit-evasion scenario involving multiple evaders. Our results show that our algorithm achieves a 4.5 times performance boost compared to flatfooted optimization, and we observe that our hierarchy leads to the development of localized strategies across multiple replanning cycles. Furthermore, we find that our approach excels in tackling dynamic target locations and encourages the development of robust strategies in response to new location announcements by other evaders. Our algorithm executes at 0.25 seconds per iteration on a 16-evader urban scenario, and we observe target capture rates of up to 80% across various difficulty levels. We also introduce an innovative evaluation metric called "reachability profile" that offers a quantitative measure of overall target capture effectiveness across all replanning cycles, and we make this metric as well as all associated data available for download. Our method's efficiency and performance milestones set a new benchmark for large-scale stochastic pursuit-evasion games. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance, including the ability to balance dose savings with image quality preservation. A key challenge in this area is the limited availability of paired high-dose and low-dose CT scans for training. An important breakthrough came with the introduction of unsupervised cycle-consistent translation methods, including the CycleGAN, which allows for the construction of a mapping between low-dose and regular-dose CT scans without needing paired data. However, one limitation of these models is their reliance on two separate networks for bidirectional translation, which can be difficult to optimize and results in significant memory requirements. In this work, we introduce the AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN, a novel framework that simplifies the dualGAN architecture by combining the two translation and reversal components into a single multi-task learning cycleGAN framework. By doing so, we achieve a substantial reduction in model size (approximately 6 times smaller) and eliminate the need for two separate training processes. Furthermore, our model leverages an adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) switch that enables the discovery of latent features that capture CT scan characteristics without relying on paired data. When compared to the original dualGAN method and our previous unsupervised low-dose CT denoising results, the AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN offers a balance between efficiency and image quality, with a mean opinion score (MOS) rating of 3.19, outperforming the baseline by a 0.23 MOS points and demonstrating the potential for dose reduction of up to 2 times while maintaining comparable image quality as reported in our previous study presented at the SIIM 2022 conference. With a relatively small model size of approximately 34 million parameters, our method exhibits great promise as a practical solution for real-world CT scan enhancements. Our code is available for download at https://github.com/ghimmesi/adasinchans. Recent successes of large-scale models in conversational understanding can be attributed to contrastive pre-training methods, which learn to distinguish encoded dialog contexts from positively related samples. However, these methods' limitations stem from relying solely on direct connections between dialog contexts, which hinders the learning of structural information essential for task-oriented dialog understanding. To address this, we introduce SPACE-2, a tree-structured semi-supervised pre-training framework that incorporates contrastive learning to effectively capture underlying structures in dialog datasets. By leveraging both supervised and unsupervised data, we design a prototype network to learn dialog context representations that conserve information across different hierarchical levels. Through experiments on four task-oriented dialog datasets, our method demonstrates superior performance when compared to popular dialog understanding baselines and showcases the benefits of learning structural information through a tree-structured approach. Specifically, our method achieves notable improvements (+3.8% F1 score) over the original SPACE model, with code available at https://github.com/THU-DLI/S4UD. Furthermore, pre-trained models are accessible at https://github.com/THU-DLI/S4UD-data for public use. Our research paves the way for the development of more sophisticated structural understanding abilities in task-oriented dialog datasets. Additionally, we explore various practical applications derived from pre-trained SPACE-2 models, including (1) improved baseline models for 20-Strong ShotGun, (2) expert training for real-world tasks like http://www.nlp2019.org/task/shotgun/, and (3) enhanced search in http://www.shotgun2019.org/search/. These experiments serve as preliminary examinations rather than primary evaluations of our method. Our primary findings are obtained from the 20-strong shotGun evaluation, which assesses the performance of pre-trained models on a diverse set of 20 tasks. Our results indicate that our method delivers superior performance in this setting, surpassing non-supervised baselines by a significant margin of 5.5% F1 score. In contrast to models pre-trained using supervised contrastive learning alone, our method exhibits a more substantial improvement of 11.1% F1 score. Notably, our method outperforms models pre-trained using supervised contrastive learning alone by an even more substantial degree on few-shot settings, with a difference of 14.5% F1 score in the 5-strong shotGun evaluation. Our method's ability to efficiently generalize to new data in the 10-strong shotGun evaluation is also noteworthy, with a performance gap of 7.5%

Multi-task reinforcement learning presents a significant challenge when tasks conflict, as their interaction can lead to a critical performance decline known as catastrophic interference. This study adapts a well-established cognitive architecture that incorporates a variety of learning elements, including both option-based reinforcement learning and relational reinforcement learning, to address this issue. By applying a learning mechanism that maintains a balance between two processes - one that forms independent relations and another that integrates them, we demonstrate in a theoretical analysis that this architecture is resistant to catastrophic interference. To validate our findings, we design multiple complex multi-task environments based on a variety of relational reinforcement learning frameworks and show that our proposed approach outperforms comparative methods with which we experimented. These results confirm that models of this type are capable of avoiding catastrophic interference and provide insights that can be applied to other models featuring interacting learning elements. Additionally, we find that introducing random connections and restrictions on connections can significantly impact the model's ability to circumvent catastrophic interference, leading to the development of a new variable that measures the degree of freedom in a nested relational reinforcement learning framework. This variable, which we term "learning depth," emerges as a crucial factor that influences the model's ability to avoid catastrophic interference and appears to be an essential component of high-performing reinforcement learning networks. To facilitate replication and advancement of these findings, we have created an open-source implementation of all the models that were tested and the instructions on how to execute them are included with the code. This research demonstrates the potential for model-based multi-task reinforcement learning to achieve high levels of performance in complex tasks by avoiding the critical issue of catastrophic interference. As a result, it presents an alternative to the widely adopted approach of using experience replay, which is known to be susceptible to this problem, and could also provide a foundation for the development of modular networks with multiple levels of free connections and constraints, a feature that is common in many cognitive architectures. This type of network is capable of solving a wide range of complex problems that involve multiple elements that interact with each other, such as navigation through multiple environments that are interconnected, by efficiently preventing catastrophic interference. To further validate the general applicability of these findings, we tested the model-based multi-task reinforcement learning approach in scenarios that are unrelated to reinforcement learning, such as in a scenario where there is a need to predict the square of a sum of two numbers based on the squares of individual numbers, and found that this architecture is also capable of avoiding catastrophic interference in these situations. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. Although traditional methods rely on multiple images from different poses, recent studies have shown the potential for single-image-based calibration. However, these approaches often assume the camera's pose and radiation conditions can be estimated or predefined, neglecting the situation where they need to be inferred from the image itself. Additionally, none of these methods have been tested on real-world datasets. This research addresses the challenge of calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using a single image, assuming unknown radiation conditions and camera poses. We demonstrate that calibrating the camera system is possible, obtaining a mean error of 0.36 mm when using synthetic data and a real-world dataset with a mean error of 0.67 mm, providing the first successful outcome of this task in both virtual and real-world environments. Furthermore, our method combines existing techniques for estimating camera poses and radiation conditions, demonstrating that the choice of these components affects the outcome, resulting in the observation that certain combinations yield significantly better results than others. Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. Traditionally, THz communication is confined to short-distance applications due to high THz signal loss, but recent research introducing laser-based transmission in outdoor scenarios has shown promising increases in system performance. However, these gains come at the cost of extended training periods for beamforming, which can now themselves be optimized through reinforcement learning techniques. We present a novel approach to reducing the training time for beamforming by dividing the process into two stages, first locating the communication link (a critical step) and then refining the beamforming in subsequent iterations. This method is the foundation for a reinforcement learning system that uses a value iteration approach to determine the optimal actions in each stage, leading to the development of efficient policies that can be implemented with reasonable complexity. Our simulations show that our proposed method can achieve significant performance gains over traditional methods, with an average improvement of 300% in Stage 2's precision and an average reduction of 50% in total training time. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that our scheme can achieve up to 80% of the optimal performance, even in challenging scenarios with large distances between communication links. We also provide a quantitative analysis of the factors influencing the system's performance and investigate various critical design parameters in detail. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Three screens were identified as responsible for major scintillation patterns and associated scattering and absorption phenomena. Estimates of these screens' physical properties, including distances, sizes, and angular widths, were calculated and are consistent with models of the interstellar medium. One screen, located ~115 pc from the Earth, with an observed angular size, showed characteristics similar to those of a turbulent cell often found in the path to the pulsar and the Earth, commonly referred to as the "local screen". This screen's size and angular width cannot be disentangled with current data, but new observations and/or higher sensitivity at smaller spatial scales may allow for their separation, providing further insight into the interstellar medium's structure and the relationship between screens and the superposed line-of-sight magnetic field. Estimates of the distance to this screen, often referred to as the "local interstellar medium", are still based on earlier measurements and need confirmation, while its other properties, such as the density and magnetic field strength, remain unknown and cannot be determined solely from scintillation data. This paper introduces a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to circumvent the limited duration issue of WaveNet. Typically, WaveNet generates audio on a millisecond timescale but requires long sequences for effective pitch and spectral reproduction. In response, QPNet divides time into two segments: a periodic segment (typically a note's duration) and a shorter nonlinear segment. Two sub-networks, one for each period, are trained and their outputs combined with a pitch-dependent dilated convolutional neural network to produce sustained sounds. By leveraging both periodic and nonlinear signal components and incorporating a network that adapts to changing pitch, QPNet outperforms WaveNet in MUSDB'18 drum and bass evaluation but struggles with bass enhancement due to pitch range issues. As a result, a modified version, quasi-periodic WaveNet with auxiliary pitch, is proposed and demonstrates improved performance on bass tracks. This approach demonstrates the effectiveness of combining periodic and nonlinear signal analysis for audio generation. Furthermore, a related discovery made during this research is the introduction of a quasi-periodic dilated convolutional network, which shows potential in classification tasks involving musical notes. Despite achieving comparable or better results in the primary evaluation, the models proposed in this research do not achieve a significant reduction in parameter count when compared to WaveNet. To differentiate between zero-energy peaks originating from Majorana and those from other causes at non-zero temperatures, our method involves swapping the normal lead in tunneling spectroscopy with a high-resistance lead (characterized by large Ohm values). The increased resistance in this setup significantly alters tunneling conductance, impacting it in distinct ways. While the Majorana peak persists in rising with temperature in a particular exponential manner, defined by the temperature of the lead, other causes will show varied temperature responses due to Ohm's influence, creating a clear distinguishing criterion. Furthermore, this method is theoretically applicable in determining the Majorana gap by taking into account various temperatures and Ohm values, even those that are currently out of reach for experimental measurement. From a practical experimentation viewpoint, there are two crucial factors to control: the temperature of the lead and the electrode's resistance. However, controlling the lead's temperature proves more challenging due to the tight balance required between it and the electrode's temperature. Nevertheless, this method remains a viable option for differentiating zero-energy peaks through tunneling spectroscopy. In our study, we also discuss an alternative method that could potentially control the lead's temperature without the need for sophisticated cryogenic systems. This alternative involves using a superconductor-insulator-superconductor (SIS) junction as the electrode in tunneling spectroscopy. This junction allows for the control of two critical factors: the temperature of the lead and the electrode's resistance, by adjusting two key points: the bias voltage in tunneling spectroscopy and the applied voltage for the SIS junction. This control offers even greater flexibility to study tunneling spectroscopy in various conditions. Through both theoretical calculations and actual measurements on the SIS junction, we have verified that this method is indeed effective in distinguishing zero-energy peaks. This includes differentiating the Majorana peak from other peaks, and potentially determining the gap size by studying tunneling conductance at non-zero temperatures. This method could also be applied to verify the existence of Majorana in other materials. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, the theory of shadows facilitates the derivation of a higher categorical version of the Oresky-Powell conjecture, concerning the interaction between THH and shadows, particularly in the context of stable categories and their relationship with Waldorf's global THH. A supplemental component explores the connection between shadows and the bicategorical version of the trace, as well as a more general conjecture about the representability of shadows within monoidal functors. A separate strand of research within this paper delves into the examination of shadows within the realm of stable categories through the lens of THH and its relation to global THH, ultimately yielding a characterization of stable categories via THH and their associated shadows, while also establishing a categorical version of the Oresky-Powell conjecture. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically excludes certain challenging elements during training and phases involving prediction, thereby expediting training process. Our algorithm achieves superior results on multiple benchmark datasets, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art in sound source localization accuracy in videos, according to comprehensive evaluation conducted across different datasets. These evaluation metrics indicate that our method not only excels in sound source accuracy but also maintains high classification confidence, outperforms existing models on unsupervised sound source localization tasks and demonstrates robustness in models trained using both classification and segmentation objectives. These findings are validated across multiple benchmark datasets in the accompanying supplementary material. Our algorithm is also capable of processing 10 frames per second on a single V100 GPU, making it suitable for real-world applications. We introduce a new sound source versus other challenging element separation metric called IOU-S3, alongside two existing metrics such as mean average precision (MAP) and mean average recall (MAR) to evaluate the performance of sound source localization algorithms. IOU-S3 is unique in that it measures the average overlap between predicted bounding boxes and ground truth bounding boxes after removing easy image elements, taking into account both precision and recall, unlike existing evaluation protocols that focus solely on mean average precision or mean average recall, without considering the underlying distribution of challenging elements within the dataset. We also introduce a new dataset called YouTube-VisualSound, comprising 3600 high-quality video sound-source-vs-other pairs, alongside corresponding IOU-S3, MAP and MAR scores, to support the IOU-S3 metric and provide a more comprehensive evaluation framework for future sound source localization research. This new dataset includes 7500 bounding box annotations, detailing the location of challenging image elements, along with corresponding class masks, along with a new evaluation metric called IOU-S3, in contrast to existing datasets such as VisualGroundingInInstructions and VGG-Sound, which solely provide sound-source-vs-all-image-data annotations, without distinguishing between easy and difficult image elements, thereby offering a more challenging yet underexplored vision-audio benchmark for future research. Our analysis of both YouTube-VisualSound and VGG-Sound datasets reveals the presence of challenging class masks that are consistently misclassified during sound source localization tasks, leading to a significant performance decline of up to 30%

Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial for personalized patient treatment and follow-up. This task can be automated through image analysis, but a significant obstacle is building a reliable model. To address this challenge, we've created UniToPatho, an Italian-language dataset consisting of 1,281 histological images of colorectal polyps, including their surrounding mucosa. These images are organized into four categories based on the degree of dysplasia and polyp type, as specified in the Paris Classification System. UniToPatho is unique in that it is the largest publicly available dataset of its kind. To train and evaluate machine learning models, we've divided the dataset into three disjoint subsets: a training set containing 672 images, a testing set containing 400 images, and a validation set containing 209 images. Our experiments demonstrate that a robust model can be developed using a combination of histopathological patch classification and characterizing the polyp's location. This approach is essential for accurate adenoma grading. UniToPatho is now available for other researchers to build upon and improve upon existing methods. Unlike Antarctic samples that originated from dry Antarctic meteorite finds, Benenitra and Chelyabinsk samples came from locations with higher water availability, yet surprisingly, their isotopic composition of hydrogen in pyroxene minerals is significantly more positive than expected, differing by 5-6 times more than initially reported. As hydrogen-rich organic materials are ubiquitous in chondrites, this process likely occurred extensively throughout the solar system, affecting many planetesimals. Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into a target language through a intermediate stage in the text domain. This complex task requires not only accurate speech recognition but also fluent and grammatically correct target-text generation, proving especially challenging for rare language pairs. To address this issue, this paper introduces a novel approach called zero-shot speech-to-text, where speech recognition and target-text generation occur automatically without explicit training, relying instead on speech recognition and machine translation capabilities for the source and target languages. We demonstrate the feasibility of this model for 10 language pairs and show it achieves state-of-the-art performance in zero-shot speech-to-text and machine translation. We also find that our system performs close to directly trained models for nine out of these 10 language pairs. The code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/kaushikparmesht/zero-shot-speech-to-text. We anticipate this work to contribute a method for speech-to-text translation that is both efficient and flexible, with potential applications in low-resource language pairs and for spoken content summarization. Despite its effectiveness, zero-shot speech-to-text remains prone to target-text overfitting in our experiments, with significant scope for further improvement through the addition of source and target-level regularization and more extensive evaluation across the NICO corpus and other speech-to-text datasets. With zero-shot speech-to-text, speech-to-text systems can be developed without the need for large-scale speech and target-text data for each language pair, making them particularly well-suited to multi-language applications involving rare language pairs and where speech-to-text systems need to be developed quickly. We investigate the impact of target-text overfitting on our system through the addition of source and target-level regularization and find this has the effect of reducing this issue by approximately half. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means, potentially yielding new connections between Hodge numbers. Furthermore, this research explores connections between relative I-functions and discrete symmetries in the context of singularities, including examples related to the Fano variety of cubic polynomials and some toric partial contact manifolds with specified divisor properties. Lastly, it outlines an approach for studying the Frobenius exactness of functors, including its application to determining the Frobenius exactness of functors related to quantum cohomology, mirror symmetry, and Landau-Ginzburg models. This research also provides a theoretical framework for potentially extending its findings to a broader class of varieties through the use of mathematical functors and symmetries, potentially yielding new insights into the geometry of these varieties. This research was presented in part at the 2021 KIAS school on birational geometry and at the 2022 University of Wisconsin-Madison algebraic geometry seminar. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize the field by linking style transfers to probabilistic models, thereby enabling the creation of realistic images that reflect specific statistical characteristics. In this study, we explore the potential of GAN-based models in disease-aware image editing by utilizing a latent space representation and incorporating a probabilistic graphical model that explains the distribution of image features. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the LIDC dataset containing chest X-rays used to diagnose lung nodules. When modifying the images to conform to specific nodule sizes, our results show that our model outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we investigate the model's ability to predict nodule locations and sizes from raw images by utilizing a novel disease-aware image-to-latent-space transformation module. Notably, our approach achieves nodule size estimation with a mean absolute error of 1.35 without the need for additional training, surpassing existing methods that demand supplementary information during the testing phase. Furthermore, the model exhibits robustness when editing images with nodules in different positions and of various sizes. Our code is available at https://github.com/ik1127/disease-aware-edition. When transferring styles using GAN, producing realistic images that reflect specific statistical characteristics has become possible. This new application of GAN has delivered outstanding results in disease-aware image editing by linking style transfers to probabilistic models, as demonstrated in our experiments. Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume into three main components: a point, a local area around the point, and the rest of the volume. By expressing the potential as a sum of these components, we can easily compute the potential using: a direct formula for the point, a local approximation for the surrounding area, and a boundary integral over the rest of the volume. For the boundary integral, we developed a new high-order method to compute the potential by summing up the contributions from many small triangles that make up the boundary. By combining these components, we can accurately compute the Newtonian potential over complex two-dimensional regions using a simple and efficient algorithm, even when the boundary is highly irregular. In this paper, we also discuss how we implemented this method in an existing code that solves volume integral equations, and we presented results for several examples of complex two-dimensional regions, comparing our method with the standard approach that uses a grid without a set pattern. These results show that our method is significantly more efficient and accurate than the standard approach, and we also found that the new method is very robust and can handle very small features and highly irregular boundaries with ease. In the case of boundaries that are not flat, we developed a new high-order method to compute the boundary integral by summing up the contributions from many small triangles that make up the boundary, and we showed that this method has an asymptotic complexity of O(k^2) when using k order polynomials to approximate the potential and the boundary, and an asymptotic complexity of O(h^-2) when using a grid without a set pattern.
